`srun` is preferred because it is fully coupled to Slurm, automatically distributes processes to allocated resources, resolves task affinity, initializes correct environment variables, and records accurate accounting information.
What is the main benefit of using `srun` for task distribution in Slurm, even if `mpiexec` might offer better performance in specific circumstances?
The main benefit of using `srun` is that it minimizes the risk of a mismatch between the resources allocated by Slurm and those used by Open MPI, ensuring proper resource management and consistency.
Where can users find more detailed documentation for `sbatch` and `srun` commands when working with Slurm on Alliance clusters?
Users can find additional documentation on the SchedMD website, with direct links provided for `sbatch` and `srun`.
What is an allocation in the context of high-performance computing resources?

An allocation is an amount of resources that a research group can target for use for a period of time, usually a year. This amount is either a maximum amount, as is the case for storage, or an average amount of usage over the period, as is the case for shared resources like computation cores. Allocations are typically made in terms of core years, GPU years, or storage space.
How does the job scheduler prioritize compute jobs based on a research group's allocation?

The scheduler uses prioritization algorithms to meet the allocation targets of all groups. It bases job priority on a research group’s recent usage of the system compared to their allocated usage on that system, giving more weight to recent usage (or non-usage) to allow groups that match their actual usage with their allocated amounts to operate roughly continuously.
Why were Reference GPU Units (RGUs) introduced, and what evaluation criteria are used to rank GPU models with RGUs?

Reference GPU Units (RGUs) were introduced in the 2024 RAC year to rank all GPU models in production and alleviate problems in the allocation process and while running jobs, which arose because all GPUs were previously treated as equivalent despite dramatic increases in performance. GPU models are ranked using an evaluation based on their FP32 score (40% weight), FP16 score (40% weight), and GPU memory score (20% weight).
What is the purpose of the Alliancecan Slurm portal, and what kind of data does it display upon initial login?

The `portal.alliancecan.ca/slurm` website provides an interface for exploring time-series data about jobs on the national clusters. When a user first logs in, it displays CPU days on an arbitrary cluster across all project accounts the user has access to. If there is no usage on that cluster, the figure will contain the text 'No Data or usage too small to have a meaningful plot'.
How can users view their resource usage for a specific project account on the Alliancecan Slurm portal?

On the Alliancecan Slurm portal, users with access to multiple Slurm accounts can select a specific project account from the 'Select user’s account' pull-down menu within the 'SLURM account' panel. If this menu is left empty, the figure will display all usage across all accessible accounts on the selected cluster. Once an account is chosen, the figure updates to show its usage, and an 'Allocation Information' panel provides project details. The histogram bars illustrate the daily metric for all users in that account, with the top seven users shown in unique colours and all others in gray.
What additional metrics and display options are available in the legend of the Alliancecan Slurm portal's usage figure?

The legend on the Alliancecan Slurm portal's usage figure allows users to toggle the display of additional metrics beyond user colour affiliation. These include 'SLURM Raw Usage', 'SLURM Raw Shares', 'CCDB allocation', 'Queued jobs' (representing pending job resources with narrow gray bars), and 'Total' (daily total text on each bar). Users can single-click items to toggle their presence or double-click to toggle all other items on or off.
What is the Reference GPU Unit (RGU) value and the recommended core and memory allocation for a whole H100-80gb GPU on the Rorqual cluster?
On the Rorqual cluster, a whole H100-80gb GPU has an RGU value of 12.2 and is recommended to be allocated 16 cores and 124 GB of memory.
For the Rorqual cluster, what are the recommended core and memory allocations for an H100-1g.10gb GPU instance?
On the Rorqual cluster, an H100-1g.10gb GPU instance is recommended to be allocated 2 cores and 15 GB of memory. It has an RGU value of 1.74.
What is the RGU value and the bundle characteristics (cores and memory) for an H100-3g.40gb GPU instance on the Rorqual cluster?

On the Rorqual cluster, an H100-3g.40gb GPU instance has an RGU value of 6.1 and a bundle of 8 cores and 62.2 GB of memory. The recommended allocation for this instance is 8 cores and 62 GB of memory.
What does the "Queued jobs" metric represent in the SLURM usage figure legend, and how is it displayed?

The "Queued jobs" metric in the SLURM usage figure legend represents the quantity of resources belonging to jobs that are pending in the job queue. It is displayed with narrow gray bars for each day in the figure window.
What information does the "Total" option in the SLURM usage figure legend provide?
The "Total" option in the SLURM usage figure legend adds text to the top of each bar, indicating the daily total of the metric across all users for that specific day.
How do users control the visibility of individual or multiple items within the SLURM usage figure legend?

Users can control the visibility of items in the SLURM usage figure legend by single-clicking an item to toggle its individual presence in the figure. To toggle all other items on or off simultaneously, users can double-click any item in the legend.
In the Slurm portal, what is the difference between "SLURM Raw Shares" and "SLURM Raw Usage," and how do these metrics help assess an account's priority?

The "SLURM Raw Shares" of an `rrg-*` or `rpp-*` allocation account is a straight line corresponding to that account's resource allocation on the cluster, while for default accounts, it's dynamic based on the number of active accounts. "SLURM Raw Usage" is a metric used by the scheduling software to determine account priority, calculated as the cumulative sum of an account's usage in billing units plus a half-life decay period. Plotting "SLURM Raw Usage" helps assess how past usage influences priority over time, with a general rule of thumb being that if "SLURM Raw Usage" is 10 times "SLURM Raw Shares," the account's usage is at par with its target share.
How can a user display their allocation target and the resources consumed by queued jobs within the Slurm portal's usage figure?

When a single account is selected for display in the Slurm portal, the "SLURM Raw Shares," which represents the allocation target, is shown as a horizontal red line. It can be toggled on or off using the "Display allocation target by default" item in the "Parameters" panel, or by clicking "SLURM Raw Shares" in the legend. The "Queued jobs" metric, which presents a sum of all resources in pending jobs at each time point, can be toggled on or off by clicking its label in the legend to the right of the figure.
What does the "Projection" area represent when a user selects an end date in the future for displaying usage in the Slurm portal?

If an end date after the present time is selected, the Slurm portal figure will display a transparent red area, labelled "Projection," over the future time. In this projection period, each running job is assumed to continue to its requested time limit, and each pending job is assumed to start at the beginning of the projected time and run until its requested time limit. It's important to note that this is not intended to be a forecast of actual future events.
How can researchers view their group's compute resource usage in the CCDB portal?
Researchers can view their group's compute resource usage by logging into the CCDB portal and navigating to 'My Account > View Group Usage'.
What types of usage metrics are available for selection in the Slurm portal's usage histogram?
In the Slurm portal, users can select from metrics such as CPU, CPU-equivalent, RGU, RGU-equivalent, Memory, Billing, GPU, and all specific GPU models available on the chosen cluster.
Do the CPU and GPU usage values summarized in the CCDB portal accurately represent core-equivalent measures for all job types?

No, the CPU and GPU core year values summarized in the CCDB portal are calculated based on the quantity of resources allocated to jobs and do not represent core-equivalent measures. For large memory jobs, these usage values may not match the cluster scheduler’s representation of the account usage.
What is the 'Projection' feature in the Slurm portal's usage display?

The 'Projection' feature in the Slurm portal's usage display is a transparent red area that appears when you select an end time after the present. It illustrates future resource usage based on assumptions about currently running and pending jobs.
How does the Slurm portal calculate resource usage within the 'Projection' period?

Within the 'Projection' period, the Slurm portal calculates resource usage by assuming that each currently running job will run to its requested time limit, and each pending job will start at the beginning of the projected time (i.e., immediately) and run until its requested time limit.
Is the 'Projection' in the Slurm portal intended to be a forecast of actual future events?
No, the 'Projection' feature in the Slurm portal is explicitly not intended to be a forecast of actual future events.
What kind of information can be found under the 'Usage by resource allocation project' tab in the CCDB portal?

Under the 'Usage by resource allocation project' tab, users can find Resource Allocation Project Identifiers (RAPIs) for the selected allocation year. It also displays tables with detailed information on each allocation project and the resources they have used across all clusters. Additionally, the top of the page summarizes details like the account name (e.g., def-, rrg- or rpp-*), the project title and ownership, and overall allocation and usage summaries.
How is GPU usage presented for resource allocation projects in the CCDB portal?
For resource allocation projects that involve GPU usage, the CCDB portal breaks down the usage data by various GPU models and measures it in Reference GPU Units (RGUs).
In the CCDB portal, how can users view the resource usage associated with individual job submitters within their group accounts?

Usage can be displayed grouped by the individual users who submitted jobs from within the resource allocation projects (group accounts). This view shows each user's aggregated usage across different systems. Users can then select from a list of submitters to display their usage broken down by cluster, and further view a monthly breakdown by clicking the 'Show monthly usage' link in the 'Extra Info' column.
What are the key criteria and their corresponding weights used to evaluate GPU models for Reference GPU Units (RGUs)?

GPU models are evaluated for Reference GPU Units (RGUs) based on three main criteria: FP32 score (for dense matrices on regular GPU cores) which accounts for 40% of the weight, FP16 score (for dense matrices on Tensor cores) also weighted at 40%, and GPU memory score which makes up the remaining 20%. The NVidia A100-40gb GPU is used as the reference model, assigned an RGU value of 4.0.
Could you list the Reference GPU Unit (RGU) scores for various whole GPU models available for allocation?

The NVidia A100-40gb GPU is the reference model with a combined RGU score of 4.0. Other whole GPU models and their combined RGU scores are: H100-80gb (12.2 RGU), A100-80gb (4.8 RGU), V100-32gb (2.6 RGU), V100-16gb (2.2 RGU), T4-16gb (1.3 RGU), P100-16gb (1.1 RGU), and P100-12gb (1.0 RGU).
What are Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) instances, and how are their Reference GPU Unit (RGU) values determined for resource allocation?

Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) technology allows scheduling a fraction of a GPU, referred to as a GPU instance or MIG instance, enabling multiple jobs or users to run simultaneously on the same GPU. For allocation purposes, the RGU values for these GPU instances are estimated by considering the whole-GPU performance numbers and the specific fraction of the GPU that the instance represents. For example, an A100-1g.5gb instance is assigned an RGU value of 0.6.
What are the primary evaluation criteria and their corresponding weights for ranking different GPU models into Reference GPU Units (RGUs)?

The primary evaluation criteria for ranking different GPU models into Reference GPU Units (RGUs) are the FP32 score (with dense matrices on regular GPU cores) at 40%, the FP16 score (with dense matrices on Tensor cores) also at 40%, and the GPU memory score at 20%.
What user usage patterns influenced the selection of the evaluation criteria for Reference GPU Units (RGUs)?

The evaluation criteria were chosen because roughly half of the users primarily utilize single-precision floating-point operations (FP32), the other half use half-precision floating-point operations (FP16), and a significant portion of all users are constrained by the amount of memory on the GPU.
What kind of information is presented in the table titled "GPU models and instances available for RAC 2026"?

The table displays a list of GPU models and instances, along with the fraction of a whole GPU each represents and its corresponding Reference GPU Unit (RGU) value, specifically for the 2026 Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) year.
For the RAC 2026 year, what is the Reference GPU Unit (RGU) value assigned to a whole A100-40gb GPU?
A whole A100-40gb GPU is assigned an RGU value of 4.0 for the RAC 2026 year.
What are the RGU value and the fraction of a whole GPU for an A100-3g.20gb instance as listed in the available models for RAC 2026?
The A100-3g.20gb instance represents 50% of a whole GPU and has an RGU value of 2.0 for RAC 2026.

When selecting a GPU model for a high-performance computing project, how do the expected operations (e.g., FP32 or FP16) influence the choice, and what are the implications for Reference GPU Unit (RGU) usage and computational efficiency?

For applications primarily using FP32 operations, an A100-40gb GPU is expected to be twice as fast as a P100-12gb GPU, but it will consume four times the resources in terms of RGUs. This means P100-12gb GPUs could allow for double the computations for an equivalent RGU allocation. Conversely, for applications heavily reliant on FP16 operations (common in AI), an A100-40gb GPU, while evaluated as using four times the resources of a P100-12gb, can compute approximately 30 times more calculations in the same timeframe, leading to about 7.5 times more overall computations for an equal RGU allocation.
How are Reference GPU Units (RGUs) incorporated into the Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) process, particularly when a project requesting GPUs needs to be moved to a different cluster?

During the Resource Allocation Competition, project proposals requesting GPUs must specify a preferred GPU model. The system then automatically calculates the total Reference GPU Units (RGUs) based on the requested GPU-years and the RGU value of the selected model (e.g., 13 A100-40gb GPU-years equals 52 RGUs). The RAC committee allocates a specific RGU amount. If an allocated project must be moved to a different cluster, the committee will adjust the number of GPU-years provided at the new cluster to ensure the total RGU value remains constant.

In the context of national clusters, what is a "core equivalent," and how does the scheduler use this concept to calculate job priority, especially when a job requests more memory than typically associated with its requested cores?

A "core equivalent" is a bundle consisting of a single core and a predefined amount of associated memory, typically 4GB per core on most clusters. The scheduler calculates job priority based on the resources that other users are prevented from utilizing, rather than just the resources actually used. For example, if a job requests only one core but requires 8GB of memory on a system where each core is associated with 4GB, the job will be counted as using two core equivalents. This is because the additional memory requirement effectively makes a second core's memory unavailable to others, impacting future job priority based on the maximum of requested cores or memory equivalents.
What is a core equivalent in the context of high-performance computing?
A core equivalent is defined as a single core bundled with the amount of memory considered to be associated with each core on a given high-performance computing system.
How is a core equivalent typically defined on most Alliance clusters?
On most Alliance clusters, a core equivalent is typically defined as a single core combined with 4GB of memory, reflecting the memory-to-core ratio found in the most common node types.
How are jobs charged for resource usage in terms of core equivalents on Alliance clusters?
Jobs on Alliance clusters are charged for core-equivalent usage at a rate of 4 GB per core.
How does the Alliance charge research groups for core equivalents when jobs request varying amounts of cores and memory on shared cluster resources?

The Alliance charges research groups for the maximum number of core equivalents they utilize from the resources. Assuming a core equivalent is 1 core and 4GB of memory, if a job requests more cores than memory (above this 1 core/4GB ratio), it will be charged based on the number of cores. If it requests more memory than this ratio, it will be charged based on the memory requested, with the job request being counted as the higher of these two equivalent amounts when priority is calculated.
What is the principle for how research groups are charged for Reference GPU Unit (RGU) equivalents, including associated cores and memory, by the scheduler on Alliance clusters?

When using GPU-based allocations, which include a Reference GPU Unit (RGU) alongside multiple cores and memory in a bundle, research groups are charged for the maximum number of RGU-core-memory bundles they use. This means if a job requests more RGUs, cores, or memory relative to the defined proportions of a fictive RGU-core-memory bundle, the charge will be calculated based on the component (RGU, cores, or memory) that represents the highest number of these equivalent bundles.
How is the RGU equivalent calculated for a job request that uses more memory than what is typically bundled with a Reference GPU Unit (RGU) and CPU cores on a High-Performance Computing cluster?

If a research group requests more memory than is associated with its requested Reference GPU Units (RGUs) or cores, they will be charged based on the maximum number of RGU-core-memory bundles used, determined by the memory requested. For instance, assuming a fictive bundle of 1 RGU, 3 cores, and 4 GB of memory, a request for 1 RGU, 2 cores, and 6 GB of memory would be counted as 1.5 RGU equivalents because the 6 GB of memory equates to 1.5 bundles (6 GB / 4 GB per bundle).
On a specific fictive High-Performance Computing cluster, what is the Reference GPU Unit (RGU) equivalent value for a bundle that includes one V100-32gb GPU, 7.8 CPU cores, and 10.4 GB of memory?
On the specified fictive cluster, a bundle consisting of one V100-32gb GPU, 7.8 CPU cores, and 10.4 GB of memory is calculated to be worth 2.6 RGU equivalents.
What defines the RGU-core-memory bundle characteristics on Alliance systems?
Alliance systems have RGU-core-memory bundle characteristics where only one ratio is applied per cluster, defining the combination of Reference GPU Units (RGU), CPU cores, and associated memory.
For the Narval cluster, what are the RGU per GPU and the recommended bundle characteristics for an A100-40gb GPU?
On the Narval cluster, an A100-40gb GPU has 4.0 RGUs per GPU, with a recommended bundle of 12 cores and 124 GB of memory.
What are the RGU per GPU and the recommended bundle characteristics for an H100-80gb GPU on the Fir cluster?
On the Fir cluster, an H100-80gb GPU has 12.2 RGUs per GPU, with a recommended bundle of 12 cores and 280 GB of memory.
What is an allocation in the context of high-performance computing resources on Alliance clusters?

An allocation is a specific amount of resources that a research group can target for use over a period, typically a year. For storage, it's a maximum amount, while for shared resources like computation cores and GPUs, it represents an average usage over the period.
How do core year and GPU year allocations differ from storage allocations on Alliance clusters?

Storage allocations provide a maximum amount of storage for exclusive use. Core year and GPU year allocations are more complex, aiming to capture average usage over the allocation period on shared resources, rather than a strict maximum.
How does the job scheduler on Alliance clusters determine the priority of jobs submitted by research groups?

The scheduler uses prioritization algorithms based on a research group's recent usage compared to their allocated usage on that system, with more weight given to recent activity. This aims to allow groups matching their allocation to operate continuously at that level.
What are the consequences if a research group overuses its CPU or GPU allocation on Alliance clusters?

If a group overuses its allocation, subsequent jobs from that group may have lower priority for a time, as the scheduler prioritizes other groups below their target. However, users are not prevented from submitting new jobs, and average usage should still remain close to the allocation target.
What is a Reference GPU Unit (RGU) on Alliance clusters, and why was it introduced?

A Reference GPU Unit (RGU) is a metric introduced in the 2024 RAC year to rank different GPU models in production based on their performance and memory. It was created to address problems in the allocation process and job running due to the varying and increasing performance of GPUs.
What evaluation criteria and weights are used to rank GPU models for RGU calculation on Alliance clusters?
The evaluation criteria are FP32 score (40%), FP16 score (40%), and GPU memory score (20%).
Which GPU model serves as the reference for RGU calculation on Alliance clusters, and what is its RGU value?
The NVidia A100-40gb GPU is used as the reference model and is assigned an RGU value of 4.0 for historical reasons.
How are Reference GPU Units (RGUs) handled during the Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) process on Alliance clusters?

During RAC, proposals for GPUs must specify a preferred GPU model. The requested gpu-years are automatically converted to RGUs in the CCDB form (e.g., 13 A100-40gb gpu-years = 52 RGUs). The RAC committee allocates RGUs, and if a project is moved to a different cluster, gpu-years are adjusted to maintain the same RGU amount.
What is a core equivalent on Alliance clusters, and how does the scheduler use it to calculate resource usage?

A core equivalent is a bundle consisting of a single core and an associated amount of memory (typically 4GB on most clusters). The scheduler charges research groups for the maximum number of core equivalents they take, whether it's based on cores requested or memory requested exceeding the standard ratio.
How does the scheduler on Alliance clusters charge for RGU-core-memory bundles?

Research groups are charged for the maximum number of RGU-core-memory bundles they use, meaning the usage is calculated based on whichever component (RGU, cores, or memory) demands the largest 'equivalent' share of the bundle ratio.
What is the purpose of the Slurm portal (portal.alliancecan.ca/slurm) for Alliance cluster users?

The Slurm portal provides an interface for exploring time-series data about jobs on national clusters, allowing users to view usage metrics like CPU-equivalent, RGU-equivalent, memory, and specific GPU models over specified time intervals.
How can users view their resource usage over an extended period into the future on the Alliance Slurm portal?

Users can select an end date in the future when setting the time interval. The portal will then display a 'Projection' as a transparent red area, showing currently running and pending jobs for their requested duration into the future, assuming they run to their time limit.
What information does the 'SLURM Raw Usage' metric provide on the Alliance Slurm portal?

The 'SLURM Raw Usage' is a metric used by the scheduling software to determine account priority. It represents the cumulative sum of an account's usage in billing units plus a half-life decay period, helping users assess how past usage affects their account's priority over time.
How can users access their group's compute resource usage information in the Alliance CCDB?
Users can access this information by logging into the CCDB and navigating to 'My Account > View Group Usage'.
What types of usage breakdowns are available in the Alliance CCDB under the 'View Group Usage' section?

Users can view usage breakdowns 'By Compute Resource' (per cluster), 'By Resource Allocation Project' (per project), and 'By Submitter' (per user who submitted jobs). GPU usage is further broken down into various GPU models and measured in RGUs for relevant projects.
What is the importance of choosing appropriate parameter values when submitting a job on a computational cluster?

Choosing appropriate parameter values ensures that your job doesn't waste resources or create problems for other users and yourself. This helps your job start more quickly, finish correctly, and produce the necessary output to advance your research.
What are some typical problems users might encounter if they don't estimate job resources correctly on a computational cluster?

Users might experience longer waiting times in the queue if they request too many resources (time, memory, CPU cores, GPUs), or their job might be stopped prematurely if it exceeds its time or memory limits due to insufficient requested resources. Additionally, resource estimation based on local computer performance can be misleading, and compute tasks might waste resources if programs don't scale well, aren't designed for multiple nodes, or processors wait excessively after read-write operations.
What is the recommended best practice for submitting initial or first jobs on a computational cluster to determine resource needs?

For initial jobs, the best approach is to submit a few relatively small test jobs, requesting a standard amount of memory (e.g., `#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=2G`) and time (e.g., one or two hours). If a job ends before completion, users should double the duration. If a job runs out of memory (indicated by an "OOM event"), users should double the requested memory. This iterative testing helps gain familiarity and make intelligent estimates for more realistic jobs.
What is the recommended memory efficiency for jobs on a cluster, and how should users specify memory requests for a whole node or a large memory node in their job submission scripts?

For most jobs, a `Memory Efficiency` of at least 80% to 85% is recommended, as shown in the output from the `seff` command. To utilize all available memory on a node, users can include `#SBATCH --mem=0` in their job submission script, though this approach might lead to the job being assigned a node with less memory due to the variable memory available on cluster nodes. If a large memory node is specifically required, users should request a specific amount, for example, `#SBATCH --mem=1500G`, but should be aware that these nodes are few, leading to potentially longer wait times.

When running a job on a cluster, how can one determine if the software supports parallel execution, and what are the best practices for configuring a job to efficiently use multiple cores within a single node or distribute processes across multiple nodes?

To determine if software supports parallel execution, consult its documentation for a section on parallel execution, or contact the development team. For parallel programs utilizing multiple cores on a single node (shared memory), users should study the software's scalability to select the optimal number of CPU cores, as requesting too many can paradoxically slow the program down. For distributed memory parallelism across multiple nodes, ensure the software uses the MPI standard, start jobs using `srun` instead of `mpirun`, and aim to avoid scattering processes. Instead, submit jobs where the number of parallel processes is an integral multiple of the number of cores per node for a more compact and performant distribution.
What is a checkpoint in the context of job submission on clusters?

A checkpoint is a mechanism where a program writes a snapshot of its current state to a diskfile. This allows the program to be restarted from that precise point in the calculation, using the saved diskfile.
Why should longer jobs on clusters consider using checkpoints?

Longer jobs, particularly those exceeding 48 hours, should consider using checkpoints because they prevent significant loss of work. If a power outage or another interruption occurs on the compute node(s) being used by the job, the program can be restarted from its last saved checkpoint, minimizing the amount of lost progress.
How frequently should a program write checkpoint files to be effective?
To minimize potential work loss, it is recommended that a program writes a checkpoint file every six or eight hours.
What is the recommended strategy for submitting parallel jobs on a cluster to optimize performance and reduce scheduler complexity?

To optimize performance and simplify the scheduler's job, it is recommended to submit parallel jobs where the number of parallel processes is an integral multiple of the number of cores available per node, assuming the parallel software is compatible with this approach. This helps ensure a more compact distribution of processes.
On a cluster with 40 cores per node, what specific numbers of parallel processes should be requested for efficient job submission?

On a cluster with 40 cores per node, you should request parallel jobs that ask for a number of processes which are multiples of 40, such as 40, 80, 120, 160, or 240 processes. This ensures the processes are assigned in the most compact fashion across the nodes.
How can a job script header be configured to assign 120 MPI processes compactly using three whole nodes, with 40 tasks per node?
To assign 120 MPI processes compactly using three whole nodes, with 40 tasks per node, the job script header should be configured with `#SBATCH --nodes=3` and `#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=40`.
How can users ensure their jobs are utilizing CPU resources effectively on the clusters?

Users should strive for a CPU efficiency very close to 100%, which is measured by the `CPU Efficiency` field in the output of the `seff` command. Any value below 90% is considered poor and indicates that the software's execution within the job needs improvement.
What are the recommended steps for evaluating if a GPU will significantly benefit a job on the clusters, given that GPU nodes are less common?

Since GPU nodes typically have longer wait times, it's advisable to first perform a small sample calculation both with and without a GPU to determine the actual speed-up. If a job only completes 5% or 10% faster with a GPU, it's likely not worth the extended wait, as the GPU may be idle for a significant portion of the job's execution. Tools such as `nvidia-smi`, `nvtop`, or `TensorBoard` (for TensorFlow-based software) can be used to monitor GPU efficiency.
What general practices should be avoided or adopted to prevent resource wastage in jobs submitted to the clusters?

To prevent resource wastage, jobs should generally not contain the `sleep` command. It is strongly recommended to use alternatives like a Python virtual environment or Apptainer instead of Conda and its variants. Additionally, read and write operations should be optimized by utilizing node-local storage.
What is the main purpose of providing tips for job submission on Alliance clusters?

The main purpose is to help users choose appropriate job parameters to avoid wasting resources, prevent problems for other users, ensure jobs start quickly, and finish correctly, thus moving research forward.
What are some common issues that can occur when submitting jobs on Alliance clusters?

Common issues include jobs waiting longer in the queue due to requesting excessive resources, jobs being stopped for exceeding time or memory limits, and wasting resources because programs don't scale well or processors wait during read-write operations.
What is the recommended best approach for submitting initial jobs on an Alliance cluster?

The best approach is to begin by submitting a few relatively small test jobs, requesting a standard amount of memory (e.g., `#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=2G`) and a short duration (one or two hours), ideally with known expected results.
How should a user adjust resource requests if a test job on an Alliance cluster runs out of memory or finishes before computation?

If a job ends with an 'OOM event' (out of memory), the user should try doubling the requested memory. If it ends before the computation finishes, they should double the duration until it's sufficient.
What is the recommended minimum duration for non-test jobs on Alliance clusters, and what should be done for shorter computations?

For non-test jobs, the recommended minimum duration is at least one hour. If a computation requires less than an hour, users should consider using tools like GLOST, META, or GNU Parallel to regroup several computations into a single Slurm job.
Why is it important to provide a relatively accurate estimate for a job's duration on an Alliance cluster?
An accurate duration estimate is important because overestimating significantly can lead to the job spending much more time waiting to start than it would with a more precise estimate.
How can users monitor the actual wall-clock time taken by their completed jobs on Alliance clusters?
Users can use monitoring tools, such as the `seff` command, and check the 'Job Wall-clock time' field in its output to see how long completed jobs took.
What is the target memory efficiency for jobs on Alliance clusters, as measured by the `seff` command?
The `Memory Efficiency` in the `seff` command's output should ideally be at least 80% to 85% in most cases.
What should users consider when requesting large memory nodes for their jobs on Alliance clusters?
Users should ensure their job genuinely requires a large memory node, as these are relatively few and requesting one will lead to significantly longer wait times in the queue.
What is the default assumption about software on Alliance clusters, and what does it imply for core requests?
By default, most software is serial and can only make use of a single core. Requesting more cores for a serial program will not make it run any faster.
How can users determine if the software they are using on an Alliance cluster can run in parallel?

The best approach is to look in the software's documentation for a section on parallel execution; if nothing is found, it usually indicates the program is serial. Users can also contact the development team.
What factors should users consider when choosing the number of cores for parallel jobs on a single node on Alliance clusters?

Users should consider that many parallel programming techniques assume a shared memory environment within a single node. It's important to study the software's scalability, as requesting an excessive number of CPU cores can slow down a program.
What type of parallelism must software support to run across multiple nodes on Alliance clusters, and what command should be used to start such jobs?
Software must support distributed memory parallelism, typically using the MPI standard. Programs parallelized to run across multiple nodes should be started using `srun` rather than `mpirun`.
What is the recommended strategy for distributing parallel processes across nodes to optimize performance and scheduler efficiency on Alliance clusters?

Users should aim for a compact distribution, submitting jobs where the number of parallel processes is an integral multiple of the number of cores per node (e.g., 40, 80, 120 processes on a 40-core/node cluster).
What is the target CPU efficiency for jobs on Alliance clusters, as indicated by the `seff` command output?
The goal is for the `CPU Efficiency` field in the `seff` command output to be very close to 100%, with any value less than 90% indicating a need for improvement in software usage.
What are important considerations for users requesting GPUs for their jobs on Alliance clusters?

Users should ensure the requested GPU is being used as efficiently as possible and genuinely contributes to improved performance, as GPU nodes are uncommon and lead to significantly longer wait times. Testing with and without a GPU is recommended.
What tools can be used to monitor the efficiency of GPU-based jobs on Alliance clusters?
Tools for monitoring GPU efficiency include `nvidia-smi`, `nvtop`, and `TensorBoard` (if using TensorFlow-based software).
What are some specific recommendations for avoiding resource waste during job execution on Alliance clusters?

Users should avoid using the `sleep` command, are strongly recommended against using Conda variants in favour of Python virtual environments or Apptainer, and should optimize read and write operations by using node-local storage.
Why do Ansys parallel jobs require special instructions on computing clusters?
Ansys parallel jobs require special instructions on computing clusters because the MPI implementations included in the Ansys software suite do not support the Slurm scheduler used on these clusters.
What is the typical procedure for running an Ansys Fluent job on a cluster?

Typically, you prepare your Fluent job using Ansys Workbench on a desktop, export the case file (and data file if needed), transfer these files to the cluster's /project or /scratch filesystem, create a journal file to load the case/data, run the solver, and write results, then run the job. After the job runs, you can download and import the data file back into Fluent.
When should one consider modifying an Ansys Fluent Slurm script to requeue a job, and what important considerations should be taken into account?

You should consider modifying your Slurm script to requeue your job (up to 4 times) if jobs frequently fail to start due to license shortages and manual resubmission is inconvenient. However, it's strongly recommended to monitor and inspect each Slurm output file to confirm that each requeue attempt is license-related, as this modification will also requeue simulations that fail due to other issues like divergence, leading to wasted compute time. If a job is requeued due to a simulation issue, you must manually kill the job progression with `scancel jobid` and correct the problem.
What is the main function of the `script-flu-bynode+restart.sh` Slurm script for Ansys Fluent?

The `script-flu-bynode+restart.sh` Slurm script is designed to run Ansys Fluent jobs on multiple compute nodes, with the added functionality of automating solution restarts. This allows simulations to continue from a previous state, which is particularly useful for jobs exceeding typical runtime limits or needing multiple attempts.
How does the `script-flu-bynode+restart.sh` script differentiate between an initial simulation run and a subsequent restart?

The script utilizes the Slurm `--array` directive (e.g., `#SBATCH --array=1-5%1`) to manage multiple job attempts or restarts. It uses the `$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` environment variable: if it's the first task (ID `== 1`), it executes the initial journal file (`MYJOUFILE`). For all subsequent tasks (ID `> 1`), it uses the restart journal file (`MYJOUFILERES`) to continue the simulation.
What are the required user-defined variables and key Slurm directives in the `script-flu-bynode+restart.sh` script?

Key user-defined variables include `MYVERSION` (e.g., `3d` for the Fluent version), `MYJOUFILE` (the initial journal filename), `MYJOUFILERES` (the journal filename for restarts), `MYCASFILERES` (the case restart filename), and `MYDATFILERES` (the data restart filename). Essential Slurm directives are `--account`, `--time`, `--nodes`, `--ntasks-per-node`, `--mem`, `--cpus-per-task`, and especially `--array` to specify the number of solution restarts.
How does the provided Slurm script for Fluent manage job restarts for multinode simulations?

The script utilizes Slurm array jobs to manage restarts. For the initial run (when `SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` is 1), it uses the primary journal file (`$MYJOUFILE`). For subsequent restarts, it switches to a dedicated restart journal file (`$MYJOUFILERES`). Upon successful completion of a task, if it's not the final restart attempt, it updates symbolic links for the restart case and data files (`$MYCASFILERES` and `$MYDATFILERES`) to point to the most recent output files, ensuring the simulation resumes from the latest state.
How does the Fluent script in the provided context configure parallel communication methods for different clusters?

The script dynamically adjusts the Fluent parallel communication method based on the cluster environment. If the `CC_CLUSTER` environment variable indicates that the job is running on the "nibi" cluster, Fluent uses the Ethernet-based MPI (`-peth`). For other clusters, it defaults to the InfiniBand-based MPI (`-pib`).
What happens if a Fluent job fails during a restart attempt when using this Slurm script?

If a Fluent job fails during an array task, the script will output a message indicating that the job attempt failed due to a license or simulation issue. If it was not the last attempt in the array (`SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` is less than `SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_COUNT`), it will indicate that it is resubmitting the job. If all attempts have failed, it will state that all job attempts failed and exit.
What is the primary purpose of the provided Slurm script for Ansys Fluent, and what key Slurm directives configure its resources for a multinode, by-core job with solution restart?

The script is designed to run Ansys Fluent simulations in a distributed memory parallel environment, specifically enabling solution restarts. Key Slurm directives used to configure resources include `#SBATCH --ntasks=16` to specify the total number of cores across all nodes, `#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=4G` for memory allocation per core, and `#SBATCH --array=1-5%1` to define the number of solution restart attempts or time steps.
How does the provided Slurm script for Ansys Fluent manage the execution of initial runs versus subsequent solution restarts within a job array?

The script differentiates between initial runs and restarts using the `$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` variable. For the first run in the array (`$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID == 1`), Ansys Fluent is executed using the initial journal file specified by `MYJOUFILE`. For all subsequent runs within the array, representing solution restarts, Fluent utilizes the restart journal file defined by `MYJOUFILERES`. This conditional logic applies whether the job is running on a single node or multiple nodes.
What is the purpose of Fluent journal files, and what functionalities do they offer for simulations?

Fluent journal files allow users to automate commands from Fluent's Text User Interface (TUI), enabling them to modify simulation parameters like temperature, pressure, and flow speed. This facilitates running multiple simulations under varying conditions using a single case file by adjusting parameters within the journal file. Additionally, these files can be configured to use either the legacy `.cas/.dat` file format (with `/file/cff-files no`) or the more efficient `.cas.h5/.dat.h5` format (with `/file/cff-files yes`). For a comprehensive list of commands, users can consult the Fluent User's Guide.
In Fluent's solution restart scripts, how are subsequent job segments managed, and how do they handle the case and data files for continuous simulations?

In Fluent's solution restart scripts, such as the `Multinode (by core + restart)` example, the `$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID` variable differentiates between the initial run (task ID 1) and subsequent restarts. The initial run utilizes the main journal file (`$MYJOUFILE`), while subsequent restarts use a dedicated restart journal file (`$MYJOUFILERES`). Upon successful completion of a job segment, the script automatically creates symbolic links from the most recent `.cas` and `.dat` output files found in the `output/` subdirectory to the designated restart case (`$MYCASFILERES`) and data (`$MYDATFILERES`) files, allowing the next job segment to seamlessly continue from the latest saved state.
What is the main purpose of Fluent journal files in Ansys simulations, and what types of commands can they include?

Fluent journal files automate the simulation process by loading case files, running the solver, and writing results. They can contain virtually any command from Fluent's Text User Interface (TUI), allowing users to adjust simulation parameters such as temperature, pressure, or flow speed, and run multiple simulations under different conditions with a single case file.
What are the essential initial steps for preparing and transferring a User-Defined Function (UDF) for use with Fluent on an Alliance cluster?

First, you must transfer your UDF source file, like `sampleudf.c`, and any dependent files to the cluster. Ensure the text mode setting of your transfer client is used, especially when uploading from Windows, so Fluent can read the file correctly. The UDF should be placed in the same directory as your journal, case, and data files. Crucially, before uploading your case file to the cluster, confirm that neither the 'Interpreted UDFs' nor the 'UDF Library Manager' dialog boxes in the Fluent GUI are configured to use any UDF; this ensures that only the journal file commands control the UDF when jobs are submitted.
How can a Fluent journal file be configured to use an interpreted User-Defined Function (UDF) during a simulation run?

To configure a Fluent journal file to interpret a UDF at runtime, you need to add a specific command line before the case/data files are read or initialized. The command is `define/user-defined/interpreted-functions "sampleudf.c" "cpp" 10000 no`, where `sampleudf.c` should be replaced with the actual name of your UDF source file. It's also important to open your case file in the Fluent GUI, remove any managed definitions, and resave it to ensure this journal command is the sole control for UDF usage during the Fluent run.
What is the process for using a compiled User-Defined Function (UDF) with Ansys Fluent on an Alliance cluster?

To use a compiled UDF, it must first be compiled on an Alliance cluster, which creates a `libudf` subdirectory containing the necessary `libudf.so` shared library. This `libudf` directory can then be transferred to other Alliance clusters if the same `StdEnv` environment module version is loaded. The UDF is subsequently loaded by uncommenting the `define/user-defined/compiled-functions load libudf` line in your journal file. It is important not to leave both the compile and load lines uncommented, as this will lead to inefficient recompilation for every job and potential build conflicts.
Why is it necessary to parallelize a User-Defined Function (UDF) for use with Ansys Fluent parallel jobs, and what are the potential consequences of not doing so?

A UDF must be parallelized before it can be used effectively with any Fluent parallel job, including single-node SMP and multinode MPI. This parallelization involves adding compiler directives, predicates, and reduction macros to the UDF's serial code to control which processes execute specific parts of the code. Failing to parallelize a UDF can result in Fluent running very slowly or, in the worst case, immediately crashing.
What is the primary purpose of User-Defined Functions (UDFs) when working with Discrete Phase Models (DPM) in Ansys Fluent?
User-Defined Functions (UDFs) are used to customize Discrete Phase Models (DPM) within Ansys Fluent simulations, allowing for tailored behaviour of particles.
What is the procedure for defining the injection of particles for a Discrete Phase Model (DPM) simulation using the Ansys Fluent graphical user interface?

To define particle injections in Ansys Fluent's GUI, users should navigate to the 'Physics panel', select 'Discrete Phase' to open the 'Discrete Phase Model' box, and then click the 'Injections' button. Within the 'Injections' dialog box, clicking 'Create' opens the 'Set Injection Properties' dialog, where users can choose an 'Injection Type' and specify 'Point Properties' such as source position, initial trajectory, mass flow rate, and temperature, or opt to read properties from an injection text file.
How can the setup for Discrete Phase Models (DPM) in Ansys Fluent, including injection definitions and interaction with the continuous phase, be automated after initial solution initialization?

After initializing the solution, DPM setup can be automated by adding specific commands to a journal file. This includes enabling coupled calculations for DPM source term updates using a command like `/define/models/dpm/interaction/coupled-calculations yes`, and defining particle injections by referencing an injection text file with commands such as `/define/models/dpm/injections/create injection-0:1 no yes file no zinjection01.inj no no no no`.
How can Discrete Phase Model (DPM) injection settings be automated in Ansys Fluent using a journal file?

DPM injection settings in Ansys Fluent can be automated by including specific commands in the journal file after solution initialization. These commands allow for enabling coupled calculations (`/define/models/dpm/interaction/coupled-calculations yes`), deleting and creating injections from a specified file (e.g., `zinjection01.inj`), and listing their particles and properties. An example injection command is `/define/models/dpm/injections/create injection-0:1 no yes file no zinjection01.inj no no no no`.
What command-line options are available for `cfx5solve` in Ansys CFX to control precision and mesh size?

For `cfx5solve` in Ansys CFX, the `-double` option can be used to run simulations in double precision, though this will double memory requirements. To handle larger meshes, specifically those with up to 2 billion elements, the `-large` option should be added. By default, `cfx5solve` runs in single precision and supports meshes up to 80 million structured or 200 million unstructured elements.
How does one configure a Slurm script to run an Ansys CFX job on a single compute node?

To configure a Slurm script for an Ansys CFX job on a single compute node, you must specify `#SBATCH --nodes=1`. You should also define the number of cores per node with `#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node` (e.g., 4) and total memory with `#SBATCH --mem` (e.g., 16G). After loading the `StdEnv/2023` and `ansys/2023R2` (or newer) modules, the `cfx5solve` command is used. The `-start-method` will be "Open MPI Local Parallel" for Narval or Fir clusters, and "Intel MPI Local Parallel" for other clusters. The number of partitions for the local parallel job is specified by `-part $SLURM_CPUS_ON_NODE`.
What are the main differences in Slurm script configuration between running an Ansys CFX job on a single node versus multiple nodes?

For a single-node Ansys CFX job, the Slurm script specifies `#SBATCH --nodes=1` and allows for explicit definition of `#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node` and `#SBATCH --mem`. The `cfx5solve` command uses a "Local Parallel" start method. In contrast, for multi-node jobs, the script requires `#SBATCH --nodes` to be set to 2 or more, and typically uses `#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=192` to utilize all cores per node and `#SBATCH --mem=0` to allocate all memory. The `cfx5solve` command employs a "Distributed Parallel" start method and uses `slurm_hl2hl.py` to determine the number of nodes for distributed parallelism (`-par-dist $NNODES`). Additionally, multi-node Intel MPI jobs on clusters other than Narval or Fir require specific environment variable settings like `export I_MPI_HYDRA_BOOTSTRAP=ssh`.
Before submitting an Ansys Workbench job to a Slurm queue, how must it be initialized?

To initialize an Ansys Workbench job, first start an OnDemand desktop on the cluster and navigate to the directory containing your project file. You should then remove the old `_ProjectScratch` cache directory. Next, load the specific Ansys module version you intend to use in your Slurm script. Open the Workbench GUI by issuing `runwb2 -f YOURPROJECT.wbpj` and answer 'No' if prompted to recover the project. In the 'Project Schematic' window, right-click on 'Model' and select 'Reset', confirming that you accept the deletion of local and generated data. Finally, save the file, exit Workbench (clicking 'No' when asked if you want to save the modified project), and then submit your job.
What is a more intuitive way to run Ansys Workbench simulations compared to submitting jobs with Slurm scripts?

Running Ansys Workbench simulations directly from within the Workbench native GUI during an OnDemand desktop session is considered a more intuitive option than submitting jobs with Slurm scripts. This is because an OnDemand desktop session can reserve a compute node with up to 96 cores, 768GB of memory, and an 8-hour runtime.
When running Fluent jobs on clusters, what are the recommended Slurm script types for general purposes, and what are their respective benefits and drawbacks?

For most Fluent jobs, the `by node` script is recommended to minimize solution latency and maximize performance over as few nodes as possible. While very large jobs might experience shorter queue wait times with a `by core` script, this approach can lead to significantly longer startup times and makes the job more vulnerable to crashing if multiple compute nodes fail during the simulation.
What considerations are important for optimizing Fluent's mesh partitioning when running parallel jobs on clusters?
For optimal efficiency in parallel Fluent jobs, the number of mesh partitions should be an integral multiple of the number of cores, and users should ensure there are at least 10,000 cells per core.
How do you submit an Ansys Workbench project file to a cluster queue using a Slurm script?

You can submit an Ansys Workbench project file to the queue by customizing one of the provided Slurm scripts, such as `script-wbpj-202X.sh`, and then executing it with the `sbatch` command, for example `sbatch script-wbpj-202X.sh`.
What is the function of the `MEMPAR` variable in the Ansys Workbench Slurm scripts for parallel processing?

In the Ansys Workbench Slurm scripts, the `MEMPAR` variable is used to configure the parallel processing type. It is set to `0` for Shared Memory Parallel (SMP) when running on a single compute node, and `1` for Distributed Memory Parallel (DMP) if multiple nodes are being utilized.
When conducting scaling tests for an Ansys Workbench job with a Slurm script, how can one prevent the solution from being overwritten upon job completion?

To prevent the solution from being overwritten when a Workbench job successfully completes, you should change `Save(Overwrite=True)` to `Save(Overwrite=False)` in the final line of the Slurm script. This modification allows for easier evaluation of simulation scaling without overwriting the initialized solution from previous test runs.
How do I run an Ansys Mechanical APDL job using Shared Memory Parallel (SMP) on a CPU cluster with a Slurm script?

To run an Ansys Mechanical APDL job with Shared Memory Parallel (SMP) on a CPU cluster, you can use a Slurm script such as `script-smp-2023-cpu.sh`. This script is typically configured for a single node (`#SBATCH --nodes=1`) and specifies the total number of cores (`#SBATCH --tasks=8`) and memory (`#SBATCH --mem=32G`). You'll need to load the appropriate `StdEnv` and `ansys` modules (e.g., `ansys/2024R1.03`), create an output directory, and then execute the job using the `mapdl -smp` command with your input file (e.g., `YOURAPDLFILE.inp`). For the Cedar cluster, an additional `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` export is required.
What is the procedure for submitting an Ansys Mechanical APDL job using Distributed Memory Parallel (DMP) on a CPU cluster with a Slurm script?

To submit an Ansys Mechanical APDL job using Distributed Memory Parallel (DMP) on a CPU cluster, you would use a Slurm script similar to `script-dmp-2023-cpu.sh`. This script allows specifying the total number of cores (`#SBATCH --ntasks=8`) and memory per CPU (`#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu=4G`), potentially across multiple nodes. After loading the required `StdEnv` and `ansys` modules (e.g., `ansys/2024R1.03`) and creating an output directory, the job is executed with the `mapdl -dis` command. The MPI implementation varies by cluster; Beluga uses Intel MPI, while other clusters use Open MPI. For Cedar, a `libstdc++.so.6.0.29` symbolic link and `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` export are also needed.
What are the recommended practices for optimizing and configuring Ansys Mechanical APDL jobs on a cluster, including memory and version compatibility?

For optimal performance, Ansys Mechanical APDL jobs allocate 1024 MB total memory and 1024 MB database memory by default. These values can be manually adjusted by adding `-m` and/or `-db` arguments to the `mapdl` command in your Slurm scripts. It's crucial to perform detailed scaling tests before running production jobs to determine the optimal number of cores and minimum memory required. The single node Shared Memory Parallel (SMP) scripts generally offer better performance than multinode Distributed Memory Parallel (DMP) scripts and should be utilized whenever feasible. Additionally, to avoid compatibility issues, the Ansys module version loaded in your Slurm script should ideally match the version used to generate the APDL input file.
How can a user manually specify memory and database memory for Ansys Mechanical APDL jobs when submitting them on a cluster?

Ansys Mechanical APDL jobs typically allocate 1024 MB of total memory and 1024 MB of database memory by default. Users can manually specify or change these values by adding arguments like `-m 1024` (for total memory) and/or `-db 1024` (for database memory) to the `mapdl` command line in their Slurm scripts.
Which parallelization method is generally recommended for Ansys Mechanical APDL jobs on a cluster, Shared Memory Parallel (SMP) or Distributed Memory Parallel (DMP)?

For Ansys Mechanical APDL jobs, the single node (Shared Memory Parallel or SMP) scripts generally perform better than multinode (Distributed Memory Parallel or DMP) scripts. Therefore, SMP scripts should be used whenever possible to achieve optimal performance.
What steps should users take to ensure optimal resource utilization and compatibility when running Ansys Mechanical APDL jobs using Slurm scripts on a cluster?

To ensure optimal resource utilization, users should perform detailed scaling tests before running production jobs, which helps in specifying the optimal number of cores and the minimum required memory in their scripts. For compatibility, the Ansys module loaded in the script should ideally match the Ansys version used to generate the input file.
What is the primary function of the Rocky software when run in a cluster queue?
Rocky software is used to solve standalone, non-coupled simulations within a cluster queue, with sample Slurm scripts provided to facilitate this process.
How can a user restart or resume a partially completed Rocky simulation?

To restart a partially completed Rocky simulation, users must set the `RESUME` parameter to `1` in the Slurm script and then resubmit the script to the queue. By default, Rocky simulations start from the beginning with `RESUME=0`.
What is the performance difference between GPU-based and CPU-only Rocky simulations for basic test cases?

For basic test cases, GPU-only Rocky simulations were observed to outperform CPU-only scripts by a factor of 3.5x. It is generally expected that GPU-based scripts will provide significantly faster solution times for standalone Rocky simulations compared to using only CPUs.
How do you resume a partially completed Rocky simulation using the provided Slurm scripts?

To resume a partially completed Rocky simulation, you need to set the `RESUME` variable to `1` in the Slurm script. This will instruct Rocky to continue the simulation from its last saved state, rather than starting a new simulation and removing previous results.
What are the key differences in resource requests between the CPU-only and GPU-based Slurm scripts for Rocky simulations?

The CPU-only script requests 6 CPUs, 24GB of memory, and a 2-hour time limit. In contrast, the GPU-based script requests 2 CPUs, 24GB of memory, a 1-hour time limit, and specifically requests one H100_1g.10gb GPU (or an a100_1g.5gb GPU when running on Narval).
What are the primary command-line options used to execute Rocky simulations within the provided Slurm scripts?

The primary command-line options used to execute Rocky simulations in these scripts are `--headless` (to run without a graphical interface), `--simulate` (to perform the simulation), `--resume=0` or `--resume=1` (to either start fresh or continue a simulation), `--ncpus=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK` (to specify the number of CPU cores), and `--use-gpu=0` or `--use-gpu=1` (to disable or enable GPU acceleration, respectively).
Where can users locate the Slurm scripts for operating Ansys Electronics Desktop (AnsysEDT)?
Slurm scripts for utilizing Ansys Electronics Desktop (AnsysEDT) are provided on the dedicated "AnsysEDT" page.
How is Ansys Fluent launched on a compute cluster using these Slurm scripts?

The Slurm scripts prepare the environment by loading the `StdEnv/2023` and `ansys/2023R2` (or newer) modules. They then configure Intel MPI settings, including cluster-specific adjustments for Narval or Nibi, create a machinefile using `slurm_hl2hl.py`, and finally execute the `fluent` command. The `fluent` command is run with parameters that specify the Fluent version (`MYVERSION`), the number of cores (`NCORES`), the MPI implementation (`-mpi=intel`), and the path to the user's journal file (`MYJOURNALFILE`).
How do the provided Slurm scripts for Ansys Fluent manage parallel execution for single versus multiple compute nodes?

For single-node execution (`$SLURM_NNODES == 1`), the `fluent` command utilizes shared memory parallel (SMP) processing by including the `-pshmem` flag. For multiple compute nodes, it employs distributed memory parallel (DMP) processing. On the Nibi cluster, the `-peth` flag is used, while on other clusters, `-pib` is specified. In both multi-node cases, a machinefile (`-cnf=/tmp/machinefile-$SLURM_JOB_ID`) generated by `slurm_hl2hl.py` is referenced, and the `-mpi=intel` flag is consistently used.
Which specific parameters in the provided Slurm script for Ansys Fluent need to be adjusted by a user before submission?

Users must specify their Slurm account name via `#SBATCH --account`, the time limit for the job with `#SBATCH --time=DD-HH:MM`, and define resource requests such as the number of compute nodes (`#SBATCH --nodes`), tasks per node (`#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node`), and memory (`#SBATCH --mem` or `#SBATCH --mem-per-cpu`). Additionally, users need to set the `MYJOURNALFILE` variable to the name of their Fluent journal file (e.g., `sample.jou`) and the `MYVERSION` variable to specify the desired Fluent solver version (e.g., `3d`, `2d`, `2ddp`, or `3ddp`). The `ansys` module version should also be specified if different from the default `ansys/2023R2`.
What is the purpose of the `slurm_hl2hl.py` command within Ansys Fluent Slurm scripts?

The `slurm_hl2hl.py` command is used to generate a machine file, typically output to `/tmp/machinefile-$SLURM_JOB_ID` or `/tmp/mf-$SLURM_JOB_ID`, which is crucial for managing parallel computations in Ansys Fluent jobs.
How does the "Multinode (by node)" Ansys Fluent Slurm script differentiate between single-node and multi-node execution for Intel MPI jobs on clusters like Nibi?

For single-node jobs, the "Multinode (by node)" Ansys Fluent script uses `fluent -g $MYVERSION -t $NCORES -mpi=intel -pshmem -i $MYJOURNALFILE` for shared memory parallel (SMP). For multi-node execution on the Nibi cluster, it uses `fluent -g $MYVERSION -t $NCORES -mpi=intel -peth -cnf=/tmp/machinefile-$SLURM_JOB_ID -i $MYJOURNALFILE` for distributed memory parallel (DMP) over Ethernet. For other clusters, it uses InfiniBand (`-pib`).
When using the "Multinode (by node, Narval)" Slurm script, what are the distinct Fluent execution commands for single-node versus multi-node simulations?

For single-node simulations, the "Multinode (by node, Narval)" script executes Fluent using `fluent -g $MYVERSION -t $NCORES -mpi=openmpi -pshmem -i $MYJOURNALFILE` for shared memory parallel. For multi-node simulations, it first exports `FI_PROVIDER=verbs` and then executes Fluent using `fluent -g $MYVERSION -t $NCORES -mpi=openmpi -pib -cnf=/tmp/machinefile-$SLURM_JOB_ID -i $MYJOURNALFILE` for distributed memory parallel via InfiniBand.
What are the common configurations for Slurm scripts used to run Ansys Fluent in multinode environments on the Narval cluster with Open MPI?

Slurm scripts for Ansys Fluent on the Narval cluster using Open MPI typically include `StdEnv/2023` and `ansys/2023R2` (or newer) module loads. They export `OPENMPI_ROOT=$EBROOTOPENMPI`, specify a journal file (`MYJOURNALFILE`) and Fluent version (`MYVERSION`), and generate a machinefile using `slurm_hl2hl.py`. The `fluent` command is executed with `-mpi=openmpi`. For multinode execution, the `FI_PROVIDER=verbs` environment variable is set, and `-pib -cnf=/tmp/machinefile-$SLURM_JOB_ID` is used, whereas single node runs use `-pshmem`.
What Slurm directives are used to allocate resources in the 'Multinode (by core, Narval)' script for Ansys Fluent?

The 'Multinode (by core, Narval)' Slurm script for Ansys Fluent allocates resources using the following directives: `--account=def-group` for the account, `--time=00-03:00` for the time limit, `--ntasks=16` to specify the total number of cores across all nodes, `--mem-per-cpu=4G` for memory per core, and `--cpus-per-task=1`. The script also indicates that `--nodes=1` can be uncommented to specify the number of compute nodes.
How does the 'Multinode (by node, Narval)' Slurm script for Ansys Fluent differentiate its `fluent` command execution based on whether it's running on a single node or multiple nodes?

In the 'Multinode (by node, Narval)' Slurm script for Ansys Fluent, if the job is running on a single node (`$SLURM_NNODES == 1`), the `fluent` command uses `fluent -g $MYVERSION -t $NCORES -mpi=openmpi -pshmem -i $MYJOURNALFILE`. If running on multiple nodes, it first exports `FI_PROVIDER=verbs` and then executes `fluent -g $MYVERSION -t $NCORES -mpi=openmpi -pib -cnf=/tmp/machinefile-$SLURM_JOB_ID -i $MYJOURNALFILE`.
How are Fluent jobs executed on the Narval cluster when using the provided scripts?
On the Narval cluster, Fluent jobs are executed using Open MPI. For single-node jobs, `pshmem` is used, while multi-node jobs utilize `pib` and a machinefile generated from Slurm host list.
Which Ansys Fluent module version is necessary for running jobs on the Trillium cluster?
Only Ansys module versions 2025R2 or newer, such as `ansys/2025R2.04`, are compatible for running Fluent jobs on the Trillium cluster.
What steps must a user take if there are missing links to writable Ansys configuration directories or files when running Fluent on Trillium?

If links to writable Ansys configuration directories (like `~/.ansys` or `~/.fluentconf`) or files (like `~/.flrecent`) are missing in the home directory on Trillium, the user must remove any existing ones and then create symbolic links from the home directory to the `$SCRATCH` directory (e.g., `ln -s $SCRATCH/.ansys ~/.ansys`).
What are the specific requirements for the `.fluentconf` directory and `.flrecent` file when running Fluent jobs on the Trillium cluster, and how are errors related to their configuration resolved?

On the Trillium cluster, the `.fluentconf` directory and `.flrecent` file in a user's home directory must be symbolic links pointing to writable locations within their `$SCRATCH` space. If these links are missing, an error will occur, and users are instructed to remove any existing directories or files with those names and then create the symbolic links using commands such as `ln -s $SCRATCH/.fluentconf ~/.fluentconf` and `ln -s $SCRATCH/.flrecent ~/.flrecent` before resubmitting their job.
What is the primary function of the "License requeue" scripts for Fluent jobs, and under what conditions should they be used?

The "License requeue" scripts for Fluent jobs are specifically designed to automatically resubmit simulations that frequently fail to start because of a temporary unavailability of licences. These scripts are appropriate for jobs that are known to complete normally without errors once they commence, but which typically require several submission attempts to acquire the necessary licences.
When should Fluent's "License requeue" scripts not be used, and what are the potential negative outcomes of using them in those situations?

Fluent's "License requeue" scripts are not recommended for jobs that might run for an extended period before crashing or for jobs that complete with unresolved warnings in their journal file. Misusing these scripts in such cases will lead to the simulation repeating from the beginning up to the maximum number of specified requeue attempts, ultimately resulting in wasted compute time.
What is the purpose of the `SBATCH --array` directive in the `script-flu-bycore+requeue.sh` Slurm script when running an Ansys Fluent job?

The `SBATCH --array=1-5%1` directive in the `script-flu-bycore+requeue.sh` Slurm script is used to specify a job array, which enables the automatic requeueing of an Ansys Fluent job. This functionality is primarily intended for jobs that frequently fail to start due to license shortages, allowing for multiple attempts (e.g., up to 5 attempts as shown) to acquire a license without manual resubmission.
How does the `script-flu-bycore+requeue.sh` Slurm script configure resources for an Ansys Fluent job running on an Alliance cluster?

The `script-flu-bycore+requeue.sh` Slurm script configures resources using several `SBATCH` directives: `--time=00-03:00` sets a time limit of 3 hours; `--ntasks=16` specifies a total of 16 cores across all allocated nodes; `--mem-per-cpu=4G` allocates 4 GB of memory for each core; and `--cpus-per-task=1` indicates that each task uses one CPU. The script also loads the `StdEnv/2023` and `ansys/2023R2` modules, and defines the journal file (`MYJOURNALFILE=sample.jou`) and Fluent version (`MYVERSION=3d`) for the simulation. Fluent is then executed using the specified number of cores and an appropriate Intel MPI configuration, adapting for single-node or multi-node execution.
What is the primary purpose of the solution restart scripts for Ansys Fluent jobs on clusters?

The solution restart scripts are provided to automate restarting very large Ansys Fluent jobs that require more than the typical seven-day maximum runtime window available on most clusters. Jobs are restarted from the most recently saved timestep files.
What are the fundamental requirements and initial setup steps for utilizing Fluent solution restart scripts for long-running jobs?

A fundamental requirement is that the first timestep must be completed within the requested job array time limit when starting a simulation from an initialized solution field. To begin, a working set of `sample.cas`, `sample.dat`, and `sample.jou` files must be present.
How should a Fluent journal file be modified to enable solution restarts, and what is the strategy to optimize the restart process?

To enable solution restarts, first edit your `sample.jou` file to contain `/solve/dual-time-iterate 1` and `/file/auto-save/data-frequency 1`. Then, create a restart journal file by copying `sample.jou` to `sample-restart.jou` and editing `sample-restart.jou` to contain `/file/read-cas-data sample-restart` instead of `/file/read-cas-data sample`. Also, comment out the initialization line (e.g., `; /solve/initialize/initialize-flow`). To optimize the process, if your second and subsequent timesteps are known to run twice as fast as the initial timestep, add `/solve/dual-time-iterate 2` to the `sample-restart.jou` file. This minimizes the number of solution restarts, which are computationally expensive, by allowing more timesteps to complete per restart.
Why are specific instructions provided for running parallel Ansys jobs on Alliance clusters?
Specific instructions are needed because the MPI implementations included with the Ansys software suite do not support the Alliance clusters' Slurm scheduler.
What is the typical procedure for preparing and submitting an Ansys Fluent job to an Alliance cluster?
Users typically prepare the job on a desktop, export case and data files, transfer them to a `/project` or `/scratch` directory, create a journal file, and then submit the job using a Slurm script.
When running Ansys Fluent on Alliance clusters, what is the primary recommendation for Slurm script usage to optimize performance?
The 'by node' script is generally recommended to minimize solution latency and maximize performance, especially when using as few nodes as possible.
What are the best practices for configuring mesh partitioning in Ansys Fluent jobs for optimal efficiency on Alliance clusters?
The number of mesh partitions should be an integral multiple of the number of cores, and for optimal efficiency, ensure at least 10,000 cells per core.
What unique setup steps are required for Trillium users submitting Ansys Fluent jobs?
Trillium users must ensure that writable symbolic links exist for `~/.ansys`, `~/.fluentconf`, and `~/.flrecent`, pointing to directories within their `/scratch` space, before submitting jobs.
When is it appropriate to use 'license requeue' scripts for Ansys Fluent jobs, and what cautionary measure should be taken?

These scripts are suitable for jobs known to complete normally but frequently fail to start due to license shortages. Users must monitor Slurm output to confirm requeues are license-related, as other failures will also trigger costly repetitions.
How do 'solution restart' scripts extend the runtime for large Ansys Fluent jobs on Alliance clusters?
They automate the process of restarting simulations from the most recently saved timestep files, allowing jobs to run beyond typical maximum Slurm time limits, such as seven days.
How can users configure Ansys Fluent journal files to change simulation parameters and specify output file formats?

Journal files can include any Fluent Text User Interface (TUI) command to modify parameters. The command `/file/cff-files no` or `/file/cff-files yes` specifies whether to use legacy (.cas/.dat) or more efficient (.cas.h5/.dat.h5) file formats, respectively.
What critical steps are involved in preparing and using User-Defined Functions (UDFs) with Ansys Fluent on an Alliance cluster?

Users must transfer the UDF source file using text mode, add specific commands to the journal file before reading case/data files, and ensure the UDF is parallelized with compiler directives, predicates, and reduction macros if used in parallel. Compiled UDFs must be built on an Alliance cluster.
What are some important command-line options available for `cfx5solve` in Ansys CFX, and how can users find more information?

Important options include `-single` (default precision), `-double` (for double precision, doubles memory), and `-large` (for meshes up to 2 billion elements). A full list can be obtained by running `cfx5solve -help`.
What is the mandatory initialization procedure for Ansys Workbench jobs on an Alliance cluster before submitting them via Slurm?

Users must start an OnDemand desktop, navigate to the project directory, remove `_ProjectScratch`, load the Ansys module, open the project GUI with `runwb2`, reset the Model, save, exit without saving modifications, and then quit Workbench.
Can Ansys Workbench simulations be run directly from the GUI on Alliance clusters, and what are the advantages?

Yes, compute nodes can be reserved for OnDemand desktop sessions, allowing simulations to run directly from the Workbench native GUI, which offers a more intuitive option than submitting jobs via Slurm scripts.
How do users obtain an input file for an Ansys Mechanical (APDL) job from an interactive Workbench Mechanical session?
Within an interactive Workbench Mechanical session, users can click on `Solution -> Tools -> Write Input Files`, then specify a file name and save it as an APDL Input File (*.inp).
What type of parallelization is generally preferred for Ansys Mechanical (APDL) jobs on Alliance clusters, and why?
Shared memory parallel (SMP) scripts typically perform better than distributed memory parallel (DMP) scripts and should be used whenever possible.
How do users control whether an Ansys Rocky simulation starts from the beginning or resumes from a partially completed state?
In the Slurm script, users set the `RESUME` variable to `0` to start from the beginning (which removes previous results) or `1` to restart a partially completed simulation.
What is a significant performance consideration for running Ansys Rocky simulations on Alliance clusters?
GPU-based scripts have been found to significantly outperform CPU-only scripts for basic test cases, suggesting faster solution times when GPUs are utilized. Users on Narval should request a100 GPUs.
Where can users find specific Slurm scripts for Ansys Electronics Desktop (AnsysEDT) on Alliance clusters?
Slurm scripts for AnsysEDT are provided on a dedicated page titled 'AnsysEDT'.
What defines a serial task in the context of job submission to a computing cluster, and what is the correct way to request CPU resources for it?

A serial task is a job that executes on a single processor or compute core at a time, without parallelism, following a strictly sequential process. To correctly request CPU resources for such a task, you should specify `--cpus-per-task=1` in your job submission script.
What happens if a user requests multiple cores, for example, 8, for a serial task, and how can this resource wastage be corrected for both CPU and memory allocation?

If a user requests multiple cores (e.g., 8) for a serial task, only one core will be actively utilized, leading to 7 wasted cores, as shown on the CPU graph where only one core is active. For memory, requesting `--mem-per-cpu=32G` with 8 cores will allocate 256 GB, but typically only about 4 GB will be used. The recommended correction is to set `--cpus-per-task=1` and adjust the memory request, for instance, to `--mem-per-cpu=6G`.
How can you determine if a submitted job is wasting GPU resources by requesting a GPU but not using it?

You can determine this by checking the GPU usage graphs, specifically the 'GPU - Cycle de calcul GPU utilisé' (GPU Compute Cycle Used) graph. If the GPU remains unused, it will show no activity or data recorded for metrics like SM Active or SM Occupancy.
