What is CephFS and where is it currently available on Alliance clusters?
CephFS (Ceph File System) is a filesystem with Ceph storage that allows data to be mounted simultaneously on multiple OpenStack instances. It is currently only available with Arbutus.
How does an Alliance compute cloud differ from a persistent cloud?

Compute clouds are resources for OpenStack instances intended to run for a limited time with very high sustained CPU and memory usage (flavours beginning with c*), while persistent clouds are for virtual machines expected to run indefinitely with low or bursty CPU requirements (flavours beginning with p*).

What steps should a user take if they are unable to log in to the cloud service?

If you are unable to log in to the cloud service, first ensure you have applied for and been granted a cloud project. Once approved, verify you are logging into the correct cloud as specified in your confirmation email, and that you are using your username (the same as for an HPC cluster), not your email address. Check the system status page for any incidents affecting the service. If your password is rejected, reset it using the provided link. If these steps do not resolve the issue, submit a ticket to cloud@tech.alliancecan.ca with your username, project name, the cloud you are trying to access, and a description of the steps you've already taken.
What are the initial troubleshooting steps if a virtual machine fails to launch in the cloud service?

If a virtual machine (VM) fails to launch, first check if the launch would exceed your project's resource limits (quotas) for VMs, CPUs, or RAM. You can do this by logging into your cloud dashboard, navigating to 'Compute,' then 'Overview.' If you encounter an error message like 'No valid host was found,' ensure that the 'Availability Zone' for the instance is set to 'Any Availability Zone' rather than a manually selected one. If the problem persists after these steps, submit a ticket to cloud@tech.alliancecan.ca.
What should a user do if they encounter an "Error: No valid host was found" message when trying to launch a virtual machine (VM) with a specific availability zone?

If you receive this "not enough hosts" error and require a particular availability zone, you should send an email to cloud@tech.alliancecan.ca. Be sure to include the cloud name, project name, the troubleshooting steps you have taken thus far, and the reason why you need that specific availability zone.
What are the initial troubleshooting steps if a user cannot connect to their virtual machine (VM) or a service running on it?

First, check the System Status page to see if there is an incident affecting your hosting cloud. If an incident is reported, wait for it to be resolved before trying to connect again. If there's no incident, try logging in to the OpenStack dashboard for your cloud project. If you cannot reach the login page for your cloud, verify your internet connectivity; if you have connectivity but still can't reach the login page, submit a ticket to cloud@tech.alliancecan.ca.
How can a user verify if their virtual machine (VM) is running from the cloud dashboard and what actions can be taken if it isn't?

After logging in to your cloud dashboard, navigate to the "Instances" screen from the left-side menu. Look at the "Power State" for your VM; it should be "Running". If it's not (e.g., "Shut Down"), try to restart it using the "Actions" menu on the right-hand side by selecting "Start Instance" or "Resume Instance". You should also check the "Action Log" and "log" tabs from the instance's details screen for any error messages that might explain why it was taken out of the running state.
What is the default setting for the "Availability Zone" when launching a virtual machine instance in the cloud service?
The default setting for the "Availability Zone" is "Any Availability Zone," which allows OpenStack to automatically choose a zone for your virtual machine instance.
How can manually selecting an Availability Zone cause a "not enough hosts" error when launching a virtual machine instance?
If you manually select an Availability Zone instead of using the default option, you may encounter a "not enough hosts" error because there might not be enough hosts available in that specific zone.
How can a user resolve the "not enough hosts" error if it appears when trying to launch a virtual machine instance due to an Availability Zone selection?
To fix this error, the user should set the "Availability Zone" back to "Any Availability Zone" in the "Details" section when launching the instance.
How can I connect to my virtual machine (VM) using SSH if I cannot reach it and the VM is running?

If you are unable to connect to your virtual machine after following prior troubleshooting steps (1-4) and confirm that your VM is running, you should attempt to connect using SSH. You can find detailed instructions for connecting to your VM with SSH in the "Connecting to your VM with SSH" section, located near the bottom of the Cloud Quick Start Guide page.
If I receive a login prompt when attempting to connect to my virtual machine via SSH, what should I verify regarding my credentials and system settings?

If you encounter a login prompt when connecting to your virtual machine via SSH, you need to verify that you are using the correct key pair and username. To check which key pair you should be using, navigate to the OpenStack dashboard, click "Compute" on the left-side menu, then "Instances", and look at the "Key Pair" column. The correct username depends on the operating system of your VM: 'debian' for Debian, 'ubuntu' for Ubuntu, 'almalinux' for AlmaLinux, 'centos' for CentOS, and 'fedora' for Fedora. This information applies unless you have explicitly changed your username with a custom CloudInit script.
What are the standard usernames required to connect to virtual machines (VMs) via SSH for various operating systems on the cloud service?

For SSH connections, the standard usernames are 'debian' for Debian, 'ubuntu' for Ubuntu, 'almalinux' for AlmaLinux, 'centos' for CentOS, and 'fedora' for Fedora. If a custom CloudInit script was used to alter the username, that modified username should be used instead.
When experiencing difficulties connecting to a virtual machine (VM) via SSH, how can a user verify and adjust their security group settings on the cloud service?

First, verify your current IP address and confirm it is permitted in the security settings. If your IP has changed, you must add a new rule to your VM's Security Group. Ensure there is an 'Ingress' rule for 'TCP' protocol on 'Port Range 22 (SSH)' that includes your IP address. If this rule is absent, add it by selecting SSH and entering your IP address followed by /32 in the CIDR field.
What are the primary reasons a user might encounter difficulties when attempting to delete a volume on the cloud service, and what troubleshooting steps are recommended?

A common reason a volume cannot be deleted is if it is currently attached to a running virtual machine (VM); it must first be detached. Another reason is the presence of snapshots; all snapshots of the volume must be deleted before the source volume can be removed. If the volume is detached but still shows an 'In-use' status, or if these steps do not resolve the issue, it is recommended to submit a support ticket including the username, project name, cloud name, and volume UUID.

What is the primary purpose of using Transport Layer Security (TLS) and Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) for web communication?

TLS and SSL enable encrypted communications over computer networks. Their primary purpose is to protect sensitive information, such as passwords, sent over the internet, and to prevent third parties from intercepting or modifying data transmitted between a web server and a client, even if the information isn't sensitive.
What are the two main types of SSL certificates, and for what situations is each type typically recommended?

The two main types are certificates signed by a third-party signing authority and self-signed certificates. Third-party signed certificates, often easily obtained through services like Let's Encrypt, are recommended for public-facing sites because the third party vouches for the web server's validity, helping to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. Self-signed certificates are useful for testing or small, locally used sites, but they are not recommended for public-facing sites as visitors will receive a security warning because no third party vouches for the server's validity.
How does Certbot assist with managing SSL certificates?

Certbot is a tool that automatically creates or renews SSL certificates signed by the Let's Encrypt Certificate Authority (CA). It also automatically configures your web server to use the SSL certificate, streamlining the process of securing a website.
What modifications are necessary in Apache's `default-ssl.conf` file to configure it to use a newly created self-signed SSL certificate?

To configure Apache to use a self-signed SSL certificate, you must edit the `/etc/apache2/sites-available/default-ssl.conf` file. Specifically, change the `SSLCertificateFile` and `SSLCertificateKeyFile` lines to point to `/etc/ssl/certs/server.crt` and `/etc/ssl/private/server.key` respectively. Additionally, ensure both `default-ssl.conf` and `000-default.conf` have the same `DocumentRoot` variables.
After configuring a self-signed SSL certificate on an Apache web server, what steps should be taken to tighten security, including forcing HTTP traffic to HTTPS?

To tighten security, first edit `/etc/apache2/sites-available/default-ssl.conf` and add `ServerName XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX.cloud.computecanada.ca`, `SSLProtocol all -SSLv2 -SSLv3`, `SSLCipherSuite HIGH:MEDIUM:!aNULL:!MD5:!SEED:!IDEA:!RC4`, and `SSLHonorCipherOrder on` inside the `<VirtualHost>` tag, replacing `XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX` with your VM's public IP. Secondly, edit `/etc/apache2/sites-available/000-default.conf` and add the line `Redirect permanent / https://XXX-XXX-XXX-XXX.cloud.computecanada.ca` inside its `<VirtualHost>` tag to force all HTTP traffic to HTTPS.
Once Apache is configured with a self-signed SSL certificate, how do you enable the SSL-enabled website and apply the changes?

What are the general steps to install the Apache web server on an Ubuntu Linux virtual machine in a cloud environment?

How can the Apache web server's root directory be changed from the default `/var/www/html` to a user's home directory, such as `/home/ubuntu/public_html`, on an Ubuntu VM for easier website management?

How do you install the Apache bandwidth module (`mod_bw`) to limit bandwidth on a web server?

How is the Apache bandwidth module (`mod_bw`) configured to limit total bandwidth from all clients to 100 Mbps?


What database servers does the Alliance currently provide to researchers, and what are the future plans for database server availability on the Graham cluster?

The Alliance offers access to MySQL and Postgres database servers for researchers on both the Cedar and Graham clusters. However, as of January 13, 2025, the Graham cluster will no longer provide a database server during its transition to the new Nibi system, due to a reduction in capacity.
How can a researcher request a MySQL account on the Cedar server?

To get a MySQL account on the Cedar MySQL server, researchers must send a request to Technical Support. The request needs to include their Alliance username and the amount of database space required for their project.
What is the naming convention for creating a MySQL database on the Cedar server?
When creating a MySQL database on the Cedar server, the name of the database is arbitrary but it must start with "username_" where "username" is your MySQL username.
What are the guidelines for running SQL commands or scripts that consume significant CPU on the Cedar MySQL server?

It is acceptable to submit a long-running SQL command from the head node, as most of the CPU usage is taken from the database server side. However, if you run a script which issues SQL commands and uses lots of CPU, then it needs to be submitted as a job to the scheduler.
How do users create MySQL databases on the Cedar cluster, and what are the naming conventions for these databases?

Users can create multiple MySQL databases on the Cedar cluster. The name of each database must start with the user's MySQL username followed by an underscore (e.g., if the username is "david", a database name must begin with "david_"). For instance, to create a database named "david_db1", the command would be `CREATE DATABASE david_db1;`. These databases are automatically accessible only to the user from the Cedar head node, Cedar compute nodes, and the Cedar Portal.
What is the procedure for sharing a specific table from a MySQL database on the Cedar cluster with another user?

To share a table from your MySQL database on the Cedar cluster, you first connect to MySQL using the `mysql` command. Then, use `USE <database_name>;` to specify the database containing the table you want to share. Finally, run the command `GRANT <priv_type> ON <mytable> TO '<user>'@'172.%';`, replacing `<priv_type>` with the type of privilege (e.g., `SELECT` for read-only), `<mytable>` with the table name, and `<user>` with the username of the person you're sharing with. For example, to grant 'SELECT' access on 'mytable' from 'david_db' to 'john', the commands would be `USE david_db;` followed by `GRANT SELECT on mytable to 'john'@'172.%';`.
How does a researcher obtain a PostgreSQL account and database on the Cedar cluster, and what information needs to be provided in the request?

To obtain a PostgreSQL account and database on the Cedar cluster, a researcher must send a request to Technical Support. The request needs to include their Alliance username, the amount of database space required for their project, and whether they need the PostGIS extension for the database. How can a user on the Cedar cluster share their PostgreSQL database or specific tables with another user?

The database owner then needs to grant `connect` access to their database to the other user, and for each specific table or view they wish to share, they must grant one or more privileges such as `select`, `update`, `insert`, or `delete` access. What is the required method for connecting to PostgreSQL and MariaDB/MySQL instances provided by the Alliance's Cloud-based Database as a Service (DBaaS), and why is it important?

What is OpenStack, and what are its primary functions and use cases?

OpenStack is a software suite used on our clouds to control hardware resources such as computers, storage, and networking. Its primary functions include the creation and management of virtual machines (VMs or instances) through software emulation, providing complete control over the computing environment, from choosing an operating system to software installation and configuration. Diverse use cases are supported, ranging from hosting websites to creating virtual clusters.
In OpenStack, what is the purpose of a project, and how are projects and their quotas managed?

OpenStack projects group virtual machines (VMs) together and provide a quota from which VMs and related resources can be created. Each project is unique to a particular cloud, and all accounts that are members of a project have the same level of permissions. Projects are considered owned by primary investigators (PIs), who are the only ones who can request new projects or quota adjustments. Requests for access to an existing project must also be confirmed by the owning PI.
What is a security group in OpenStack, and what rules are typically included in the default security group?

A security group in OpenStack is a set of rules used to control network traffic into and out of your virtual machines. The default security group contains rules that allow a VM to access outside networks, for example, to download operating system upgrades, but it does not allow other machines to access it, except for other VMs belonging to the same default security group. Specifically, it includes two egress rules (one for IPv4 and one for IPv6) to allow outbound access, and two ingress rules (one for IPv4 and one for IPv6) to allow communication among VMs within that security group.

How can new users, along with their SSH keys and sudo permissions, be added to an OpenStack virtual machine during its initial launch using cloudInit, and what crucial considerations should be kept in mind?

Users can be added during VM creation by pasting a cloudInit script into the 'Customization Script' field of the OpenStack dashboard. The script, formatted in YAML, specifies user names, shell, SSH public keys, and whether they have sudo access (e.g., `sudo: ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL`). It's crucial to note that if the `users:` section doesn't include `- default`, the script will overwrite any default users normally created by the operating system, making the listed users the *only* ones on the VM. Therefore, at least one user with sudo permission is vital. To preserve default users while adding new ones, explicitly include `- default` in the script.
What is CIDR, or Classless Inter-Domain Routing, and how is it used in OpenStack security rules to specify IP address ranges?

CIDR, or Classless Inter-Domain Routing, is a standardized method for defining IP address ranges in OpenStack security rules. It appends a `/XX` (e.g., `/24`) to an IP address, indicating how many of the leftmost bits of an IP address must match for the rule to apply. For instance, `192.168.1.1/24` means any IP address starting with `192.168.1` will match. A `/32` ensures an exact IP address match, while a `/0` means no bits must match, effectively allowing any IP address.
What are the default rules typically included in a new OpenStack security group, and what is the recommended approach for modifying or adding to these rules?

The default OpenStack security group includes two Egress rules (one for IPV4 and one for IPV6) that allow your instance to access outside networks without limitation. It also includes two Ingress rules (one for IPV4 and one for IPV6) that permit communication among all VMs belonging to the same security group. It is generally recommended not to remove these default rules as doing so can cause issues when creating new VMs. However, it is safe and common practice to add new rules to the default security group, such as those required for SSH or RDP access.
What is the primary function of the default security group for a virtual machine?

The default security group enables a virtual machine (VM) to access the internet for tasks such as downloading operating system upgrades or installing packages. It also facilitates communication among other VMs within the same default security group, while preventing access from external machines.
Why is it recommended not to remove rules from the default security group?
It is recommended not to remove rules from the default security group because doing so may cause problems when creating new virtual machines (VMs).
What types of rules are typically included in a default security group?

A default security group typically includes two Egress rules, one for IPv4 and one for IPv6, to allow the virtual machine access to an outside network. It also includes two Ingress rules, one for IPv4 and one for IPv6, to permit communication among all virtual machines belonging to that same security group.
What is important to remember about YAML formatting when creating cloudInit scripts for virtual machines?
YAML is very particular about white space formatting, so you must include a space after the hyphen before your public key string in a cloudInit script.
What happens to the default user if a custom cloudInit script is specified during the creation of a new virtual machine?

If a custom cloudInit script is specified, it overwrites the default user that would normally be added, meaning only the users explicitly listed in your configuration script will be present on the newly created virtual machine.
When defining users with a cloudInit script for a new virtual machine, what is a vital consideration regarding user permissions?

It is vital to ensure that at least one user defined in the cloudInit script has sudo permissions, as the script overwrites default users, making the listed users the only ones on the new virtual machine.
How can I add new users to a virtual machine using cloudInit while preserving the existing default distribution user?

To add new users while keeping the default user (such as `debian`, `centos`, or `ubuntu`) on a virtual machine, you should include `- default` under the `users:` section in your `cloud-config` script, followed by the new user definitions.
What details should be included when defining new users in a cloudInit script for a virtual machine, specifically regarding SSH keys and permissions?

When defining new users in a `cloud-config` script, you should specify the user's `name`, `shell` (e.g., `/bin/bash`), `sudo` permissions (e.g., `ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL` for sudo access), and their `ssh_authorized_keys` as a list of public keys.
After a virtual machine has launched with a cloudInit script to add new users, how can I confirm that the public keys for those users were correctly added?

To confirm that public keys for new users have been correctly added after a VM launches, navigate to the "Compute->Instances" panel, click on the instance name, and then select the "log" tab. The log should display `ci-info` messages indicating that the authorized keys have been set up for each user.

In OpenStack, what is the 'dashboard' and what OpenStack sub-project developed it?
The 'dashboard' is the web browser user interface used to manage cloud resources, developed under an OpenStack sub-project referred to as Horizon.
What is the purpose of 'projects' in OpenStack and how do they relate to user permissions and resources?

OpenStack projects group VMs together and provide a quota for creating VMs and related resources. All accounts that are members of a project have the same level of permissions, meaning anyone can create or delete a VM within that project if they are a member.
Who can request new OpenStack projects or quota adjustments, and who confirms access to existing projects?

New projects and quota adjustments can only be requested by primary investigators (PIs), who are also considered the owners of the projects. Requests for access to an existing project must be confirmed by the PI owning that project.
What are availability zones in OpenStack and how do they differ across Alliance clouds like Beluga, Graham, and Arbutus?

Availability zones in OpenStack allow users to specify the group of physical hardware their VM will run on. Beluga and Graham clouds have only one zone, 'nova', while Arbutus has three: 'Compute', 'Nova', and 'Persistent'.
What is an advantage of using two persistent availability zones on the Arbutus cloud?

An advantage of using two persistent zones on the Arbutus cloud is to ensure continuous availability, for example, by running two instances of a website in different zones, so if one site goes down, the other remains operational.
What is an OpenStack security group, and where can users manage them?

An OpenStack security group is a set of rules that control network traffic into and out of virtual machines. Users can manage security groups by navigating to 'Project->Network->Security Groups' in the dashboard.
What are the default rules of an OpenStack security group, and is it recommended to remove them?

The default security group allows VMs access out to the internet (2 Egress rules for IPv4/IPv6) and permits communication between VMs within the same security group (2 Ingress rules for IPv4/IPv6). It is not recommended to remove rules from the default security group as this may cause problems when creating new VMs.
When managing OpenStack security groups, what general principles should users consider for ingress rules?
When managing security groups, users should carefully consider what needs to be accessed and who needs to access it, striving to minimize the IP addresses and ports in their Ingress rules.
What does CIDR stand for, and how are CIDR rules used in OpenStack security groups?

CIDR stands for Classless Inter-Domain Routing, a standardized way of defining IP ranges. In OpenStack security groups, CIDR rules are used to specify the allowed IP or IP range for network traffic, such as '192.168.1.1/24' to match any IP address starting with 192.168.1.
What is cloudInit, and when can it be used to customize an OpenStack instance?

cloudInit is a tool used to customize an OpenStack instance the first time it is launched. This can be done either via the OpenStack command-line interface or by pasting a cloudInit script into the 'Customization Script' field in the OpenStack dashboard.
How can users add new user accounts with or without sudo permissions to an OpenStack VM during its creation using a cloudInit script?

Users can add new user accounts by including a YAML-formatted cloudInit script during VM creation, specifying usernames, shells, and SSH authorized keys. Sudo permissions can be granted by adding `sudo: ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL` under a user's configuration.
When using cloudInit to add users, how can the default distribution user (e.g., debian, centos, ubuntu) be preserved?
To preserve the default distribution user when adding new users via cloudInit, users should include `- default` as the first entry under the `users:` section in their cloudInit script.
How can a user verify if public SSH keys have been correctly added for new users configured via cloudInit on an OpenStack VM?

After the VM has finished spawning, users can verify if public SSH keys have been added correctly by checking the instance's log. This log is accessible by clicking on the instance name on the 'Compute->Instances' panel and then selecting the 'log' tab, which should display information about authorized keys.
How do you create a new user account on an Ubuntu virtual machine (VM)?

To create a new user account on an Ubuntu VM, use the command `sudo adduser --disabled-password USERNAME`. Additionally, the new user will require a key pair, and their public key must be added to `/home/USERNAME/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the VM, ensuring correct permissions and ownership.
How can administrative or root user privileges be granted to a new user on an Ubuntu virtual machine (VM)?

On an Ubuntu VM, administrative or root user privileges can be granted by using the command `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/90-cloud-init-users`. This command opens an editor where you can add a line similar to `USERNAME ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL`.

This document provides assistance with common tasks for managing Linux virtual machines (VMs).
Which operating systems are primarily discussed for VM management in this document?
The document primarily focuses on the Linux Operating System for VMs, but also mentions Microsoft Windows.
What are some common Linux distributions used on VMs, as mentioned in the document?

What is required for a new user to connect to a Linux VM after their account has been created?
The new user will need to have a key pair, and their public key must be added to `/home/USERNAME/.ssh/authorized_keys` on the VM with correct permissions and ownership.
What is the command to grant administrative or root user privileges to a new user on an Ubuntu Linux VM?
Administrative privileges can be granted by using the command `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/90-cloud-init-users` and adding a specific line to the opened editor.
What line should be added to the sudoers file using `visudo` to grant a user full administrative privileges without requiring a password on an Ubuntu Linux VM?
The line `USERNAME ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL` should be added to the sudoers file to grant a user full administrative privileges without a password.
Where can users find guidance on recovering data from a compromised VM?
Users can find guidance on recovering data from a compromised VM in the 'Recovering data from a compromised VM' guide.
How can a VM be recovered from the dashboard?

Yes, the document links to guides for 'generating SSH keys in Windows' and 'creating a key pair in Linux or Mac'.
What is the primary method for a virtual machine hosted on the Cloud to access `/project` filesystems on national HPC clusters?

VMs hosted on the Cloud do not have direct access to the filesystems on the national HPC clusters; to access `/project` files from a VM, users must utilize SSHFS, which mounts the `/project` folder inside the virtual machine.
What are the key security requirements to observe when using SSHFS to mount a `/project` folder inside a virtual machine?

When using SSHFS to mount a `/project` folder inside a VM, it is required not to store passwords in plain text, to create an SSH key specifically for SSHFS use only (not reusing login keys), and to keep the VM updated while only opening required and secured ports.
What is the main purpose of this document regarding virtual machines and file systems?
This document describes how to let a virtual machine (VM) access /project filesystems on national systems, specifically when hosted on the Alliance Cloud.
What method is recommended to access files stored on /project from a virtual machine?
To access files stored on /project from a virtual machine, users should use SSHFS.
What functionality does SSHFS provide for virtual machines?
SSHFS enables mounting your /project folder inside your virtual machine, making it appear like a regular folder that can be accessed via standard Linux commands.
Where can users find a reference for SSHFS?
A reference for SSHFS can be found at https://wiki.archlinux.org/index.php/SSHFS.
Why are specific requirements necessary when mounting /project inside a virtual machine using SSHFS?
Specific requirements are needed to avoid security issues when mounting /project inside a virtual machine using SSHFS.
What is the security requirement regarding storing passwords on a virtual machine when using SSHFS?
Users must not store their password in plain text on the virtual machine.
What is the requirement for SSH key usage when setting up SSHFS for a virtual machine?
Users must create an SSH key specifically for use with SSHFS, use it only for that purpose, and not reuse the same SSH key used for logging in.
What maintenance practices are required for a virtual machine that uses SSHFS to access /project?
The virtual machine must be kept up to date, and only required and secured ports should be open.
How do mounted SSHFS folders appear and function within a virtual machine?
SSHFS mounts appear like regular folders in the virtual machine and can be accessed via regular Linux commands.
What is the Alliance Nextcloud service and what are its primary features?

The Alliance Nextcloud service is a Dropbox-like encrypted cloud storage service provided for all Alliance users. Users can log in with their Alliance username and password at https://nextcloud.computecanada.ca/. It offers a fixed quota of 100 GB per user, daily backups without an offsite copy, and is hosted at Simon Fraser University in Burnaby, BC. Access is available via a web interface, Nextcloud Desktop Sync Client, Nextcloud mobile apps, and any WebDAV client.
What are the main differences between the Alliance Nextcloud and SHARCNET Nextcloud services?

While both Alliance and SHARCNET Nextcloud services offer 100 GB per user and similar access methods, they differ in several ways. The Alliance Nextcloud server is located at Simon Fraser University, Burnaby, BC, with a daily backup without offsite copy. SHARCNET's Nextcloud server is located at the University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON, with daily backups to a tape library. Additionally, SHARCNET's Nextcloud can be mounted directly on the Nibi cluster, and researchers can request a quota increase by contacting help@sharcnet.ca.
Which methods can users employ to access their files on the Alliance Nextcloud service?

Users can access their files on the Alliance Nextcloud service through several methods: using the web interface via a browser, installing the Nextcloud Desktop Sync Client to synchronize data between their computer and Nextcloud, utilizing Nextcloud mobile apps, or connecting with any WebDAV client to mount the Nextcloud folder on their computer.
What are the key distinctions between using a WebDAV client and a Synchronization client to access Alliance Nextcloud storage, including their respective advantages?

A WebDAV client mounts your Nextcloud storage directly on your computer, meaning files are not copied locally and any edits are made directly on the original file on the Alliance Nextcloud system at Simon Fraser University. This method requires continuous network connectivity. Conversely, a Synchronization client initially copies all your Nextcloud files to a local folder on your computer, allowing you to work on files offline. When network connectivity is re-established, changes are re-copied to all synchronized systems to ensure consistency, though this process can be time-consuming if files are changed frequently.
How can a user configure and use the `rclone` command-line utility to upload and download files to Nextcloud, and what is its primary advantage over `curl`?

To use `rclone`, first ensure it is installed on your computer or utilize the version available on Alliance clusters. Then, configure a remote storage device profile by running `rclone config`. You'll select 'New remote', name it (e.g., 'nextcloud'), choose 'WebDAV' as the storage type, provide the URL `https://nextcloud.computecanada.ca/remote.php/dav/files/<your CCDB username>`, specify 'Nextcloud' as the service, enter your CCDB username and password, and then save the configuration. Once configured, you can upload a file using `rclone copy /path/to/local/file nextcloud:remote/path` and download a file using `rclone copy nextcloud:remote/path/file .`. The main advantage of `rclone` over `curl` is that it allows you to create a configuration once for each remote device, storing your encrypted password, eliminating the need to re-enter service details and your password for every subsequent operation.
How do you connect to the Alliance Nextcloud service using a WebDAV client on a Mac?

On a Mac, you can connect by selecting 'Go' then 'Connect to the Server' from the Finder menu. Enter the WebDAV URL 'https://nextcloud.computecanada.ca/remote.php/webdav/' as the Server Address, click 'Connect', and then provide your Alliance username and password. This will mount a WebDAV drive on your Mac.
What is the process for mapping a WebDAV network drive to the Alliance Nextcloud service on Windows?

To map a WebDAV drive on Windows, use the 'Map Network Drive...' option. Select a drive letter, and then input the WebDAV URL 'https://nextcloud.computecanada.ca/remote.php/webdav/' into the 'Folder' field.
Are there any alternative WebDAV clients recommended for accessing Alliance Nextcloud on Mac or Windows?
Yes, Cyberduck is an alternative WebDAV client that can be used on both Mac OSX and Windows for accessing the Alliance Nextcloud service.
What is the purpose of the Nextcloud service provided for Alliance users?
The Nextcloud service for Alliance users is a Dropbox-like cloud storage service intended for users with relatively small datasets, up to 100 GB.
How do Alliance users log into the Nextcloud server?
Alliance users can log into the Nextcloud server at `https://nextcloud.computecanada.ca/` using their Alliance username and password.
What is the recommended service for Alliance users with datasets larger than 100 GB?
For datasets larger than 100 GB, Alliance recommends using the Globus service.
What are the key details of the Alliance Nextcloud service, including its location and fixed quota?
The Alliance Nextcloud service server is located at Simon Fraser University, Burnaby, BC, and has a fixed quota of 100 GB per user.
What is the backup policy for the Alliance Nextcloud service?
The Alliance Nextcloud service has a daily backup policy without an offsite copy.
What unique feature does the SHARCNET Nextcloud service offer compared to the general Alliance Nextcloud service?
The SHARCNET Nextcloud service can be mounted directly on the Nibi cluster, allowing users to access files without needing to transfer them manually.
How can users request additional storage beyond the default 100 GB for the SHARCNET Nextcloud service?
Users of the SHARCNET Nextcloud service requiring additional storage may submit a request for a quota increase to `help@sharcnet.ca`.
What access methods are available for the Nextcloud services provided by Alliance?
Nextcloud services can be accessed via a web interface, Nextcloud Desktop Sync Client, Nextcloud mobile apps, and any WebDAV client.
How does a WebDAV client differ from a Nextcloud Desktop Synchronization client in terms of file storage and access?

A WebDAV client mounts the Nextcloud storage, meaning files are edited directly on the server, whereas a Synchronization client copies files to the local computer and keeps them synchronized, allowing offline work.
What command-line tools can Alliance users utilize to copy files between a UNIX computer and Nextcloud?
Alliance users can use WebDAV command-line clients like `curl` and `cadaver`, or `rclone` to copy files between a UNIX computer and Nextcloud.
How can an Alliance user upload a file to Nextcloud from a UNIX-like command line using `curl`?
An Alliance user can upload a file using `curl` with the command: `curl -k -u <username> -T <filename> https://nextcloud.computecanada.ca/remote.php/webdav/`.
What is the advantage of using `rclone` for Nextcloud transfers compared to `curl`?
Unlike `curl`, `rclone` allows users to create a configuration once for a remote device, storing the password encrypted, and use it repeatedly without re-entering service details.
What specific URL is used when configuring `rclone` for the Alliance Nextcloud service?
The URL for configuring `rclone` with the Alliance Nextcloud service is `https://nextcloud.computecanada.ca/remote.php/dav/files/<your CCDB username>`.
How can Alliance users share files with other Alliance users or groups using Nextcloud?
Alliance users can share files by typing a user’s first name, last name, or username, or a CCDB group name; matched options will be displayed.
How can files be shared from Nextcloud with people who do not have an Alliance account?
Files can be shared with non-Alliance account holders by using the 'Share link' option and providing their email address, which sends them an email notification with a link to access the file.
How do you install the OpenStack command line tools on a Linux machine with administrative privileges?

The OpenStack command line tools are Python-based. For Ubuntu, run `sudo apt-get install python python-dev python-pip` followed by `sudo pip install python-openstackclient`. For CentOS 7, execute `yum install epel-release`, then `yum install gcc python python-dev python2-pip`, and finally `pip install python-openstackclient`. On Fedora, use `sudo dnf install python-openstackclient`.
What commands are available within the `openstack volume` command group?
The `openstack volume` command group includes commands such as `create`, `delete`, `list`, `set`, `show`, and `unset` for managing volumes.
What functionalities are provided by the `openstack security group` command group in the OpenStack CLI?

The `openstack security group` command group allows users to `create`, `delete`, `list`, `set`, and `show` security groups. It also provides commands for managing security group rules, including `rule create`, `rule delete`, `rule list`, and `rule show`.
How can a user manage floating IP addresses using the `openstack ip` command group?

Within the `openstack ip` command group, users can manage floating IP addresses using commands like `floating add`, `floating remove`, `floating create`, `floating delete`, `floating list`, `floating pool list`, and `floating show`. Additionally, it includes `fixed add` and `fixed remove` for fixed IP addresses.
How can a user view available commands and their details within the OpenStack command-line interface?

Users can view available commands categorized by groups by typing `help` at the OpenStack prompt. To see commands belonging to a specific command group, type `help <command group>`. For details on a particular command, including its options and arguments, type `help <command group> <command>`.
Why are OpenStack CLI commands grouped by category in the documentation, especially considering administrator access?

OpenStack CLI commands are grouped by category in the documentation because many commands are only available to OpenStack administrators and would return an error if a non-administrator tried to use them. These lists help average users easily identify which commands are available for their use.
Which commands are available for managing objects directly within the `object` command group of the OpenStack command line tool?
The `object` command group in the OpenStack command line tool provides commands such as `create`, `show`, `delete`, `list`, `save`, `set`, and `unset` for direct object management.
How can OpenStack command line users manage object storage accounts using the `object` command group?
Within the `object` command group, users can manage object storage accounts with `store account set`, `store account show`, and `store account unset`.
What commands are listed for managing containers in the OpenStack command line interface based on the provided command groups?
The listed commands for managing containers include `delete`, `show`, `list`, `unset`, and `save`.
What is the purpose of using separate command-line interfaces in OpenStack, distinct from the main `openstack` command?
Separate command-line interfaces for OpenStack components offer extra functionality compared to what is available through the main `openstack` command.
How are the separate OpenStack command-line interfaces, such as `nova` or `glance`, installed?
The separate OpenStack command-line interfaces are installed at the same time as the main `openstack` command, so no further installation steps are required to use them.
Which specific OpenStack command-line tools are used for managing servers, images, volumes, and orchestration, respectively?
The `nova` command is used for working with servers, `glance` for images, `cinder` for volumes, and `heat` for orchestration.
What is the main purpose of the OpenStack command line tool?
The OpenStack command line tool allows users to perform many actions available through the OpenStack dashboard GUI and offers additional functionalities that the dashboard does not provide.
What are the basic prerequisites for using the OpenStack command line tool?
To use the OpenStack command line tool, you need an internet connection and the client installed on your machine.
How can users install the OpenStack command line tools on a Linux machine with administrative privileges?

Users can install the Python-based OpenStack command line tools using their Linux distribution's package manager (e.g., `apt-get` for Ubuntu, `yum` for CentOS 7, `dnf` for Fedora) or by running `sudo pip install python-openstackclient`.
What is the process for installing the OpenStack command line tools into a user's home directory if administrative privileges are not available?

If administrative privileges are unavailable, users first need to install Python and pip by other means, then install the command line tools into their home space using `pip install --user python-openstackclient`.
What is the most convenient way to configure the OpenStack command line client to connect to an OpenStack project?

The most convenient way is to download an OpenStack environment setup file (RC file) from the OpenStack dashboard (Project -> API Access) and then source it using a command like `source <project name>-openrc.sh`.
What password is required when connecting the OpenStack command line client to a project after sourcing the RC file?
When connecting the OpenStack command line client to a project, the system will ask for your CCDB password after you source the RC file.
How can a user verify if their OpenStack command line client setup is functioning correctly?
A user can test their OpenStack command line client setup by typing `openstack image list` after sourcing the RC file and providing their password.
What precaution should users take when switching between different OpenStack RC files?

When switching between RC files, users should be cautious of environment variables that might still be set from the previous file, which could cause commands to fail. It is recommended to either unset these variables or start a new session.
What are the two primary ways to execute commands using the OpenStack command line tool?

Commands can be executed interactively by typing `openstack` and then issuing commands at the prompt, or as one-off commands by preceding each command with `openstack`, for example, `openstack server list`.
How can users find help or a list of available commands within the OpenStack command line interface?

In interactive mode, users can type `help` for a list of available commands, `help <command group>` for commands within a specific group, or `help <command group> <command>` for details on a particular command, including its options and arguments.
What are some common server management tasks that can be performed using the OpenStack command line tool?
Common server management tasks include creating, deleting, listing, showing, starting, stopping, rebooting, suspending, resizing servers, and adding or removing security groups or volumes.
Which command group is specifically used for managing volumes within the OpenStack command line interface, and what basic operations does it support?
The `volume` command group is used for managing volumes and supports basic operations such as `create`, `delete`, `list`, and `show` volumes.
What command group allows users to manage images using the OpenStack command line tool?
The `image` command group allows users to manage images, providing functionalities to `create`, `delete`, `list`, `save`, `set`, and `show` images.
How can users manage keypairs through the OpenStack command line interface?
Users can manage keypairs using the `keypair` command group, which enables them to `create`, `delete`, `list`, and `show` keypairs.

Yes, separate command-line interfaces are available for specific OpenStack components, such as `nova` for servers, `glance` for images, `cinder` for volumes, and `heat` for orchestration, often offering extra functionality.
What is the process that occurs when a compromised virtual machine (VM) is detected?

When a compromised VM is detected, the Alliance support team first confirms the compromise by investigating network traffic logs and other sources. Subsequently, the VM is shut down and locked at the sysadmin level, and the user is notified by email.
Why is it necessary to rebuild a new virtual machine (VM) after an existing one has been compromised?

It is necessary to rebuild a new VM because an administratively locked VM cannot be started, and the contents of the compromised VM are no longer trustworthy. While the data can be safely extracted, a new VM must be built for continued operation.
What are the initial steps a user should take to recover data from a compromised virtual machine (VM) volume?

To begin data recovery from a compromised VM volume, first send an email to cloud@tech.alliancecan.ca outlining your recovery plan. If filesystem access is needed, the cloud support team will unlock the volume. Next, log in to the OpenStack admin console and launch a new instance specifically for data rescue operations.
What is the primary responsibility of a user when a virtual machine (VM) has been compromised on Alliance clusters?
Users are responsible for recovering data out of a VM that has been compromised.
How does the Alliance support team confirm that a virtual machine (VM) has been compromised?
The support team confirms a compromised VM by investigating network traffic logs and other sources.
What actions are taken by the sysadmin team immediately after a compromised virtual machine (VM) is detected on Alliance clusters?
The VM is shut down and locked at the sysadmin level, and the user is notified by email.
Can an administratively locked virtual machine (VM) be started on Alliance clusters?
No, an administratively locked VM cannot be started.
Is it considered safe to extract data from a compromised virtual machine (VM) on Alliance clusters?
Yes, it is relatively safe to extract data from a compromised VM.
What is the first step a user should take to initiate data recovery from a compromised virtual machine (VM) on Alliance Cloud?
Users should send an email to cloud@tech.alliancecan.ca outlining their recovery plan.
How can a user request access to the filesystem of a compromised volume during the recovery process on Alliance Cloud?
A user can request access by sending an email to cloud@tech.alliancecan.ca, and the cloud support team will unlock the volume if required for filesystem access.
Which administrative console should a user log into to perform data rescue operations for a compromised VM on Alliance Cloud?
Users should log in to the OpenStack admin console.
What is the purpose of launching a new instance during the recovery process for a compromised virtual machine (VM) on Alliance Cloud?
The new instance is launched to be used specifically for data rescue operations, allowing the compromised volume to be attached to it.
How do you detach a compromised volume from its original virtual machine (VM) within the OpenStack admin console for recovery?
Under 'Volumes,' select 'Manage Attachments' for the compromised volume and click 'Detach Volume'.
After detaching a compromised volume, how is it attached to the new recovery instance in OpenStack?
Under 'Volumes,' select 'Manage Attachments' for the compromised volume, then choose 'Attach To Instance' and select the recovery instance.
Once attached to a recovery instance and accessed via SSH, how is the old, compromised volume typically identified?
The old, compromised volume will typically be available as the 'vdb' disk when SSHing into the recovery instance.
What is the final step in accessing data from a compromised volume attached to a recovery instance, and why is external help suggested?
The final step is mounting the appropriate filesystem, but users should contact someone with experience because instructions vary greatly depending on how the base OS image was created.
On the cloud, who is responsible for the security of virtual machines?
On the cloud, you are responsible for the security of your virtual machines.
What is the recommended authentication method for cloud instances, and why is it preferred over passwords?
Cloud instances use SSH key authentication by default, and it is recommended because enabling password-based authentication is significantly less secure.
Which specific services should generally NOT be made publicly accessible on a virtual machine for security reasons?

Services such as ssh (22), RDP (3389), mysql (3306), VNC (5900-5906), and postgresql (5432) should generally not be made publicly accessible, as they allow interactive login or database access to your instance.
What is the user's primary responsibility concerning virtual machine security on the Alliance cloud?
Users are responsible for the security of their virtual machines when operating on the Alliance cloud.
What is the purpose of this document regarding virtual machines on the Alliance cloud?
This document outlines key considerations for users regarding security when creating a virtual machine on the Alliance cloud.
Is there a recommended resource for learning basic security considerations for virtual machines in the cloud?
Yes, there is a YouTube recording titled "Safety First!" which covers basic security considerations for VMs in the cloud.
What are some key practices for keeping a virtual machine's operating system secure?
Key practices include applying security updates regularly, avoiding packages from unknown sources, using recent images, employing SSH key authentication, and installing `fail2ban`.
Why is SSH key authentication recommended over passwords for cloud instances?
SSH key authentication is recommended because cloud instances use it by default, and enabling password-based authentication significantly reduces security.
What is `fail2ban` and why is it recommended for VM security?

Which services should generally *not* be made publicly accessible from a VM on the cloud?

Which services are typically meant to be accessible from the internet on a VM?

What is the recommended protocol for web servers configured on a virtual machine?

What actions are required the very first time you start the VNC server using the `vncserver` command?
