The standard software environment on tamIA is `StdEnv/2023`.
What Slurm options should be used when requesting H100 and H200 GPUs for jobs on tamIA?
For H100 GPU nodes, use `--gpus=h100:4`, and for H200 GPU nodes, use `--gpus=h200:8`. For multiple GPUs per node, use `--gpus-per-nodes=h100:4` or `--gpus-per-nodes=h200:8`.
How can users monitor their jobs and resource usage on the tamIA cluster?
Users can monitor their CPU, memory, and GPU usage in real-time or examine past jobs through the tamIA portal at `https://portail.tamia.ecpia.ca/`.
How do users obtain access to the Trillium cluster, including its CPU, GPU, and HPSS components?

Users must opt-in for the Trillium cluster via the CCDB webpage at https://ccdb.alliancecan.ca/me/access_systems. Users who had opted into Niagara or Mist, or HPSS through Niagara, before August 5, 2025, will be automatically opted-in. Opting into Trillium grants access to both its CPU and GPU subclusters, while HPSS requires a separate opt-in on the same CCDB page.
How do users log into the Trillium CPU and GPU subclusters using a terminal, and what essential command should be run after the first login?

To log into the Trillium CPU subcluster, users should SSH to `USERNAME@trillium.alliancecan.ca`. For the Trillium GPU subcluster, users should SSH to `USERNAME@trillium-gpu.alliancecan.ca`. Both login methods require the use of SSH keys and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) enabled on your CCDB account. After the first successful login, it is highly recommended to run the command `trisetup` to set up initial configuration files like `.bashrc` and create important directories and symbolic links to your scratch and project directories.
Could you describe the hardware specifications for the compute nodes in both the CPU and GPU subclusters of the Trillium cluster?

Each compute node in the Trillium CPU subcluster features 192 AMD Zen 5 (Turin) cores and 755 GB of available memory, with a total of 1224 such nodes. For the GPU subcluster, each compute node is equipped with 96 AMD Zen 4 (Genoa) cores, 755 GB of available memory, and 4 NVIDIA H100 GPUs. There are 61 GPU compute nodes in total.
What are the changes to the default directory locations for home, scratch, and project on Trillium compared to Niagara, and how can users conveniently access these new locations?

On Trillium, your home directory is now located at `/home/USERNAME` and your scratch directory at `/scratch/USERNAME`, neither of which are nested under a group anymore. For project directories, existing groups will find them at `/project/RRG-NAME`, and all groups now also have a `/project/def-PINAME` directory with a 1 TB quota. To easily find and link to your scratch and project directories, users should run the `trisetup` command after their initial login, which populates symbolic links within a `links` directory in their `$HOME`.
What is the standard software environment on Trillium, and how should users load a comprehensive set of modules for general use or for GPU development?

Trillium utilizes the CVMFS software stack, consistent with other national clusters. By default, only the `gentoo/2023` and `CCconfig` modules are loaded. To load a more comprehensive set of standard modules, including a default GCC compiler, users should execute `module load StdEnv/2023`. For compiling GPU code with CUDA, it is also necessary to load the appropriate `cuda` module, for example, `module load StdEnv/2023 cuda/12.6`. The `cuda` module is exclusively available on Trillium's GPU login and compute nodes.

How do file and directory permissions on Trillium differ from Niagara, particularly regarding group ownership for home and scratch directories, and what are the implications for sharing files or running compute jobs?

On Trillium, files and directories within your home and scratch directories now have group-ownership set to your own private group, a change from Niagara where they might have been owned by your PI's group. To share files with other group members, you will need to utilize Access Control Lists (ACLs) or manually change group ownership. Project directories, conversely, are configured for sharing with group-membership corresponding to their allocation. An important operational change is that home and project file systems are read-only on Trillium's compute nodes, meaning all compute jobs must write their data to the scratch directory.
What are the hardware specifications for a single compute node within the Trillium GPU subcluster?
Each compute node in the Trillium GPU subcluster is equipped with 96 AMD Zen 4 (Genoa) cores, 755 GB of available memory, and 4 NVIDIA H100 GPUs.
What type of CPUs and GPUs are used in the Trillium GPU subcluster?
The Trillium GPU subcluster utilizes AMD Zen 4 (Genoa) chips for its CPUs and NVIDIA H100 GPUs.
How many GPU compute nodes are there in Trillium's GPU subcluster, and what is the total number of GPUs available?
The Trillium GPU subcluster comprises 61 GPU compute nodes, making a total of 244 GPUs available within the subcluster.
What modules are loaded by default on the Trillium cluster, and what is required for other software modules?
On Trillium, only the `gentoo/2023` and `CCconfig` modules are loaded by default. All other modules, including those for compilers, libraries, and Python, must be explicitly loaded by the user.
How can users load the standard set of default modules, including the GCC compiler, on Trillium to match other national clusters?
To get the same set of default modules as available on other national clusters, including the gcc compiler, users should load the `StdEnv/2023` module by running `$ module load StdEnv/2023`.
How do you compile GPU code with CUDA on Trillium, and which nodes support the CUDA module?

To compile GPU code with CUDA on Trillium, users need to load both the `StdEnv/2023` and `cuda/12.6` modules. The `cuda` module is only available on the Trillium GPU login node and GPU compute nodes; it is not available on the Trillium CPU nodes.
What is the recommendation for recompiling code after migrating to the Trillium cluster?

Even though all files, including binaries, were copied over, codes that did not use the CVMFS software stack or that used absolute paths will have to be recompiled. It is highly recommended to recompile all code, even if it previously used the CVMFS stack on Niagara.
What action is required for virtual Python environments after migrating to Trillium, and what should users do if they previously used Anaconda?

Users must recreate their virtual Python environments because of the user directory change, as existing environments will not work. If users had Anaconda virtual environments, they should switch to using standard virtual environments instead, as there is no Anaconda module available on Trillium.
Where can users find support and documentation for the Trillium cluster?

Users can refer to the Trillium Quickstart guide, contact support via email at trillium@tech.alliancecan.ca, or take the self-guided 'Intro to SciNet and Trillium' course available at education.scinet.utoronto.ca.
What is the initial step for users to gain access to the Trillium cluster and its HPSS nearline system?
Users must opt-in via the CCDB webpage at https://ccdb.alliancecan.ca/me/access_systems for both the Trillium cluster and its HPSS nearline system.
How can users log in to the CPU and GPU subclusters of Trillium, respectively?
To access the CPU subcluster, users should `ssh USERNAME@trillium.alliancecan.ca`. For the GPU subcluster, `ssh USERNAME@trillium-gpu.alliancecan.ca` is used. Both require SSH keys and MFA.
What command should users run after their first login to Trillium to set up their environment?

Users should run the `trisetup` command, which populates essential configuration files like `.bashrc` and creates directories and symbolic links to scratch and project directories in their home directory.
What are the key hardware specifications for the Trillium CPU subcluster compute nodes?
Each compute node in the CPU subcluster has 192 AMD Zen 5 (Turin) cores and 755 GB of available memory.
What are the key hardware specifications for the Trillium GPU subcluster compute nodes?
Each compute node in the GPU subcluster has 96 AMD Zen 4 (Genoa) cores, 755 GB of available memory, and 4 NVIDIA H100 GPUs.
How was user data from Niagara migrated to Trillium, and what data might users need to copy manually?

Data on home, scratch, and project directories on Niagara as of July 31st, 2025, that was not changed afterwards, was automatically copied. Users need to manually copy any data added or modified on Niagara after that date.
What is the new directory layout for home, scratch, and project directories on Trillium?
Home directories are at `/home/USERNAME`, scratch at `/scratch/USERNAME`, RRG project directories at `/project/RRG-NAME`, and default project directories at `/project/def-PINAME`.
What are the default storage quotas for home and scratch directories on Trillium?
The default quota is 100 GB for home directories and 25 TB for scratch directories.
What is the backup policy for the different file systems on Trillium?
Home and project directories are backed up, but the scratch directory is not backed up.
How do file and directory permissions for home and scratch directories differ on Trillium compared to Niagara, particularly for sharing?

On Trillium, new files in home and scratch have group-ownership set to the user's private group. Sharing files requires using ACLs or changing group ownership. Project directories are configured for sharing with research group ownership.
Where should compute jobs write their output on Trillium, and why?
Compute jobs must write their output to the scratch directory because the home and project file systems are read-only on Trillium compute nodes.
What software stack is used on Trillium, and what modules are loaded by default?
Trillium uses the CVMFS software stack. By default, only the `gentoo/2023` and `CCconfig` modules are loaded. Users can load `StdEnv/2023` for a broader set of common modules.
Are existing binaries and virtual Python environments from Niagara expected to work on Trillium?

No, most codes, especially those not using the CVMFS stack or absolute paths, will require recompilation. Virtual Python environments also need to be recreated due to directory changes, and Anaconda is no longer supported.
How do users load the necessary modules for compiling GPU code with CUDA on Trillium?
On the GPU login or compute nodes, users need to load `StdEnv/2023` and then the appropriate `cuda` module, for example: `module load StdEnv/2023 cuda/12.6`.
What is the Trillium cluster, when will it be available, and which institution hosts it?
The Trillium cluster is a large parallel computing system built by Lenovo Canada. It is hosted by SciNet at the University of Toronto and is scheduled to be available on August 7, 2025.
How do users log in to the Trillium cluster, and what are the specific login node addresses for its CPU and GPU subclusters?

Users must log in to the Trillium cluster using SSH Keys and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), as password access is disabled for the login nodes. The login node for the CPU subcluster is `trillium.alliancecan.ca`, and for the GPU subcluster, it is `trillium-gpu.alliancecan.ca`.
What are the primary storage systems available on the Trillium cluster and their respective capacities?

The Trillium cluster provides 29 petabytes of NVMe SSD-based parallel storage from VAST Data for high-performance file systems. Additionally, there is an extra 114 petabytes of HPSS tape-based archive available for nearline storage, which supports dual-copy archiving and is managed by Atempo backup software.
What are the limitations for writing data to the `$HOME` and `$PROJECT` directories when running compute jobs on Trillium, and how can these limitations be circumvented for `$HOME`?
On Trillium, compute jobs cannot write data to either the `$HOME` or `$PROJECT` directories. However, Interactive Apps accessed through Open OnDemand do have write access to the `$HOME` directory.
How can users access the nearline storage on Trillium, given it is not directly mounted on the nodes?
Nearline storage on Trillium is not mounted directly on the nodes. Users must access it either by submitting jobs to the HPSS SLURM partition or by using Globus.
What is Open OnDemand on Trillium, and what applications does it support for users?

Open OnDemand on Trillium replaces JupyterHub and allows users to access a variety of applications from their web browser. These include JupyterLab, VS Code, RStudio, MATLAB, ParaView, the DDT debugger, a terminal, and job submission tools.
How do users access the Trillium cluster's login nodes?
Users must employ SSH Keys and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) to access Trillium's login nodes, as direct password access is disabled.
Is internet access available from all types of nodes on the Trillium cluster?
No, internet access cannot be reached from Trillium's compute nodes. However, Interactive Apps on Open OnDemand do have internet access.
What are the storage limitations for a user's `$HOME` directory on the Trillium cluster?
Users on the Trillium cluster will have space for up to 100 GB or 1 million files in their `$HOME` directory.
What is the Trillium cluster on Alliance clusters?
Trillium is a large parallel cluster built by Lenovo Canada and hosted by SciNet at the University of Toronto.
What is the login node address for the CPU subcluster on the Trillium cluster?
The login node address for the CPU subcluster on Trillium is trillium.alliancecan.ca.
What is the login node address for the GPU subcluster on the Trillium cluster?
The login node address for the GPU subcluster on Trillium is trillium-gpu.alliancecan.ca.
Which nodes are designated for data transfer operations like rsync, scp, or sftp on the Trillium cluster?
The data transfer nodes for Trillium are tri-dm{1,2,3,4}.scinet.utoronto.ca.
What is the Globus collection name for accessing the Trillium file system?
The Globus collection for the Trillium file system is alliancecan#trillium.
What is the total capacity of the parallel storage system on the Trillium cluster?
The Trillium cluster has 29 petabytes of NVMe SSD based parallel storage from VAST Data.
What is the network bandwidth for CPU nodes connected to the Nvidia “NDR” Infiniband network on Trillium?
The network bandwidth for CPU nodes on Trillium is 400 Gbit/s.
What kind of GPUs are used in the Trillium GPU subcluster nodes, and how much memory do they have?
Trillium GPU subcluster nodes use 4 x NVidia H100 SXM GPUs, each with 80 GB memory, connected via NVLink.
How is the Trillium cluster's cooling system designed for energy efficiency and environmental impact?
Trillium uses fully direct liquid cooling with warm water (35–40 °C input), resulting in a PUE below 1.03, avoiding new water usage, and supplying excess heat to nearby facilities.
What are the read and write bandwidths of the VAST high-performance file system on Trillium?
The VAST high-performance file system on Trillium has a 714 GB/s read bandwidth and 275 GB/s write bandwidth.
What is the capacity of the HPSS tape-based archive storage available on Trillium?
An additional 114 PB of HPSS tape-based archive is available for nearline storage on Trillium.
What are the required authentication methods for logging into Trillium login nodes?
Users must use SSH Keys and Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) to log into Trillium login nodes, as password access is disabled.
Is it possible to access the internet directly from compute nodes on the Trillium cluster?
The internet cannot be reached from compute nodes on Trillium, although Interactive Apps on Open OnDemand do have internet access.
Are there any restrictions on writing to the $HOME directory from compute jobs on Trillium?
The $HOME directory cannot be written to from compute jobs on Trillium, but Interactive Apps on Open OnDemand do have write access.
What is the default project space quota for a group on Trillium, and how can more be requested?
Default accounts on Trillium have access to a project space of 1 TB per group, but it is not possible to request more project space through RAS.
How can users access the nearline storage on Trillium, given that it is not mounted on the nodes?
Nearline storage on Trillium needs to be accessed via jobs submitted to the HPSS SLURM partition or via Globus.
Do Trillium nodes provide local disk storage, and if not, what alternative is available for temporary files?
Trillium nodes have no local storage; however, the $SLURM_TMPDIR environment variable points to a folder on the RAM disk, which can be used for certain workflows.
What is Open OnDemand on Trillium, and what types of applications does it support for users?
Open OnDemand on Trillium supports various applications from a browser, including JupyterLab, VS Code, RStudio, MATLAB, ParaView, the DDT debugger, as well as a terminal and job submissions.
How are resources allocated for jobs in the CPU subcluster on Trillium?
Resources in the Trillium CPU subcluster are scheduled by whole 192-core nodes.
What are the key scheduling policies for resources in the GPU subcluster on Trillium?
Resources in the Trillium GPU subcluster are scheduled by whole GPU (no "MIG") or by whole node.
What is the Vulcan cluster, what is its primary purpose, and who manages it?

The Vulcan cluster is dedicated to supporting the Canadian scientific Artificial Intelligence community. It is located at the University of Alberta and is jointly managed by the University of Alberta and Amii. This cluster is also a component of the Pan-Canadian AI Compute Environment (PAICE).
What are the requirements for researchers to be able to use the Vulcan cluster?

To use the Vulcan cluster, researchers must be conducting AI research or applying AI methods. Specifically, to log in, access must be requested in CCDB. For submitting jobs, researchers need to be members of an AIP RAP, and Principal Investigators (PIs) can apply for General Access to PAICE Systems if they don't have one.
Describe the types of storage available on the Vulcan cluster and their key characteristics.

The Vulcan cluster's storage system combines NVMe flash and HDD on a Dell PowerScale platform, offering about 5PB of usable capacity. It provides three types of spaces: Home space for /home directories with small fixed quotas and daily backup; Scratch space for active, temporary data with large fixed user quotas, no backup, and inactive data purging; and Project space with large adjustable quotas per project and daily backup.
What is the primary purpose of the Vulcan cluster within the Alliance national systems?
The Vulcan cluster is dedicated to supporting the needs of the Canadian scientific Artificial Intelligence community.
When will the Vulcan cluster become available for use?
The Vulcan cluster will be available starting April 15, 2025.
What is the login node address for the Vulcan cluster?
The login node for the Vulcan cluster is vulcan.alliancecan.ca.
Where is the Vulcan cluster located and which organizations manage it?
The Vulcan cluster is located at the University of Alberta and is managed by the University of Alberta and Amii.
What is the maximum duration allowed for jobs submitted to the Vulcan cluster?
The maximum duration for jobs on the Vulcan cluster is 7 days.
Who is eligible to conduct research on the Vulcan cluster?
Vulcan is open to all researchers doing research on AI or applying AI methods in their research.
What is the initial requirement for a user to log in to the Vulcan cluster?
To be able to log in to Vulcan, users must request access in CCDB.
What must a Principal Investigator do if they need to submit jobs on the Vulcan cluster but do not currently have an AIP RAP?
Principal Investigators must apply for 'General Access to PAICE Systems' in CCDB if they do not already have an AIP RAP to submit jobs.
How can a Principal Investigator add other researchers to their AIP RAP for the Vulcan cluster?

Principal Investigators can add members by going to the 'Resource Allocation Projects' table on the CCDB home page, locating their AIP project, clicking 'Manage RAP memberships,' and entering the user's CCRI.
What are the CPU specifications for the nodes in the Vulcan cluster?
Each node in the Vulcan cluster features 2 x Intel Xeon Gold 6448Y CPUs with 64 cores and 512 GB of system memory.
How many total GPUs are available across all nodes in the Vulcan cluster?
The Vulcan cluster has a total of 1008 NVIDIA L40s 48GB GPUs.
What type of storage system does the Vulcan cluster utilize, and what is its total usable capacity?
The Vulcan cluster's storage system uses a combination of NVMe flash and HDD storage running on the Dell PowerScale platform, with approximately 5PB of total usable capacity.
What are the characteristics of the Home space on the Vulcan cluster's storage system?
The Home space is for /home directories, has a small fixed quota, is not allocated via RAS or RAC, and includes daily backup.
What is the policy for inactive data stored in the Scratch space on the Vulcan cluster?
Inactive data in the Scratch space on the Vulcan cluster will be purged.
How is Project space allocated and managed on the Vulcan cluster?
Project space has a large adjustable quota per project and includes daily backup.
Which job scheduler does the Vulcan cluster use to manage user workloads?
The Vulcan cluster uses the Slurm scheduler to run user workloads.
What is the Canadian Common CV (CCV) and its primary purpose?

The Canadian Common CV (CCV) is a software system funded by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) aimed at standardizing CV submissions to granting agencies for funding competitions. It is used by major funding agencies such as NSERC, SSHRC, NCE, CIHR, and the Alliance.
Who should an Alliance account holder contact for support regarding the Canadian Common CV (CCV)?

Alliance account holders with specific questions about the information required in the Alliance CCV template or issues submitting their CCV to the Alliance should contact support@tech.alliancecan.ca. For forgotten CCV usernames/passwords or technical access issues with ccv-cvc.ca, the CCV helpdesk should be contacted directly at support@cihr-irsc.gc.ca or by phone at 613-954-1968 or 1-888-603-4178.
How do users identify and correct missing or incorrect information when filling out the Alliance CCV template?

Users can identify missing content by a red x-mark next to a row. To correct this, they should click on the pencil icon, and the CCV interface will inform them which specific fields are missing or filled out incorrectly.
What is the purpose of the confirmation number assigned after submitting an Alliance CCV?

The confirmation number assigned upon submission of an Alliance CCV is mandatory to enter on the CCDB. Its purpose is to link a user's Resource Allocation Competitions (RAC) application with their CCV submission.
Which specific Canadian Common CV (CCV) template must be used when submitting a CCV to the Digital Research Alliance of Canada?

When submitting a CCV to the Digital Research Alliance of Canada, only confirmation numbers for CCVs submitted using the Alliance template will be accepted. Confirmation numbers from other CCV templates, such as NSERC or CIHR, are not valid.
What are the mandatory sections that must be completed in the Alliance Canadian Common CV (CCV) template?

The mandatory sections for the Alliance CCV template include Personal Information (Identification, Correspondence language), Education (Degrees), Employment (Academic Work Experience, Non-Academic Work Experience, Affiliations, Leaves of Absence and Impact on Research), and Research Funding History over the last five years.
Who is required to submit a Canadian Common CV (CCV) for Alliance account renewal, and what is the validity period for the submission?

Submitting a CCV for Alliance account renewal is mandatory for all users with Faculty and Adjunct Faculty roles. It is optional for Emeritus Professors, Retired Faculty, and Librarians. To renew an account, the CCV must have been submitted within the last 300 days.
What are the requirements for Co-Principal Investigators (Co-PIs) regarding their Canadian Common CV (CCV) when they are part of a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application with the Alliance?

All Co-PIs on a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application must have an updated Canadian Common CV (CCV) on file, meaning it must have been submitted within the last 90 days. The Academic Principal Investigator (PI) will not be able to submit their RAC application until this requirement is met for all Co-PIs.

When an Academic Principal Investigator submits a new Canadian Common CV (CCV) for a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application to the Alliance, how do they report publications enabled by computational resources?

After submitting a new Canadian Common CV (CCV), the publications from the Alliance CCV template will appear in the 'CCV Publications Reporting' section on CCDB, initially surrounded by a red border. To submit the RAC application, the PI must provide an answer for all publications to remove these red borders. This can be done by checking individual publications, clicking 'Select all new' to mark all as enabled, or clicking 'Clear all new' if none were enabled. To mark a publication as *not* enabled by computational resources, the PI must click on it twice.

What action is required from an Academic Principal Investigator if their Canadian Common CV (CCV) on file is older than 90 days when they are applying for a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) with the Alliance?

If an Academic Principal Investigator's Canadian Common CV (CCV) on file is older than 90 days, they are required to submit a new CCV with their Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application. This involves visiting the CCV website to make necessary changes to the Alliance CCV template, submitting it, and then entering the new CCV confirmation code on CCDB and clicking 'Update CCV'.
How does an Academic Principal Investigator (PI) or their delegated user initiate or resume a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application on CCDB?

An Academic Principal Investigator (PI) or their delegated user should navigate to the Resource Application page on CCDB at https://ccdb.computecanada.ca/allocation/resource_applications. From there, they should go to the 'Ongoing Competitions' tab under the 'Resource Allocation Competitions' section and click 'Apply' to start a new application or 'Edit' to continue an existing one in the corresponding RRG or RPP section.
Where in the Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application form can an Academic Principal Investigator (PI) locate the Canadian Common CV section?
Within the Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application form on CCDB, an Academic Principal Investigator (PI) should scroll down to find the 'Canadian Common CV' section.
When an updated Alliance CCV is submitted that is older than 90 days, how are publications that are new to the CCV identified, and what must be done with them?

When an updated Alliance CCV is successfully uploaded, any new publications that have been added (compared to the ones on file) will be marked with a red border. To complete the reporting process and submit your application, you must review and address all these newly marked publications.
How do you indicate that a new publication in your Alliance CCV was *not* enabled by computational resources?

To mark a new publication as not enabled by computational resources, you must click on it twice. The first click will show a checkmark, indicating it was enabled by resources. The second click on the same box will remove the checkmark, signifying that the new publication was not enabled by computational resources.
What happens to previously reported publications when an updated Alliance CCV is successfully uploaded?

When an updated Alliance CCV is successfully uploaded, the system will display the list of publications included in the most recently submitted CCV, remembering how you previously marked them as enabled by computational resources.
What is required if an Academic Principal Investigator's Canadian Common CV (CCV) on file is older than 90 days when applying for a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC)?
If an Academic Principal Investigator's Canadian Common CV (CCV) on file is older than 90 days, they will be required to submit a new CCV with their Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application.

What are the steps for an Academic Principal Investigator to submit a new Canadian Common CV (CCV) if their existing one on file is older than 90 days for a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application?

An Academic Principal Investigator must go to the CCV website, make any necessary changes to the Alliance CCV template, and submit it. Afterwards, they need to enter the new CCV confirmation code on CCDB and click the "Update CCV" button.
What is the Canadian Common CV (CCV) system?
The Canadian Common CV (CCV) is a software system funded by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) that aims to standardize CV submissions to granting agencies for funding competitions.
Which types of Alliance users are optionally required to submit a Canadian Common CV (CCV) for account renewal?
Emeritus Professors, Librarians, and Retired Faculty have the option not to submit a CCV when renewing their Alliance account.
Who should be contacted for technical support if an Alliance account holder forgets their Canadian Common CV (CCV) username or password?

Alliance account holders needing technical support for CCV access or forgotten login credentials should contact the CCV helpdesk directly by email at support@cihr-irsc.gc.ca or by phone at 613-954-1968 or 1-888-603-4178.
What contact information should be used for questions specific to the information required in the Alliance Canadian Common CV (CCV) template or issues submitting it to the Alliance?
For specific questions about the information required in the Alliance CCV template or issues submitting it to the Alliance, contact support@tech.alliancecan.ca.
What are the mandatory steps to register for a new Canadian Common CV (CCV) account?

To register for a new CCV account, go to ccv-cvc.ca, select your preferred language, click 'Login', then 'Register', fill out the form with a valid email, set your password and security questions, complete the 'I'm not a robot' verification, and click 'Submit'.
What is the specific "Funding Source" and "CV Type" that must be selected when submitting a Canadian Common CV (CCV) to the Alliance?
When submitting a CCV to the Alliance, the 'Funding Source' must be 'Digital Research Alliance of Canada' and the 'CV Type' must be 'Alliance'.
What is the purpose of the confirmation number provided after successfully submitting an Alliance Canadian Common CV (CCV)?
The confirmation number assigned upon submission of an Alliance CCV is mandatory to enter on the CCDB to link a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application with the CCV submission.
Can a confirmation number from a NSERC or CIHR Canadian Common CV (CCV) template be used for Alliance submissions?
No, only confirmation numbers for CCVs submitted using the Alliance template will be accepted; confirmation numbers from other CCV templates (e.g., NSERC, CIHR) cannot be used.
What is the validity period for a Canadian Common CV (CCV) when renewing an Alliance account?
To renew an Alliance account, the Canadian Common CV (CCV) must have been submitted within the last 300 days.
What is the validity period for a Co-Principal Investigator's Canadian Common CV (CCV) when applying for a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) with the Alliance?
For Co-Principal Investigators of a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application, their Canadian Common CV (CCV) must have been submitted within the last 90 days.
What happens if an Academic Principal Investigator (PI) of a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application has a Canadian Common CV (CCV) on file older than 90 days?

If an Academic Principal Investigator's (PI) Canadian Common CV (CCV) on file is older than 90 days, they will be required to submit a new CCV with their Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application.

When an Academic Principal Investigator (PI) uploads a new Canadian Common CV (CCV), how are publications for which an answer has not yet been provided identified in the CCV Publications Reporting section?
When a new CCV is uploaded, publications for which an answer has not yet been provided are identified by a red border in the CCV Publications Reporting section of the CCV submission form on CCDB.
How does an Academic Principal Investigator (PI) indicate that a publication was *not* enabled by Alliance computational resources in the Canadian Common CV (CCV) Publications Reporting section?

To mark a publication as not enabled by Alliance computational resources, an Academic PI must click twice on the publication's checkbox; the first click indicates it was enabled, and the second click removes the check mark, indicating it was not enabled.
What should an Academic Principal Investigator (PI) do if they add new publications to their Alliance Canadian Common CV (CCV) after submitting an initial RAC application?

If an Academic PI adds new publications, they should go to the CCV website, make the changes to the Alliance CCV template, submit it, enter the new confirmation code on CCDB, and then address only the newly added publications (those with a red border) in the CCV Publications Reporting section.
What are the two ways a Co-Principal Investigator (Co-PI) can update their Canadian Common CV (CCV) for a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application?

Co-Principal Investigators can update their CCV either by clicking 'Update CCV' under the 'Ongoing Competitions' tab in the Resource Applications menu, or by clicking 'View reporting' in the 'My Account' menu.
Who is eligible for Alliance support regarding Canadian Common CV (CCV) submissions?
Alliance provides support only for Alliance account holders who need to submit a CCV to renew an account or apply for a Resource Allocation Competition (RAC).
Who is eligible to contribute to the Alliance Wiki, and what are the requirements for making edits?

Anyone with an Alliance account can contribute to the Wiki. To make edits, users must log in with their Alliance credentials, as anonymous editing is not permitted. Contributions can range from correcting minor issues like dead links or typos to authoring entire pages about specific installed software.
What types of content are appropriate for the Alliance Wiki, and what should be excluded?

The Alliance Wiki is suitable for technical documentation on available services, clusters, or instructions on how to use existing applications. Content that should be excluded includes communications for the general public, media, or funding agencies, training and outreach materials, daily status updates (which belong on status.alliancecan.ca), and information primarily for prospective users or internal CC technical staff.
If a contributor is uncertain whether specific content belongs on the Alliance Wiki, what steps should they take for clarification?

If staff members have doubts about publishing content, they should consult the #rsnt-documentation channel in Slack. Non-staff contributors, on the other hand, should contact Technical Support for guidance.
How can a contributor mark a wiki page as a draft on this technical documentation site?

To mark a wiki page as a draft, a contributor should insert `{{Draft}}` at the very top of the page's source code. This allows them to work on a new page in stages or receive feedback before deciding it is complete.
What are the key writing style guidelines for creating effective and user-friendly technical documentation on this wiki?

Key writing style guidelines include designing each paragraph around one idea, presenting the most important information first, addressing the reader directly (e.g., "Click on the button."), using simple words and phrases, employing the present tense and active voice, staying positive, and using consistent terms to avoid confusion. Additionally, when referring to a "system," it's recommended to use a more precise word like "cluster," "storage space," or "scheduler" whenever possible.
What are the recommended layout style guidelines for contributing to this technical wiki regarding graphic design, screenshots, and capitalization?

Contributors should separate graphic design from content, avoiding extra line breaks or indents. Screenshots are encouraged, particularly in how-tos and tutorials, but they should float to the right, be scaled down, and include a caption suggesting clicking for a larger version if needed. For titles and headings, only the first word and proper nouns should be capitalized, with a preference for APA sentence case for all titles.
What is the general multi-step process for translating a page on this wiki?

To translate a page, one first writes the content in the original language, then marks the page for translation. Next, a human translates the page using the MediaWiki Translate extension's organizational tools. Finally, a second human reviews the translation to ensure accuracy.
What are translation units on the wiki, and what is their purpose when a page is marked for translation?

When a wiki page is marked for translation, the content is analyzed and split into 'translation units' by the translation extension. These units can be small segments like a title, a paragraph, or an image. Their purpose is to allow these smaller parts to be translated individually, meaning that a minor modification to a page won't necessitate retranslating the entire page. This system also enables tracking the percentage of a page that has been translated or has become outdated.
What are the essential steps for marking a newly written page on the wiki for translation?

To mark a new wiki page for translation, you must first ensure the original language is correctly set (e.g., French on Special:PageLanguage, if applicable). Next, enclose all content intended for translation within `<translate>` and `</translate>` tags, while simultaneously enclosing code blocks and wiki markup (like tables or tags) in `</translate><translate>` tags to exclude them from translation. You must also place the `<languages />` tag at the very top of the page. After these preparations, switch to 'View' mode, click on 'Mark this page for translation', review the generated translation units to confirm proper inclusion/exclusion, specify 'fr' or 'en' as the priority language for translation, and finally, click 'Mark this version for translation'.
What specific actions should contributors avoid when dealing with translation tags on the wiki?

Contributors must avoid directly interacting with translation tags, which are automatically managed by the translation extension. This means you should absolutely NOT edit, copy, move, create, or duplicate translation tags. The only safe action a contributor can take with these tags is to DELETE them, and then allow the extension to re-tag the page when it is marked for translation again.
What should an Alliance wiki contributor do if they encounter a lone translation tag at the end of a section's wikicode while making an edit?

If a contributor finds a lone translation tag at the end of a section's wikicode, they should stop editing that section. They should then copy any edits they've made into a local text editor, cancel their changes in the wikicode editor, and instead begin editing the wikicode of the entire page.
What is the procedure for marking changes on an already translated Alliance wiki page so that the new content can be translated?

To mark changes on an already translated page, first ensure the page is stable and do not manually alter automatically generated translation tags (e.g., `<!--T:3-->`). After making your edits, new text intended for translation must be enclosed within `<translate> </translate>` tags, while code blocks and wiki markup should be excluded from translation using `</translate> <translate>` tags. Next, go into 'View' mode and click the 'marked for translation' link that appears at the top of the page. Review the translation units, confirm 'fr' or 'en' as the priority language, and then click 'Mark this version for translation'.
Why are code blocks typically not translated on the Alliance wiki, and what are the recommended methods for conveying information from comments within these blocks to users reading translated pages?

Code blocks are typically not translated on the Alliance wiki because professional human translators may struggle to differentiate between code and comments across various programming languages. To ensure explanatory comments are still accessible to users reading translated pages, contributors are advised to move the information from comments into the surrounding text, which will be translated. Alternatively, they can use index comments (e.g., 'NOTE 1') to link external, translated text to specific lines of code. Bilingual contributors familiar with the translation apparatus may also choose to translate the code block themselves.
Who is eligible to contribute to the Alliance Wiki technical documentation?

Anyone with an Alliance account can contribute to the Alliance Wiki. While staff members have primary responsibility, ordinary users are welcome to fix issues like dead links or typos, or even write entire pages on familiar software.
Are there any login requirements for editing the Alliance Wiki?
Yes, anonymous editing is not permitted. Users must log in with their Alliance credentials before they are allowed to edit, to ensure accountability for changes.
What types of content should NOT be published on the Alliance technical documentation Wiki?

What should a contributor do if information they want to publish has security implications for Alliance systems or data?
If information has implications for the security of Alliance systems or data, the contributor must consult the Director of Cybersecurity before publishing.
What is the recommended approach for including content from PDFs on the Alliance Wiki?
Contributors should avoid simply uploading PDFs. Instead, they should copy the relevant text from the PDF, add it to a Wiki page, and apply appropriate Wiki formatting, including internal links.
How can a contributor mark a new page on the Alliance Wiki as a draft?
To mark a new page as a draft, contributors should insert `{{Draft}}` at the top of the source code for that page.
What are some key writing style guidelines for content on the Alliance Wiki?

What are the steps to mark a new page on the Alliance Wiki for translation?

What actions should contributors avoid with translation tags (`<!--T:20-->`) on the Alliance Wiki?
Contributors must NOT edit, copy, move, create, or duplicate translation tags. The only safe action is to delete them, allowing the extension to re-tag the page when it is marked for translation.
How are code blocks handled during the translation process on the Alliance Wiki?
Code blocks are generally excluded from human translation because professional translators may not be able to distinguish between code and comments in various programming languages.
What is the recommended way to handle explanatory comments within code blocks that need to be understood by users reading translated pages on the Alliance Wiki?

How can a new item be added to the sidebar of the Alliance Wiki for translation?

To add a translatable item to the sidebar, one should add the new content to `MediaWiki:Sidebar` (e.g., `some-tag` or `{{(}}int:some-tag{{)}}`), add the tags to `MediaWiki:Sidebar-messages`, define the English content on `MediaWiki:some-tag`, and then translate the content on the special translation page for wiki-sidebar.
How are the tables on the 'Available software' page generated and updated on the Alliance Wiki?

The tables on the 'Available software' page are automatically generated from module files located in CVMFS. To add a link to new documentation in these tables, an entry must be added to the `module_wiki_page.json` file on GitHub.
How long does it typically take for changes to the `module_wiki_page.json` file to appear on the 'Available software' page of the Alliance Wiki?
Changes made to the `module_wiki_page.json` file may take up to six hours to propagate and become visible on the 'Available software' page of the Alliance Wiki.
What is the purpose of the 'Do not invalidate translations' checkbox when marking changes to an already translated page on the Alliance Wiki?

The 'Do not invalidate translations' checkbox should only be selected if the change is minor, such as a typo, which does not require the existing translated versions of that unit to be adjusted or re-translated.
What are the advantages of hosting Software Carpentry-style lessons on a wiki?

Hosting Software Carpentry-style lessons on a wiki offers several advantages, including support for translation, the ability to write lessons with Markdown syntax, and access to many pre-formatted styles.
What are some of the specialized templates available on the wiki for creating content boxes in Software Carpentry-style lessons?

What is the primary purpose of discussing Software Carpentry-style lessons on this wiki page?
The primary purpose is to explore using the wiki to host Software Carpentry-style lessons and to provide useful templates to facilitate their writing.
What is an advantage of hosting Software Carpentry-style lessons on a wiki compared to platforms like GitHub?

How can one add a 'Getting ready' section to a Software Carpentry lesson hosted on the wiki?

Which wiki template helps define the 'Learning Objectives' for a Software Carpentry lesson?
The `{{Objectives}}` template helps define the 'Learning Objectives' for a Software Carpentry lesson on the wiki.
What is the function of the `Callout` template in a wiki-hosted Software Carpentry lesson?
The `Callout` template is used to create a 'callout' box, which can highlight specific information or tips within a Software Carpentry lesson.
How can a 'Challenge' section be incorporated into a Software Carpentry lesson being written on the wiki?
A 'Challenge' section can be incorporated by using the `{{Challenge}}` template, providing a title and content for the challenge.
What common parameters are used when implementing the `Prerequisites`, `Getready`, `Objectives`, `Callout`, and `Challenge` templates on the wiki?
The common parameters used for these templates are `title` and `content`.
What kind of information typically goes into the content of a 'Getting ready' box for a wiki-hosted Software Carpentry lesson?
The 'Getting ready' box typically includes instructions like 'You should download the following files prior to starting the lesson.'
Are there any existing examples of Software Carpentry lessons that use a similar hosting approach?
Yes, an example like 'http://swcarpentry.github.io/shell-novice/' is mentioned as a Software Carpentry lesson typically hosted on Github.
What is the Database as a Service (DBaaS) offering, and what types of databases are currently available through this service?
The Database as a Service (DBaaS) is a managed database solution designed for loads that exceed the capacity of a virtual machine. It currently offers MySQL/MariaDB and Postgres on a physical system.
How does a user request access to the Database as a Service (DBaaS), and what critical information must be included in the request?
To request access to the DBaaS, users need to contact Technical support. It is crucial to provide the client network or IP address from which the database will be accessed in the request.
What is the required connection method for accessing Database as a Service (DBaaS) hosts, and what is the consequence of attempting a different connection method?
An SSL connection is enforced for connecting to DBaaS hosts. Attempting a plain text connection will result in authentication failure.
What is the primary purpose of the Database as a Service (DBaaS) offering described in the document?
The DBaaS offering is designed for situations where a virtual machine is not sufficient to handle a database load, providing managed database services on a physical system.
What specific types of managed databases are currently available through the Database as a Service (DBaaS)?
The current DBaaS offering includes MySQL/MariaDB and Postgres databases.
How frequently are databases backed up within the Database as a Service (DBaaS), and for how long are these backups retained?
All databases in the DBaaS are backed up once a day, and these backups are archived for a period of 3 months.
What specific information must a user provide when requesting access to the Database as a Service (DBaaS)?
When requesting access to the DBaaS, users must provide the client network or IP address from which they will access the database.
What is the common hostname and the specific TCP ports for connecting to the MySQL/MariaDB and PostgreSQL databases offered by the Database as a Service (DBaaS)?
The common hostname is dbaas101.arbutus.cloud.computecanada.ca. For MySQL/MariaDB, the TCP port is 3306, and for PostgreSQL, it is 5432.
Where can users download the CA certificate that is used to sign the host certificate for the Database as a Service (DBaaS)?
The CA certificate is available for download at http://repo.arbutus.cloud.computecanada.ca/dbaas-ca.pem.
What type of connection is enforced for PostgreSQL databases when using the Database as a Service (DBaaS), and what happens if a plain text connection is attempted?
An SSL connection is enforced for PostgreSQL databases in the DBaaS, and any attempt to use a plain text connection will fail.
How does one connect to a PostgreSQL database instance using an SSL connection with the Database as a Service (DBaaS)?
An example command to connect is `psql --set "sslmode=require" -h dbaas101.arbutus.cloud.computecanada.ca -U user01 -d dbinstance`.
What type of connection is required for MariaDB/MySQL databases with the Database as a Service (DBaaS), and what is the outcome if a plain text connection is tried?
An SSL connection is required for MariaDB/MySQL databases. If a plain text connection is attempted, authentication will fail, resulting in an 'Access denied' error.
What is an example command for connecting to a MariaDB/MySQL database instance using an SSL connection with the Database as a Service (DBaaS)?
An example command to connect is `mysql --ssl -h dbaas101.arbutus.cloud.computecanada.ca -u user01 -p dbinstance`.
What are the web links used to access Ansys programs in graphical mode on OnDemand or JupyterHub desktops for Alliance clusters like Nibi, FIR, RORQUAL, Narval, and Trillium?

Users can access Ansys programs in graphical mode via: NIBI: `https://ondemand.sharcnet.ca`, FIR: `https://jupyterhub.fir.alliancecan.ca`, RORQUAL: `https://jupyterhub.rorqual.alliancecan.ca`, Narval: `https://jupyterhub.narval.alliancecan.ca/`, and TRILLIUM: `https://ondemand.scinet.utoronto.ca`.
After starting an interactive desktop session for Ansys programs, how do you load an Ansys module, distinguishing between JupyterLab and OnDemand desktops?

If a JupyterLab-powered desktop was started, the Ansys module can be loaded by clicking in the menu on the left. For an OnDemand desktop started manually, users need to type `module load ansys/version` on the command line.
What are the command-line steps to start Ansys Fluent on an OnDemand desktop?
To start Ansys Fluent from the command line on an OnDemand desktop, open a terminal window and run `module load StdEnv/2023 ansys/2025R2.04` followed by `fluent`.
What environment variables must be set when running Ansys Fluent on an OnDemand desktop session configured without a GPU?

When running Ansys Fluent on an OnDemand desktop session without a GPU, you need to set `I_MPI_HYDRA_BOOTSTRAP=ssh` (which is required on Nibi when using intelmpi). Additionally, for graphics, set `HOOPS_PICTURE=opengl2-mesa` if using version 2025R1 or newer, or `HOOPS_PICTURE=x11/lin` if using version 2024R2.04 or older. After setting these, click the 'Start' button in the Fluent Launcher.
How do you enable hardware-accelerated graphics for Ansys Fluent on Nibi when using an OnDemand desktop session?

To enable hardware-accelerated graphics with Fluent on Nibi, you must choose a 't4 (15GB)' GPU from the pulldown list during your OnDemand desktop session setup. Once the desktop appears, open a terminal window and set the environment variables: `I_MPI_HYDRA_BOOTSTRAP=ssh` (required on Nibi) and either `HOOPS_PICTURE=opengl2` (for version 2025R1 or newer) or `HOOPS_PICTURE=opengl` (for version 2024R2.04 or older). Finally, click the 'Start' button.
Why is the `I_MPI_HYDRA_BOOTSTRAP=ssh` environment variable critical when running Ansys Fluent on the Nibi cluster with intelmpi?

The `I_MPI_HYDRA_BOOTSTRAP=ssh` environment variable is critical because it must be manually set when running Fluent on Nibi with intelmpi. Failure to do so will cause Fluent to crash when started inside OnDemand Compute Desktop sessions, producing an error. If a crash occurs, you must completely exit Fluent, cleanly shut down Workbench, and restart the process.
How do users launch the CFX program from an OnDemand desktop, specifying whether a GPU resource was requested?
To start CFX from an OnDemand desktop, use the command `cfx5 -graphics mesa` if you did not request a GPU for your session. If a GPU was requested, use the command `cfx5 -graphics ogl`.
What are the command-line steps required to launch the Mechanical APDL (Mapdl) GUI from a terminal window on an OnDemand desktop?

To start the Mechanical APDL (Mapdl) GUI, first load the necessary module by typing `module load StdEnv/2023 ansys/2022R2` (or a newer version). After loading the module, you can launch the GUI using either `mapdl -g` or by typing `launcher` and then clicking on the `RUN` button.
How does one start Ansys Workbench on an OnDemand desktop, and subsequently launch Fluent from within Workbench, considering if a GPU was utilized for the session?

To start Ansys Workbench on an OnDemand desktop, regardless of GPU usage, first load the module `module load StdEnv/2023 ansys/2025R2.04`, then run `runwb2`. To launch Fluent from within Workbench, navigate to the 'Analysis' menu, click on 'Fluid Flow (Fluent)' or 'Fluent with Fluent Meshing', then click 'Setup'. In the 'Fluent Launcher' selector panel, go to the 'Environment' tab and copy/paste `I_MPI_HYDRA_BOOTSTRAP=ssh` (required on Nibi when using intelmpi). For sessions without a GPU, add `HOOPS_PICTURE=opengl2-mesa` (optional for 2025R1 or newer), and for sessions with a GPU, add `HOOPS_PICTURE=opengl2` (optional for 2025R1 or newer), then click 'Start'.
What are the steps to start Ansys Fluent from within Workbench on an OnDemand desktop session if no GPU was requested?

If accelerated graphics are not required for your desktop session, first load the Ansys module (e.g., `module load StdEnv/2023 ansys/2025R2.04`) and then run `runwb2` from a terminal. To start Fluent from Workbench, click 'Fluid Flow (Fluent)' or 'Fluent with Fluent Meshing' in the left-hand 'Analysis' menu, click 'Setup,' and in the 'Fluent Launcher' popup, go to the 'Environment' tab. There, copy/paste `I_MPI_HYDRA_BOOTSTRAP=ssh` (required on the Nibi cluster only when using intelmpi) and `HOOPS_PICTURE=opengl2-mesa` (optional for 2025R1 or newer), then click 'Start.'
How do you launch Ansys Fluent from within Workbench on an OnDemand desktop session with GPU acceleration on the Nibi cluster?

First, choose 't4 (15GB)' from the GPU selector pulldown list for your OnDemand desktop session on the Nibi cluster. Once your desktop appears, open a terminal window, load the Ansys module (e.g., `module load StdEnv/2023 ansys/2025R2.04`), and then run `runwb2`. To start Fluent from within Workbench, click 'Fluid Flow (Fluent)' or 'Fluent with Fluent Meshing' in the left-hand 'Analysis' menu, click 'Setup,' and in the 'Fluent Launcher' popup, go to the 'Environment' tab. Copy/paste `I_MPI_HYDRA_BOOTSTRAP=ssh` (required on the Nibi cluster only) and `HOOPS_PICTURE=opengl2` (optional for 2025R1 or newer), then click 'Start.'
What steps should be taken if graphics appear corrupted when running an application within Workbench on a JupyterHub desktop session without a GPU?

If graphics appear corrupted, you can try two approaches. If you are starting Fluent, set the `HOOPS_PICTURE=opengl2-mesa` variable in the 'Fluent Launcher' window. Alternatively, you can create a custom Workbench desktop icon to start Workbench in Mesa mode: exit Workbench, open a terminal, and copy `cd ~/Desktop; cp -p $(realpath workbench.desktop) workbench-mesa.desktop`. Then, open `~/Desktop/workbench-mesa.desktop` in a text editor (e.g., nano) and change all instances of `runwb2` to enable Mesa mode. Save your changes, then refresh the Jupyter desktop by pressing 'control-R' for the new icon to appear.
How can users fix corrupted graphics when running applications such as Fluent within Workbench on a JupyterHub desktop if no GPU was requested?

If graphics appear corrupted, first try setting the `HOOPS_PICTURE=opengl2-mesa` variable in the 'Fluent Launcher' window. If the issue persists, exit Workbench, open a terminal, and create a custom desktop icon by copying `$(realpath workbench.desktop)` to `~/Desktop/workbench-mesa.desktop`. Edit this new file (`nano ~/Desktop/workbench-mesa.desktop`) to change all instances of `runwb2`. Save the changes, then refresh the Jupyter desktop (Control-R). Double-click the new 'workbench-mesa' icon to start Workbench, which will now launch in Mesa mode. This custom icon will remain available for future sessions unless manually deleted.
What are the required commands and steps to launch Ensight from a terminal window?

To launch Ensight, begin by loading the necessary modules: `module load StdEnv/2023 ansys/2022R2; A=222; B=5.12.6`. Next, set the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` environment variable using `export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$EBROOTANSYS/v$A/CEI/apex$A/machines/linux_2.6_64/qt-$B/lib`. Finally, execute `ensight -X` to start the Ensight application.
What are the web addresses for accessing Ansys programs in graphical mode on Alliance clusters like Nibi, FIR, RORQUAL, Narval, and Trillium?

Users can access Ansys programs via these links: NIBI: `https://ondemand.sharcnet.ca`, FIR: `https://jupyterhub.fir.alliancecan.ca`, RORQUAL: `https://jupyterhub.rorqual.alliancecan.ca`, Narval: `https://jupyterhub.narval.alliancecan.ca/`, and TRILLIUM: `https://ondemand.scinet.utoronto.ca`.
What resource should a user specify when configuring an interactive desktop session for Ansys programs if accelerated graphics or computations are required?
Users should be sure to specify a GPU resource if either accelerated graphics or computations will be conducted from within their desktop session.
How do users load an Ansys module on a JupyterLab-powered desktop compared to an OnDemand desktop?
On a JupyterLab-powered desktop, load the Ansys module by clicking in the menu on the left. For an OnDemand desktop, type `module load ansys/version` on the command line.
How do users start Ansys Fluent from the command line on an OnDemand desktop without a GPU, including necessary environment variables?

Load modules `StdEnv/2023 ansys/2025R2.04` and run `fluent`. In the Fluent Launcher's 'Environment tab', set `I_MPI_HYDRA_BOOTSTRAP=ssh` (if on Nibi with intelmpi) and `HOOPS_PICTURE=opengl2-mesa` (for 2025R1+) or `HOOPS_PICTURE=x11/lin` (for 2024R2.04 or older), then click 'Start'.
What environment variable must be manually set when running Fluent on the Nibi cluster using intelmpi, and why?
The environment variable `I_MPI_HYDRA_BOOTSTRAP=ssh` must be manually set on Nibi when using intelmpi; otherwise, Fluent will crash when started inside OOD Compute Desktop sessions.
How do users start Ansys Fluent from the command line on an OnDemand desktop with a GPU requested, including necessary environment variables?

How do users start Ansys CFX from an OnDemand desktop, differentiating between sessions with and without a GPU?
Use `cfx5 -graphics mesa` if no GPU was requested, and `cfx5 -graphics ogl` if a GPU was requested when the desktop was started.
What are the steps to start the Mechanical APDL (Mapdl) GUI from the command line on an OnDemand desktop?
Load the module `StdEnv/2023 ansys/2022R2` (or newer), then run `mapdl -g` or use the `launcher` command and click the `RUN` button.
How do users start Ansys Workbench on an OnDemand desktop if accelerated graphics are not required?
Specify 'GPU Node' to select a compute node without a GPU for the OOD session, then load `StdEnv/2023 ansys/2025R2.04` and run `runwb2`.
When launching Fluent from within Workbench on an OnDemand desktop without a GPU, what are the recommended environment variables?
In the Fluent Launcher's 'Environment' tab, set `I_MPI_HYDRA_BOOTSTRAP=ssh` (for Nibi only when using intelmpi) and `HOOPS_PICTURE=opengl2-mesa` (optional for 2025R1 or newer), then click 'Start'.
What should a user do if the graphics of an application started within Workbench appear corrupted on a JupyterLab desktop without a GPU?

Users can create a custom `workbench-mesa.desktop` icon by copying the existing one and changing `runwb2` to use Mesa mode, or try setting `HOOPS_PICTURE=opengl2-mesa` in the Fluent Launcher window if using Fluent.
How do users start Ansys Ensight on an Alliance cluster?

Load modules `StdEnv/2023 ansys/2022R2`, then set the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` environment variable as `export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$EBROOTANSYS/v222/CEI/apex222/machines/linux_2.6_64/qt-5.12.6/lib` and run `ensight -X`.
What are the main commands available for running Ansys Rocky programs?
The `Rocky` command starts Rocky in graphical mode, `RockySolver` runs the solver directly from the command line, and `RockyScheduler` starts a GUI for submitting/running jobs on the current node.
What is the `{{Command}}` template used for in the wiki?
The `{{Command}}` template is used to include a single command within the wiki, and it automatically detects bash syntax.
How can a user include special characters such as the equality sign (`=`) or pipe symbol (`|`) within the `{{Command}}` template?
To include an equality sign, users should use the `{{=}}` meta-template. For a pipe symbol, the `{{!}}` meta-template must be used, as these characters are normally interpreted by the wiki.
What is the primary difference between the `{{Command}}` and `{{Commands}}` templates, and how can the command prompt be customized for either?

The `{{Command}}` template is for displaying a single command, while the `{{Commands}}` template is used for a set of commands, where each command is written on a separate line and prefixed by a pipe character. To customize the command prompt for either template, a `prompt` argument can be included.
What is the main purpose of the `{{Command}}` and `{{Commands}}` templates within a wiki environment?
The main purpose of these templates is to include command-line instructions within the wiki content.
Which wiki template should be used to include a single command, and what syntax does it detect?
The `{{Command}}` template should be used for a single command, and it detects bash syntax.
How do you correctly include an equality sign (`=`) when using the `{{Command}}` template in a wiki?
To include an equality sign, you must use the meta-template `{{=}}`.
What is the method for including a pipe symbol (`|`) within a command when using wiki templates?
To include a pipe symbol, you must use `{{!}}`.
Which wiki template is designed for including a set of multiple commands?
The `{{Commands}}` template is used to include a set of multiple commands.
When using the `{{Commands}}` template, how should individual commands be structured?
Each command should be written on a separate line and prepended with the `|` character.
How can a user customize the command prompt displayed when using the `{{Command}}` template?

What are Meltdown and Spectre, and which CPU architectures and systems do they affect?

Meltdown and Spectre are bugs related to speculative execution in CPU architectures developed over the past ten to fifteen years, notably affecting Intel and AMD processors, including those used on Compute Canada clusters.
What performance impacts have been observed after applying operating system patches for the Meltdown and Spectre vulnerabilities on Compute Canada clusters?

Performance impacts vary, with some benchmarks showing up to a 30% or 50% hit, while others are minimal. Tasks involving heavy input/output, such as databases or file transfers (e.g., rsync), appear most affected. Most high-performance computing jobs are expected to be minimally impacted, as their runtime is primarily spent computing, and older processor generations generally report more significant performance degradation.
What are users operating virtual machines on the Compute Canada Cloud advised to do regarding the Meltdown and Spectre security patches?

Users operating their own virtual machines on the Compute Canada Cloud are responsible for frequently updating their VM's operating system to the latest version to ensure it incorporates the necessary security patches to address these bugs.
What are Meltdown and Spectre, and which CPU architectures do they primarily affect on Compute Canada clusters?

Meltdown and Spectre are bugs related to speculative execution in various CPU architectures developed over the past 10 to 15 years, particularly affecting processors from Intel and AMD, including those on Compute Canada clusters.
What actions has Compute Canada taken regarding systems vulnerable to Meltdown and Spectre?
Compute Canada personnel have patched systems deemed sensitive to these vulnerabilities, and all vulnerable equipment operated by Compute Canada has been patched.
What were the availability impacts of applying patches for Meltdown and Spectre vulnerabilities on Compute Canada compute nodes?
Updates required updating the operating system and rebooting the nodes; for compute nodes, this was typically done in a rolling fashion, was largely transparent to users, and is now complete.
When were the Meltdown and Spectre vulnerability updates applied to the Graham cluster?
Updates were applied at the Graham cluster between January 5 and January 31, 2018, with most nodes updated by January 13.
What range of performance impacts have been reported after applying operating system patches for Meltdown and Spectre vulnerabilities?
Cited figures vary from alarming (up to a 30% or even 50% performance hit) to very minimal impacts.
Which types of computing tasks are most heavily affected by the Meltdown and Spectre security patches on Compute Canada clusters?
Tasks involving a lot of input/output (reading and writing files), such as databases or file transfers (e.g., rsync), seem to be most heavily affected.
Are most high-performance computing (HPC) jobs significantly affected by the Meltdown and Spectre security patches?
Most high-performance computing jobs should be minimally affected since the vast majority of the run time is spent computing rather than doing input and output.
How do different processor generations respond to the performance degradation caused by Meltdown and Spectre patches?
Different processor generations are affected to different degrees, with the most notable performance degradation reported for older processors.
What is Compute Canada's ongoing commitment regarding new vendor patches for Meltdown and Spectre vulnerabilities?
If and when vendors release new patches, these will also be applied to Compute Canada systems.
What should users of Compute Canada systems understand about the security of their applications in light of Meltdown and Spectre?
Users can rest assured that Compute Canada team members are taking every action possible to ensure that systems we run are secure.
What should a user do if they believe their application's performance is severely impacted by the Meltdown and Spectre security patches on Compute Canada systems?
Users should contact the Technical support team and are encouraged to provide comparative performance numbers of their application (e.g., job run times before and after the announcement).
What is the responsibility of users operating their own virtual machines on the Compute Canada Cloud regarding Meltdown and Spectre vulnerabilities?
Users operating their own virtual machines are responsible for updating their operating system frequently to include the latest security patches addressing these bugs.
Can users expect that mitigating the performance impact of Meltdown and Spectre security patches will always be possible?
Mitigating the performance impact of the security patches is likely to require some modification to the code a user is running, and may not always be possible.
Where can users find specific instructions for updating Linux virtual machines to address security patches on the Compute Canada Cloud?
Users can find specific instructions on updating their VM in the 'Security_considerations_when_running_a_VM' section.
Where can users find additional general information about Spectre and Meltdown, including links to vendor patch sites?
Other general information about Spectre and Meltdown is available on the US-CERT web site, which includes comprehensive links to vendor patch sites.
What is the general process for translating a wiki page using the organizational tools provided by the wiki extension?

To translate a wiki page, one first writes the content in the original language. Second, the page is marked for translation. Then, a human translates the page using organizational tools provided by the wiki extension. Finally, a second human reviews the translation.
What is the purpose of splitting wiki page content into 'translation units' when a page is marked for translation?

Marking a page for translation triggers an analysis that splits the content into 'translation units,' such as a title, a paragraph, or an image. These small units can then be translated one by one, which ensures that a modification to a page does not trigger the translation of the whole page. This also allows for tracking the percentage of a page that is translated or outdated.
What are the required steps to mark a new wiki page for translation?

To mark a new wiki page for translation, you must first ensure that the wiki code to be translated is enclosed within `<translate>` tags, and that the `<languages />` tag appears at the very top of the page. Then, go to 'View' mode and click on 'Mark this page for translation'. Review the translation units, making sure to avoid translating wiki code by breaking the page into multiple `<translate>` sections if necessary. In the 'Priority languages' section, specify either 'fr' or 'en' as the priority language, and finally, click on 'Mark this version for translation'.
What is the general process for translating a wiki page using the described method?

First, content is written in the original language, then the page is marked for translation. A human translates the page using organizational tools, and finally, a second human reviews the translation.
Which specific wiki extension facilitates the translation of pages as described in the process?
The MediaWiki extension called 'Translate' is used for page translation.
Who is responsible for translating and reviewing wiki pages once they are marked for translation?
A human translates the page using organizational tools, and a second human reviews the translation.
In the context of wiki page translation, what are 'translation units'?
Translation units are small segments of page content, such as a title, a paragraph, or an image, into which the wiki page is split by the translation extension.
What are the advantages of splitting wiki page content into translation units for the translation process?

Splitting content into translation units ensures that a modification to a page does not trigger the translation of the whole page, and it allows tracking the percentage of a page that is translated or outdated.
What do users see if a wiki page has not yet been translated into their preferred language?
Users can see the page in its original language if it has not yet been translated.
What do users see if a wiki page translation has been completed but not yet reviewed?
Users can see the non-reviewed translation if a translation has not yet been reviewed.
What is the initial step for preparing the wiki code of a *new* page to be marked for translation?
The wiki code to be translated must be enclosed within <translate> and </translate> tags.
Which specific tag needs to be placed at the very top of a *new* wiki page to enable the display of language options for translation?
The tag <languages /> must appear at the very top of the page.
After adding the necessary tags to a *new* wiki page, how does one proceed to mark it for translation?
One goes into 'View' mode and then clicks on the 'Mark this page for translation' option.
What should be carefully considered when reviewing translation units for a *newly* marked wiki page?
One should try to ensure that no wiki code (such as tables or tags) gets translated, which can be achieved by breaking the page into multiple <translate> sections.
According to the document, which languages are specified as priority options when marking a wiki page for translation?
Either 'fr' (French) or 'en' (English) should be written as the priority language.
What is a key recommendation regarding the stability of a wiki page before it is marked for translation for the first time?
It is recommended to try and mark a page for translation only once it is stable.

Tags of the form <!--T:3--> should not be changed, as they are automatically generated.

One goes into 'View' mode, where a message 'This page has changes since it was last marked for translation' should appear at the top, and then clicks on 'marked for translation'.

The new text to be translated must be enclosed within <translate> and </translate> tags.

Tutorials for the Translate extension can be found on MediaWiki's website, specifically at https://www.mediawiki.org/wiki/Help:Extension:Translate.
What is the main purpose of the Digital Research Alliance of Canada's technical documentation wiki?
The Digital Research Alliance of Canada's technical documentation wiki serves as the primary source for users with questions regarding the Alliance's national equipment and services.
What types of compute clusters are offered by the Digital Research Alliance of Canada?

The Digital Research Alliance of Canada offers general-purpose clusters for CPU or GPU jobs (Fir, Nibi, Narval, Rorqual), the Trillium cluster designed for large parallel jobs, and GPU clusters that are part of the Pan-Canadian AI Compute Environment (Killarney, tamIA, Vulcan). What are some of the key services provided by the Digital Research Alliance of Canada?
