Why is it crucial for Principal Investigators to make arrangements for data management with sponsored users before their accounts are deactivated on Alliance systems?

It's crucial because the deactivation of a sponsored user's account may restrict the Principal Investigator's ability to access their files. Intellectual property rules vary, meaning PIs aren't automatically allowed access, and there's a risk of the user becoming incommunicado, making data retrieval difficult or impossible after deactivation.
What is the simplest way for group members to prevent future problems with data access after their account is deactivated on an Alliance cluster?
The easiest way to avoid any problems with data access is for group members to agree to the storage access policy in their CCDB account, which can be found under the My Account/Agreements tab.
While a departing sponsored user's account is still active on an Alliance system, what specific actions should Principal Investigators take to manage their data?

Principal Investigators should ask the user to compress many files with tools like `tar` or `zip`, identify and copy essential data to a portable USB drive, an external hard drive, or the PI's own Alliance account, ask the user to delete any data that can reasonably be deleted, and move any important data from the user's account to the PI's own account before the person leaves to avoid potential intellectual property issues.
What is the primary purpose of the information provided regarding sponsored users and file management on Alliance clusters?

The information aims to guide Principal Investigators (PIs) on managing data belonging to their sponsored users, especially concerning account deactivation and file access, to mitigate potential problems.
Who is the main audience for the guidance on managing sponsored users' accounts and files on Alliance systems?
The information is primarily directed at Principal Investigators (PIs) who have sponsored users as part of their research teams.
What is a potential consequence if a sponsored user's account is deactivated on an Alliance cluster?
Deactivation of a sponsored user's account may restrict the Principal Investigator's ability to access files owned or produced by that group member.
Why can't Principal Investigators automatically access files owned by their sponsored users, even if they control a filesystem quota, after an account is deactivated?
Intellectual property (IP) rules vary, and it is not automatically assumed that the sponsor is allowed to access files owned or produced by group members.
What is the most important general action Principal Investigators should take with a group member before their Alliance account is deactivated?
It is crucial to make arrangements with the group member to manage their data before account deactivation to mitigate the risk of them becoming incommunicado later.
What is the easiest way for group members to avoid problems with file access on Alliance clusters if their account is deactivated?
Group members should agree to the 'storage access policy' in their CCDB account under the 'My Account/Agreements' tab.
If a departing user owns many files on an Alliance system, what initial action should a Principal Investigator ask them to take?
The Principal Investigator should ask the user to compress their files first using tools such as `tar` or `zip`.
What options are available for a departing user to archive important data from their Alliance account?
They can copy the data to a portable USB drive, an external hard drive in the lab, or directly to the Principal Investigator's own account on an Alliance system.
Besides archiving, what should a Principal Investigator ask a departing user to do regarding data in their Alliance account to manage storage?
The Principal Investigator should ask the user to delete everything that can reasonably be deleted to free up valuable storage space once important data are secured.
Why is it important for a Principal Investigator to move data from a departing user's Alliance account to their own account before the user leaves?
If the person becomes incommunicado, intellectual property rules may delay or even forbid the transfer of data from their account to the PI's.
How can one inquire if data from an expired Alliance account has been migrated to tape?
One can contact Alliance technical support to inquire about data migration to tape.
Where can users find help with archiving large collections of files on Alliance clusters?
Users can find assistance by referring to the 'Handling large collections of files' wiki page.
Where can users find information regarding directory access permissions for sharing data on Alliance systems?
Users can consult the 'Sharing data' wiki page and its parent page, 'Storage and file management,' for information on directory access permissions.
What is the primary purpose of the annual account renewal process?

The annual account renewal process, which typically occurs in the spring, is critical for deactivating accounts that are no longer needed and for collecting information required by funding agencies and partners for reporting purposes.
What happens if a Principal Investigator's (PI) CCDB account expires?
If a Principal Investigator (PI) allows their CCDB account to expire, their account, as well as the accounts of all users they sponsor, will also be deactivated.
How can a user reactivate an expired CCDB account?
Accounts can be reactivated at any time by logging into CCDB (https://ccdb.alliancecan.ca/) and completing the account renewal form.
Why is the information collected from researchers during the account renewal important?
The information collected about researchers and their results is important for reports to funding agencies and the digital research infrastructure (DRI) ecosystem.
How do active account holders receive instructions for their account renewal?
Users with an active account will receive an email during the account renewal period directing them to the account renewal form.
What happens if a regular user allows their CCDB account to expire?
If a user lets their CCDB account expire, they will no longer be able to log into any of our systems.
What are the consequences if a Principal Investigator (PI) lets their account expire?
If a Principal Investigator (PI) allows their account to expire, their account as well as the accounts of all sponsored users will also be deactivated.
How can a deactivated account be reactivated?
Accounts can be reactivated at any time by logging into CCDB and completing the account renewal form.
What should users do if they don't want to renew their CCDB account but still need to recover their files?
Users who do not want to renew their CCDB account but still want to recover their files can request a temporary extension by sending an email to support@tech.alliancecan.ca.
Where can users find more information about account renewals?
More information about account renewals can be found on the Account Renewals FAQ page or by contacting renewals@tech.alliancecan.ca.
What kind of information is collected during the annual account renewal for reporting purposes?
Information about researchers and their results is collected for reports to funding agencies and the digital research infrastructure (DRI) ecosystem.
Why is the annual renewal of Digital Research Alliance of Canada accounts necessary, and what are the general consequences if an account is not renewed?

The annual renewal of Alliance accounts is essential for collecting up-to-date information required by granting agencies and for deactivating accounts that are no longer in use. If an account is not renewed between May 6 and June 9, 2026, it will be automatically deactivated, meaning the user will lose access to their data, although the data will not be immediately deleted. Deactivated accounts can still be renewed at any time.
What is considered a primary role within the Digital Research Alliance of Canada system, and why is it important to keep it updated and renewed?

A primary role in the Alliance system corresponds to a user's main position, typically the one they will hold for the longest period (e.g., a full-time faculty appointment or a student's role with their primary supervisor). It is important because it assists in managing accounts with multiple roles, facilitates communication with users, and helps with reporting. Critically, if a primary role is not renewed during the annual renewal period, the associated Alliance account will be deactivated.
What specific impact does a faculty member's (Principal Investigator's) failure to renew their Digital Research Alliance of Canada account have on their sponsored users?

If a faculty member (Principal Investigator) with sponsored users allows their Alliance account to expire without renewal by the deadline, their own account as well as the accounts of all users they sponsor will be deactivated. This will result in any jobs submitted by them or their sponsored users being paused, and their research group will lose access to their files until the sponsor's account is reactivated.
What steps must a Principal Investigator (PI) take to renew their Alliance account and manage their sponsored users?

Principal Investigators (PIs) must update their contact information and Field of Research on the account renewal form, complete a User Satisfaction Survey, and update the status of their sponsored roles (e.g., students, postdocs). University faculty who sponsor other users must specifically confirm whether those accounts are continuing or have ended. Once all information is updated and confirmed, the PI must click the 'REQUEST ACCOUNT RENEWAL' button on the left side of the form to initiate the renewal.
If a Principal Investigator (PI) with a faculty role moves to a different Alliance institution, will users sponsored by their old role be automatically transferred to their new role?

No, users sponsored by the PI's old faculty role will not be automatically transferred to their new role. Any user the PI wishes to sponsor with their new faculty role will have to apply for a new role sponsored by that new position. If the PI has a RAC allocation, sponsored users with the old role will lose access to the associated Resource Allocation Project (RAP) and may need to be re-added to the RAP once their new roles are activated.
Why might a sponsored Alliance account remain deactivated on CCDB even after the sponsored user has completed their renewal?

A sponsored Alliance account may remain deactivated even after the sponsored user completes their renewal because their sponsor has not yet renewed or reactivated their own account. The sponsored role will only be activated once the sponsor renews their account and confirms that the sponsored role is continuing.
What happens if a faculty member with sponsored users allows their Alliance account to expire?

If a faculty member with sponsored users allows their Alliance account to expire, both their account and the accounts of all users they sponsor will be deactivated. Additionally, any job submitted by them or their sponsored users will be paused, and their research group will lose access to their files until the sponsor account is reactivated.
What should a faculty member do if their Alliance account or the accounts of their sponsored users are no longer needed, or if their situation changes?

If the accounts are no longer needed, the faculty member can let them expire. Otherwise, they must request that the accounts be renewed or apply for a new role if their situation or that of their sponsored user(s) has changed.
What should I do if I have renewed my Alliance account with the wrong role?

If you have renewed your Alliance account with the wrong role, you should create a new role using your current information. You can do this by logging into CCDB, navigating to 'My Account' in the main menu, and selecting 'Apply for a new role'. Your sponsor will then receive an email to confirm this new role.
What happens to an old Alliance account role if a user creates a new role after an incorrect renewal?

If a user creates a new role after incorrectly renewing their Alliance account with the wrong role, the old role will automatically expire and be deactivated on the morning of June 11, 2025, if it is not renewed.
How can I add multiple roles to my Alliance account, and can I set more than one as my primary role?

To add multiple roles to your account, visit https://ccdb.alliancecan.ca/me/add_role and click on “disable old roles” on that page. While it is possible to submit several applications for different roles, you can only set one of them as your primary role.
What should I do if my sponsor is unable to confirm an old sponsored role that I am trying to reactivate?
If you are trying to reactivate an old sponsored role and your sponsor cannot confirm it, please send an email to renewals@tech.alliancecan.ca for assistance.
Why do users need to renew their Alliance accounts annually?
Annual renewal of Alliance user accounts is essential to collect up-to-date information required by granting agencies and to deactivate accounts that are no longer in use.
Who is required to renew their Alliance account and when?
All Alliance users must renew their account between May 6 and June 9, 2026, unless they created their account after January 1 of the current year.
What happens if an Alliance account is not renewed by the deadline?
If an Alliance account is not renewed by the deadline, it will be automatically deactivated, preventing access to data, but the data will not be immediately deleted.
Are there any exceptions for recent Alliance account holders regarding the annual renewal?
Yes, if an Alliance account was created after January 1, it does not need to be renewed at that time, but the user must still accept new policies and consents on CCDB.
Where can an Alliance user find the Privacy Policy and other agreements they have accepted?
All agreements that an Alliance user has accepted, including Policies, Standards, Terms, and Procedures, can be viewed on the 'Agreements' page within CCDB.
What is considered a primary role within the Alliance account system and why is it important?

A primary role in the Alliance account system should correspond to a user's main or longest-held position, and it is important for managing multiple roles, facilitating communication, and reporting purposes.
Can a user change their primary role on their Alliance account?
Yes, users with multiple active roles can change their primary role at any time on CCDB's 'Home' page by clicking the 'Make this role primary' checkbox next to the desired role.
What should an Alliance user do if their situation changes, such as moving to a new faculty position or transitioning from a Master's to a PhD program?
If an Alliance user's situation changes, they must apply for a new role through CCDB's 'My Account' section, and they can choose to disable old roles if they are no longer needed.
If an Alliance account has expired and been deactivated, but the user still needs access to their data, what action should they take?
If an Alliance account has expired but the user needs access to their data to move it off the Alliance Federation clusters, they should send an email to support@tech.alliancecan.ca for assistance.
What are the consequences for a faculty member (PI) if they do not renew their Alliance account by the deadline?

If a faculty member (PI) does not renew their Alliance account, their account, as well as the accounts of all sponsored users, will be deactivated, pausing jobs and causing their research group to lose file access until the PI's account is reactivated.
How does a Principal Investigator (PI) renew their Alliance account?

A PI renews their Alliance account by following a link in an email to the CCDB form, updating contact and research information, completing a user satisfaction survey, updating sponsored roles, and then clicking the 'REQUEST ACCOUNT RENEWAL' button.
If a Principal Investigator (PI) with a faculty role moves to a different institution, will their sponsored users automatically transfer to their new role?

No, if a PI with a faculty role moves to a different institution, any user they want to sponsor with their new role must apply for a new role sponsored by the PI's new faculty position, and they may need to be re-added to any Resource Allocation Project (RAP).
What should a Principal Investigator (PI) do to access files of a sponsored user who is no longer under their sponsorship?

A PI needing to access files of a sponsored user who has moved on should make arrangements with that user for their consent as soon as possible to mitigate the risk of the user becoming incommunicado.
What is the process for a user with a sponsored role (e.g., Doctoral, Masters) to renew their Alliance account?

A user with a sponsored role receives an email with a link to the CCDB renewal form, where they must update their contact information, complete a user satisfaction survey, and click 'REQUEST ACCOUNT RENEWAL,' provided their sponsor has indicated they are continuing.
Why might a sponsored user's Alliance account remain deactivated even after they have completed their own renewal on CCDB?

A sponsored user's Alliance account may remain deactivated even after their own renewal because their sponsor has not yet renewed or reactivated their own account and confirmed the sponsored user's role.
What should a sponsored user do if they mistakenly renewed their Alliance account with the wrong role?

If a sponsored user mistakenly renewed their account with the wrong role, they should create a new role with their current information by logging into CCDB and going to 'My Account' then 'Apply for a new role', and their sponsor will then confirm this new role.
Who should an Alliance user contact if their account renewal question is not answered in the FAQ?
If an Alliance user's account renewal question is not answered in the FAQ, they should send an email to renewals@tech.alliancecan.ca for assistance.
When should researchers acknowledge the Digital Research Alliance of Canada and its regional partner organizations in their publications or reports?

Researchers are requested to acknowledge the Digital Research Alliance of Canada and its regional partner organizations (ACENET, Calcul Québec, Compute Ontario, the BC DRI Group, and Prairies DRI) when publications or reports are published on research that utilized resources provided by either organization. These resources include computing, visualization or storage hardware, software, collaboration facilities, staff expertise/consultation, or data sets.
What is the recommended wording for acknowledging the Digital Research Alliance of Canada and its regional partner organizations in research publications or reports?

For research that used resources from a regional partner and the Alliance, the guideline is: “This research was enabled in part by support provided by (name of the regional partner organization) (Web address) and the Digital Research Alliance of Canada (alliance​can​.ca).” If only using the publicly available Alliance software environment, the guideline is: "This research was enabled in part by software provided by the Digital Research Alliance of Canada (alliance​can​.ca)."
Why is it important to notify the Digital Research Alliance of Canada about acknowledgments, and who should researchers contact to share news about their research successes?

Notifying the Digital Research Alliance of Canada about acknowledgments is valuable for their annual impact reports to the Canada Foundation for Innovation, which helps build a case for long-term and sustainable funding. The Alliance is also interested in showcasing research success stories on their website or in their community newsletter. Researchers can contact communications@alliancecan.ca to share news about research that uses Alliance or regional partner resources.
Why are researchers requested to acknowledge the Digital Research Alliance of Canada and its regional partner organizations?
Researchers are requested to acknowledge them when publications or reports are published on research that used their provided resources.
Which specific resources, if utilized, necessitate an acknowledgment to the Digital Research Alliance of Canada and its regional partners?
Acknowledging is required for the use of computing, visualization or storage hardware, software, collaboration facilities, staff expertise/consultation, or data sets.
What organizations must be mentioned in an acknowledgment when using resources from the Digital Research Alliance of Canada?
Both the Digital Research Alliance of Canada and the relevant regional partner organization (e.g., ACENET, Calcul Québec, Compute Ontario, the BC DRI Group, or Prairies DRI) must be mentioned.
What is the recommended guideline for acknowledging the Digital Research Alliance of Canada and its regional partners in research publications?
The guideline is: “This research was enabled in part by support provided by (name of the regional partner organization) (Web address) and the Digital Research Alliance of Canada (alliancecan.ca).”
How should a researcher acknowledge the Digital Research Alliance of Canada if they only used its publicly available software environment and are not an Alliance user?
The guideline is: “This research was enabled in part by software provided by the Digital Research Alliance of Canada (alliancecan.ca).”
What does the Digital Research Alliance of Canada request from researchers who have included an acknowledgment in their publications?
They would appreciate being sent references of these acknowledgments.
Why is it important for the Digital Research Alliance of Canada to receive references of acknowledgments from researchers?
These references are valuable for their annual impact reports to the Canada Foundation for Innovation, helping to build a case for long-term and sustainable funding.
How does the Digital Research Alliance of Canada help showcase researchers' success stories?
They are interested in showcasing success stories in their website's Research Showcase section, in their community newsletter, or by collaborating on media releases.
To whom should researchers send news or acknowledgments regarding research that used resources from the Digital Research Alliance of Canada or its regional partners?
Researchers should contact communications@alliancecan.ca.
What are some of the regional partner organizations of the Digital Research Alliance of Canada mentioned in the document?
The regional partner organizations include ACENET, Calcul Québec, Compute Ontario, the BC DRI Group, and Prairies DRI.
What is the primary recommendation for users considering the instructions on configuring and submitting a JupyterLab job on a national cluster?

The content of this page, which details configuring and submitting a JupyterLab job, is intended for advanced users only and is not recommended; users are advised to consider using the preconfigured JupyterLab environment instead.
According to the guidelines, where should a JupyterLab server be deployed on a cluster, and what kind of tasks is it designed for?

A JupyterLab server should only be deployed on a compute node or a cloud instance, as cluster login nodes have limitations. It is designed for short interactive tasks such as testing, debugging, or quickly visualizing data; longer analyses should be performed using non-interactive sbatch jobs.
What are the initial steps to install JupyterLab on a national cluster using the provided instructions?

The installation of JupyterLab on a national cluster involves creating and activating a Python virtual environment, which includes loading a Python module, then using `pip install jupyterlab` within that environment.
What is the purpose of the Jupyter Lmod extension for JupyterLab, and what are the steps to install it?

The Jupyter Lmod extension allows users to interact with environment modules, such as loading, unloading, or saving a collection, directly from within the JupyterLab interface before launching kernels. It achieves this by utilizing the Lmod's Python interface. To install it, one must first load the `nodejs` module, then execute `pip install jupyterlmod`, and finally run `jupyter labextension install jupyterlab-lmod`.
What is the RStudio Server extension for JupyterLab, and how does its installation differ from a standard JupyterLab setup?

The RStudio Server extension enables users to develop R code within an RStudio environment that appears in a separate web browser tab, integrated with JupyterLab. The key differences in its installation procedure, compared to a standard JupyterLab setup, are that the `rstudio-server` module must be loaded before the `python` module and before creating a new Python virtual environment. Subsequently, after JupyterLab is installed in the virtual environment, the `jupyter-rsession-proxy` package needs to be installed using `pip install --no-index jupyter-rsession-proxy`.
How do you enable RStudio Server functionality within an installed JupyterLab environment on a national cluster?

To enable RStudio Server functionality within an installed JupyterLab environment, you must first load the `rstudio-server` module before the `python` module and before creating a new virtual environment using `module load rstudio-server python`. After JupyterLab is installed in the new virtual environment, you then install the Jupyter RSession proxy by executing `pip install --no-index jupyter-rsession-proxy`.
What is the command to start a JupyterLab server on a compute node on a national cluster, assuming the Python virtual environment is already activated?

To start a JupyterLab server on a compute node, you need to submit an interactive job using `salloc`. An example command is `salloc --time=1:0:0 --ntasks=1 --cpus-per-task=2 --mem-per-cpu=1024M --account=def-yourpi srun $VIRTUAL_ENV/bin/jupyterlab.sh`. You should adjust parameters like time, tasks, CPUs, memory, and account based on your specific needs, and ensure your Python virtual environment is active.
How can a user access a JupyterLab server running on a compute node from their local web browser if the compute node is not directly accessible from the internet?

To access a JupyterLab server running on a compute node from a local web browser, a user must create an SSH tunnel from their local computer through the cluster. On Linux or macOS, the `sshuttle` Python package is recommended, used with a command like `sshuttle --dns -Nr <username>@<cluster>.alliancecan.ca`. On Windows, an SSH tunnel can be created using MobaXTerm or any terminal supporting `ssh` by port-forwarding (e.g., `ssh -L 8888:<hostname:port> <username>@<cluster>.alliancecan.ca`), and then navigating to `http://localhost:8888/?token=<token>` in a web browser.
How do Windows users connect to a JupyterLab instance running on a compute node?

Windows users can connect to a JupyterLab instance running on a compute node by creating an SSH tunnel. This can be done using MobaXTerm or any terminal that supports the `ssh` command, after extracting the `hostname:port` and `token` from the JupyterLab's provided HTTP address.
What information must be extracted from the JupyterLab HTTP address to establish an SSH tunnel from Windows?

To establish an SSH tunnel from Windows, users must extract the `hostname:port` (e.g., `node_name.int.cluster.alliancecan.ca:8888`) and the `token` (the alphanumerical value after `token=`) from the first provided HTTP address generated when JupyterLab is launched.
Once an SSH tunnel is established from Windows, what is the address used in a web browser to access JupyterLab?

After establishing an SSH tunnel from Windows, users should open their web browser and go to `http://localhost:8888/?token=<token>`, replacing `<token>` with the alphanumerical value extracted from the original JupyterLab server URL.
How can a user connect to a JupyterLab server running on a compute node from a Windows machine?

To connect to a JupyterLab server running on a compute node from a Windows machine, you need to create an SSH tunnel using MobaXTerm. First, extract the `hostname:port` and `token` from the HTTP address provided by the JupyterLab server. Then, open a new Terminal tab in MobaXTerm and execute the command `ssh -L 8888:<hostname:port> <username>@<cluster>.alliancecan.ca`, replacing the bracketed placeholders with your specific values. Finally, open your web browser and navigate to `http://localhost:8888/?token=<token>`, substituting `<token>` with the extracted alphanumerical value.
What is the two-step process for adding a new kernel for a programming language or a different Python version to JupyterLab?

The installation of a new kernel in JupyterLab is accomplished in two main steps. First, you must install the packages that enable the language interpreter to communicate with the Jupyter interface. Second, you need to create a kernel spec file, which informs JupyterLab on how to initiate a communication channel with the language interpreter, and save this file in a subfolder of `~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels`.
What are the initial steps to configure a custom Python kernel for JupyterLab in a new Python virtual environment?

To configure a custom Python kernel for JupyterLab, begin by creating and activating a Python virtual environment. This involves loading a Python module, creating the environment (e.g., using `virtualenv --no-download $HOME/jupyter_py3`), and then activating it with `source $HOME/jupyter_py3/bin/activate`. Next, create the common `kernels` folder using `mkdir -p ~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels`. Finally, install the `ipykernel` library with `pip install --no-index ipykernel` and generate the kernel spec file by running `python -m ipykernel install --user --name <unique_name> --display-name "Python 3.x Kernel"`, replacing `<unique_name>` with a unique identifier for your kernel. It is important to start or restart a new JupyterLab session before using the new Python kernel.
What are the steps to configure a custom Python kernel within a Python virtual environment for JupyterLab?

To configure a custom Python kernel for JupyterLab, you must first ensure a Python virtual environment is created and activated. Next, create a common `kernels` folder by running `mkdir -p ~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels`. Finally, install the `ipykernel` library using `pip install --no-index ipykernel` and then generate the kernel spec file by executing `python -m ipykernel install --user --name <unique_name> --display-name "Python 3.x Kernel"`. After these steps, it's important to start or restart your JupyterLab session.
How can you install additional Python libraries into a custom Python virtual environment that is already configured as a JupyterLab kernel?

To install additional Python libraries, ensure your custom Python virtual environment is active. If using the Jupyter Terminal via JupyterHub, ensure the activated Python virtual environment is running in a clean Bash environment. Then, you can install any required library using the `pip install --no-index <library_name>` command. For example, to install `numpy`, you would use `pip install --no-index numpy`. Once installed, these libraries will be available for use in any notebook utilizing the `Python 3.x Kernel`.
What are the prerequisites and steps to configure an R kernel for JupyterLab, and why is a login node required for some parts of the installation?

Prerequisites for configuring an R kernel in JupyterLab include having a Python virtual environment and a `kernels` folder. The installation must be performed in a remote shell session on a login node because R packages require access to CRAN (Comprehensive R Archive Network) for installation. The steps involve: loading an R module (e.g., `module load r/4.1`), then within an R shell, installing R kernel dependencies (`crayon`, `pbdZMQ`, `devtools`) using `install.packages`, followed by installing the R kernel itself via `devtools::install_github` and finally installing the R kernel spec file with `IRkernel::installspec()`. After completing these steps, you must start or restart your JupyterLab session.
What are the initial steps for setting up a custom Python kernel for JupyterLab within a new Python virtual environment?

The initial steps involve creating and activating a Python virtual environment. This process includes optionally starting from a clean Bash environment (if using the Jupyter Terminal via JupyterHub), loading a Python module, creating a new Python virtual environment (e.g., `virtualenv --no-download $HOME/jupyter_py3`), and activating it (e.g., `source $HOME/jupyter_py3/bin/activate`). Following this, a common `kernels` folder must be created in `~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels`.
After preparing a Python virtual environment and `kernels` folder, what are the final steps to install and register a Python kernel for use with JupyterLab?

The final steps involve installing the `ipykernel` library using `pip install --no-index ipykernel` within the activated virtual environment. Following this, the kernel spec file is generated using the command `python -m ipykernel install --user --name <unique_name> --display-name "Python 3.x Kernel"`, replacing `<unique_name>` with a unique identifier. It is crucial to start or restart a new JupyterLab session afterward for the new kernel to be recognised.
How do users install additional R packages for a JupyterLab R kernel on a national cluster?

To install additional R packages for an R kernel in a JupyterLab environment, users must perform the installation from a login node, not directly from a Jupyter notebook. First, load the specific R module (e.g., `r/4.1`). Then, launch an R shell using `R --no-save` and execute `install.packages('package_name', repos='http://cran.us.r-project.org')`, replacing 'package_name' with the desired package. The Python virtual environment can be deactivated during this process.
Why can't R packages be installed directly from notebooks within a JupyterLab environment on a national cluster?

R packages cannot be installed directly from notebooks within a JupyterLab environment on a national cluster because notebooks do not have access to CRAN (the Comprehensive R Archive Network), which is essential for installing R packages.
How can additional R packages be installed for use with an R kernel in JupyterLab?

To install additional R packages for an R kernel, first ensure the appropriate R module is loaded. Then, from a login node (as installation cannot be done from notebooks due to lack of CRAN access), start the R shell using `R --no-save` and execute `install.packages('your_package_name', repos='http://cran.us.r-project.org')`, replacing 'your_package_name' with the desired package like 'doParallel'.
Why is it necessary to convert Jupyter notebooks to Python scripts for execution on national clusters?

Jupyter notebooks need to be converted to Python scripts for longer runs or analyses that should be submitted as non-interactive jobs using a job scheduler like `sbatch`, as interactive tasks are meant for short durations.
What is the process for converting a Jupyter notebook to a Python script and submitting it as a non-interactive job?

From a login node, first create and activate a Python virtual environment, then install `nbconvert` if it's not already available using `pip install --no-index nbconvert`. Next, convert the notebook to a Python script using `jupyter nbconvert --to python mynotebook.ipynb`. Finally, create a submission script that includes `python mynotebook.py` to run the converted script, and submit it as a non-interactive job using `sbatch my-submit.sh`.
What are the recommended use cases for JupyterLab and Jupyter notebooks for users on Alliance clusters?

JupyterLab and notebooks are meant for short interactive tasks like testing, debugging, or quickly visualizing data (a few minutes). Longer analysis tasks should be done in a non-interactive job using `sbatch`.
What is Project Jupyter, as described in the documentation for advanced Jupyter configuration on Alliance clusters?
Project Jupyter is a non-profit, open-source project born from the IPython Project in 2014, supporting interactive data science and scientific computing across all programming languages.
What is JupyterLab, according to the documentation for advanced Jupyter configuration on Alliance clusters?

JupyterLab is a web-based interactive development environment for notebooks, code, and data, offering a flexible interface and modular design for various workflows in data science, scientific computing, and machine learning.
Why is it not recommended to run a JupyterLab server on cluster login nodes on Alliance clusters?

Cluster login nodes impose various limits that can stop applications consuming too much CPU time or memory, making them unsuitable for running a JupyterLab server. It should run on a compute node or cloud instance instead.
What is the general procedure for installing JupyterLab on an Alliance national cluster using a Python virtual environment?

The general procedure involves creating and activating a Python virtual environment, then using `pip` to install JupyterLab within that environment, followed by creating and making executable a wrapper script to launch JupyterLab.
Which specific module must be loaded before the Python module and virtual environment creation if a user intends to use RStudio Server with JupyterLab on an Alliance cluster?
If a user intends to use RStudio Server, they must load the `rstudio-server` module before loading `python` and creating a new Python virtual environment.
What command is used to activate a Python virtual environment containing a JupyterLab installation on an Alliance cluster?
The command `source $HOME/jupyter_py3/bin/activate` is used to activate a Python virtual environment named `jupyter_py3`.
How do users start a JupyterLab server on a compute node on an Alliance cluster using an interactive job?

Users start a JupyterLab server by submitting an interactive job with the `salloc` command, specifying resources like time, CPU cores, memory, and account, then running the JupyterLab wrapper script via `srun`.
Why is an SSH tunnel necessary to connect to a JupyterLab server running on a compute node from a local web browser on Alliance clusters?

What is the recommended tool for creating an SSH tunnel to a JupyterLab server from a Windows operating system when connecting to an Alliance cluster?
MobaXTerm is the recommended tool for creating an SSH tunnel to a JupyterLab server from a Windows operating system.
How can a user manually shut down a running JupyterLab server before its allocated walltime limit on an Alliance cluster?
A user can manually shut down the JupyterLab server by pressing **Ctrl-C twice** in the terminal where the interactive job was launched.

What are the prerequisites for configuring a Julia kernel for JupyterLab on an Alliance cluster, particularly regarding Python and internet access?

Prerequisites include having an available and activated Python virtual environment and a `kernels` folder. The configuration process, including installing Julia packages, must be done from a remote shell session on a login node to access the internet.
How are additional Julia packages installed for use with the Julia kernel in JupyterLab on an Alliance cluster?

Additional Julia packages are installed by loading the appropriate Julia module on a login node and then using `Pkg.add("PackageName")` via the Julia shell. The Python virtual environment can be deactivated for this step.
How are additional Python libraries installed for a custom Python kernel within a JupyterLab environment on an Alliance cluster?
Additional Python libraries are installed by ensuring the correct Python virtual environment is activated and then using `pip install --no-index <library_name>` within that environment.
What are the prerequisites and steps for installing additional R packages for an R kernel in JupyterLab on an Alliance cluster?

Prerequisites include an active R kernel with dependencies installed. Users must load the same R module on a login node and use `install.packages('PackageName', repos='http://cran.us.r-project.org')` from the R shell, as installation cannot be done directly from notebooks due to lack of CRAN access.
For longer analysis tasks, how can a Jupyter notebook be run as a non-interactive job on Alliance clusters?

For longer analysis, a Jupyter notebook can be converted into a Python script using `jupyter nbconvert --to python mynotebook.ipynb` after installing `nbconvert`. This Python script is then executed within a submission script for a non-interactive `sbatch` job.
What is the purpose of the CCDB portal and who is eligible to register for an account to access Alliance Federation resources?

The CCDB portal is a gateway to account and allocation information for the Advanced Computing Platform managed by the Digital Research Alliance of Canada, allowing users to access resources hosted by the Alliance Federation. Eligibility extends to faculty members at CFI-eligible Canadian universities, who can then sponsor their students, research staff, and collaborators. Researchers from government, non-profits, and industry may also be eligible, and should direct inquiries to accounts@tech.alliancecan.ca.
What are the initial steps for a new user to create a CCDB account with the Digital Research Alliance of Canada?

To create a new CCDB account, a user must go to the login page, click the 'Register' link, and read and accept the required agreements. After accepting and submitting, they complete a form with all required information, including their institutional email address. Following the submission, they will receive a confirmation email, and must click on the confirmation link within that email to proceed.
How does the CCDB account registration and approval process differ for Principal Investigators (PIs) compared to Group Members?

Principal Investigators (PIs) must register first, and their account requests are processed by an administrator, typically within 2 business days. Once approved, PIs receive a Role Identifier (CCRI). Group Members follow a similar registration process but must provide their sponsor's CCRI and do not need to provide research area information. Their applications are subject to approval by their sponsor, who receives an email confirmation request once the Group Member completes the first registration step.
When can a Group Member access their CCDB account after completing their registration's first step?
A Group Member can only log in to their CCDB account once their Sponsor has approved their application request, even after completing the first step of registration.
What is the process for a Sponsor to approve a Group Member's account application for the CCDB?

Once a Group Member confirms their email in Step 1 of registration, their Sponsor will receive an email containing a confirmation link. New application requests will also appear on the Sponsor's CCDB home page. To approve, the Sponsor must click this confirmation link, verify the accuracy of the Group Member's provided information (especially ensuring it's their institutional email), and then click the 'Confirm this role' button.
What information is provided to a user after their CCDB account request has been approved?
Once a CCDB account request has been approved, the user will receive a notification email that includes their Role Identifier (CCRI).
What is the primary responsibility of a Principal Investigator (PI) regarding Group Members after their own CCDB registration is complete?

After completing their own CCDB registration, a Principal Investigator (PI) must provide their CCRI to all Group Members they sponsor, and then confirm every individual Group Member who registers for a CCDB account using that CCRI.
What is the purpose of the CCDB portal in the context of the Alliance Federation?

The CCDB portal is a gateway for users to access resources hosted across Canada by the Alliance and its regional partners, providing account and allocation information for the Advanced Computing Platform.
Who is eligible to register for a CCDB account with the Alliance Federation?

Faculty members at CFI-eligible Canadian universities are eligible, and they can sponsor students, research staff, and collaborators. Researchers from government, non-profits, and industry may also be eligible.
What should a user do if they already possess a CCDB account, even if it is currently deactivated?
Users who already have a CCDB account, even if deactivated, do not need to apply for a new one and should instead consult the Account Renewals FAQ.
How many user roles does the CCDB classify, and where can users find detailed descriptions of each?
The CCDB has 12 classifications of user roles, and detailed descriptions and key characteristics of each are available on the User Roles page.
What is the initial step for a Principal Investigator (PI) when registering for a new CCDB account?
A Principal Investigator must first go to the CCDB login page, click on the 'Register' link, and then read and accept the required agreements before proceeding with the application.
What is a CCRI, and how long does it typically take for a Principal Investigator to receive it after their CCDB registration is approved?
A CCRI is a Role Identifier included in a confirmation email sent to a Principal Investigator upon approval of their CCDB registration. The approval process can take up to two business days.
What specific information must a Group Member provide during their CCDB registration that differs from a Principal Investigator's requirements?
A Group Member must indicate their sponsor’s CCRI and is not required to provide information about their research area.
What is the significance of the 'Consent to Access User Data' agreement during the CCDB account creation process?
Accepting the 'Consent to Access User Data' is optional, but declining this agreement may restrict the Alliance's ability to provide necessary support in certain situations.
What type of email address should users utilize when registering for their CCDB account?
Users should register using their institutional email address.
Who is responsible for approving a Group Member's CCDB account application, and what is the general procedure?

A Group Member's account application is approved by their Sponsor. The Sponsor receives a confirmation email or can find the request on their CCDB home page, where they review the Group Member's information and click 'Confirm this role'.
What happens after a Principal Investigator (PI) submits their CCDB account application and confirms their email?

After a PI submits their application and confirms their email, an administrator will process their account request within two business days, verifying their faculty status at the specified institution.
What should a Group Member do if their sponsor does not receive the email prompting them to confirm the Group Member's application?
New sponsored role requests pending approval will also appear on the Principal Investigator's CCDB home page, providing an alternative confirmation link for the sponsor.
Where can applicants access the full text of the policies, standards, terms, and procedures they must accept during the CCDB registration process?
Applicants can read the full text of the policies by visiting the dedicated page on alliancecan.ca.
What should a user do if they have general questions regarding the process of obtaining a CCDB account?
If users have any questions about getting a CCDB account, they should send an email to accounts@tech.alliancecan.ca.
Once a Principal Investigator has their CCRI, what is their responsibility regarding the Group Members they wish to sponsor?
Once a Principal Investigator has their CCRI, they must provide it to all Group Members they intend to sponsor, as Group Members need it to register for their own CCDB accounts.
What is the primary benefit of following this procedure to connect to computing clusters from Windows using WSL?

The main benefit is the ability to leverage ControlMaster under Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), allowing users to log into clusters with several native Windows applications for a certain period without needing multifactor authentication for every session.
How does the general SSH connection flow work when using this ControlMaster setup with WSL for accessing a cluster like Cedar?

The general connection flow involves an SSH client on your Windows machine (e.g., 'smart'), which connects to an SSH relay server in your Ubuntu VM (e.g., 'ubuntu'), and this relay server then connects to the final SSH target server, such as Cedar.
What specific software package needs to be installed on the Ubuntu VM to enable SSH connections as part of this ControlMaster setup?

To enable SSH connections as part of this setup, the `openssh-server` package must be installed on your Ubuntu VM. This is done by running `sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y` followed by `sudo apt install openssh-server -y`.
How does the alternative SSH setup, which may be more suitable for Windows GUI applications like WinSCP, work to connect to Alliance clusters via WSL?

In the alternative setup, to better support Windows GUI applications that cannot explicitly set a `RemoteCommand`, the `RemoteCommand ssh cedar` line is commented out or removed from the `~/.ssh/config` file on the Windows machine. Instead, the `authorized_keys` file on the Ubuntu VM is modified to include `command="ssh cedar"` directly before the public SSH key, allowing the command to be executed upon authentication. Users can still connect from a Windows shell using `ssh ubuntu -p 2222`.
What is a notable limitation when using native Windows applications (like WinSCP) with the ControlMaster setup under WSL for connecting to Alliance clusters?

A key limitation is that native Windows applications using this setup may display the file system of the Ubuntu relay server rather than the local Windows drives. This means users cannot directly list or access files on their Windows host from within these applications when attempting to transfer data to or from an Alliance cluster like Cedar. What are the common reasons why a job might be stuck in a pending state (`PD`) on an Alliance cluster, and how can a user check the reason?

Users can determine why their jobs are in the `PD` (pending) state by running the `squeue -u <username>` command on the cluster and examining the `(REASON)` column. Common reasons include `Resources`, indicating the cluster is busy and patience or fewer resource requests are needed, or `Priority`, meaning the user or their research group has recently over-consumed their fair share of cluster resources. Resource consumption can be tracked using the `sshare` command and its `LevelFS` column.
What do the messages "Nodes required for job are DOWN, DRAINED or RESERVED for jobs in higher priority partitions" or "ReqNodeNotAvailable" mean in the "Reason" field of Slurm's `squeue` output?

These messages, which are new to Slurm 19.05, indicate that one or more of the nodes Slurm considered for your job are currently unavailable, either because they are down, deliberately taken offline, or reserved for other jobs. These are not error messages; your job is actually in the queue and will eventually be processed. They effectively convey the same information as the "Resources" reason in Slurm version 17.11.
How accurate is the `START_TIME` displayed in the `squeue` command's output for pending jobs on Alliance clusters?

The `START_TIME` that Slurm forecasts for high-priority pending jobs is often not very useful because it depends on rapidly changing conditions. Slurm computes these expected start times based on available resources and higher-priority jobs, but frequently invalidates and recomputes its future plans if jobs end early or if prioritization changes. On general-purpose clusters, new jobs are submitted about every five seconds, and 30-50% of jobs end early, leading to frequent recomputations. Most waiting jobs will show "N/A" (not available) for `START_TIME`, meaning Slurm is not attempting to project a start time for them. However, for jobs that are already running, the start time reported by `squeue` is perfectly accurate.

How is the `LevelFS` column used to track resource consumption on an Alliance cluster, and what impact does it have on job priority?

The `LevelFS` column provides information about your over- or under-consumption of cluster resources. If `LevelFS` is greater than one, you are consuming fewer resources than your fair share, whereas if it is less than one, you are consuming more. The more you overconsume resources, which makes the `LevelFS` value closer to zero, the more your pending jobs decrease in priority.
Does the `LevelFS` calculation for resource consumption on Alliance clusters retain historical data indefinitely, and is its value consistent across all clusters?

No, the `LevelFS` calculation has a memory effect, meaning the scheduler gradually 'forgets' about any over- or under-consumption of resources from months past. Furthermore, the `LevelFS` value is unique to each specific cluster.
