What is the CCDB and what functionalities does it offer users?

The CCDB is the Alliance's online portal for managing user accounts. Through the CCDB, users can access information about their roles in projects, allocated resources, and usage statistics. It also enables users to register, manage personal information and roles, apply for the Resource Allocation Competition (RAC), and manage Resource Allocation Project (RAP) information and membership.
What is a Resource Allocation Project (RAP) in the Alliance system, and what is its purpose?

A Resource Allocation Project (RAP) is the primary method for Principal Investigators (PIs) to access national computational resources within the Alliance system. RAPs are designed to allocate computing resources to groups of researchers, not individuals, and are essential for providing accurate usage statistics to governmental funding agencies.
What are the two main types of Resource Allocation Projects (RAPs) in the Alliance system?

The two main types of Resource Allocation Projects (RAPs) are the Default RAP and the RAC RAP. A Default RAP is automatically created when a PI role is activated, managing quotas for storage and cloud resources, and allowing opportunistic, low-priority use of compute resources. A RAC RAP is established when a PI receives an award through the Resource Allocation Competition (RAC) application process.
Who automatically gains access to a Principal Investigator's (PI's) Default RAP, and how does this differ for RAC RAPs with HPC versus Cloud resources?

For a PI's Default RAP, all of their activated sponsored user roles are always members. For RAC RAPs created with HPC resources (e.g., CPU, GPU, project storage), CCDB automatically adds all of the PI's sponsored user roles, all associated Co-PI roles, and all sponsored user roles of the associated Co-PIs as members. Any new role the PI sponsors after the RAP's creation will also be automatically added. If the RAC RAP has Cloud resources, only the PI is added as a member at the time of its creation.
What are the three different permission levels for managing membership in a RAC RAP, and what specific actions can users at each level perform?

There are three RAP membership permission levels: Owner, Manager, and Member. The PI is the sole Owner and can add or remove RAP managers and members. A Manager, delegated by an Owner or another Manager, has elevated permission (on CCDB only) to make membership changes and can use the PI's allocation in the corresponding cluster(s), but cannot make changes on the project/nearline file systems on behalf of the PIs. A Member can use the PI’s allocation in the corresponding cluster(s) but cannot make any modifications to the RAP membership.
If an Alliance account holder's position or sponsor changes, or if they have lost their password, what steps should they take instead of creating a new Alliance account?

Each person is allowed only one Alliance account (one CCI). If your position or sponsor has changed, you should apply for a new role (which will have a new CCRI) instead, by logging into your existing account and visiting the 'apply for a new role' form. If you have forgotten your password, you may reset it. If you can no longer access the email address on file, you should email accounts@tech.alliancecan.ca for assistance.
What is a group name in the context of Resource Allocation Projects (RAPs) with the Alliance?

A group name serves as an alias for the Research Allocation Project Identifier (RAPI). While each RAPI has a unique group name (a one-to-one mapping), the group name is generally easier for users to remember.
What are the typical naming conventions for different types of Resource Allocation Project (RAP) group names?

Group names follow specific conventions, where 'xx' represents a sequence of digits and letters:
- Default RAP: `def-[profname][-xx]`
- RRG/HPC resource RAP: `rrg-[profname][-xx]`
- RPP/HPC resource RAP: `rpp-[profname][-xx]`
- RRG/Cloud resource RAP: `crg-[profname][-xx]`
- RPP/Cloud resource RAP: `cpp-[profname][-xx]`
How do users sign up for an Alliance account?

Users can sign up for an Alliance account by going to the register link on the CCDB portal. It is required to accept certain policies and agreements, which can be reviewed on the Alliance website, to complete the account registration.
Where can users view the policies and agreements they have accepted for their Alliance account?
Once an Alliance account has been approved, users can view the agreements they have accepted at any time on CCDB by navigating to 'My Account --> Agreements'.
What are the two main types of roles users can select when applying for an Alliance account?
There are two main types of roles users can select when applying for an Alliance account: sponsor roles, often referred to as Primary Investigators (PIs), and sponsored roles.
What are the two main types of roles available when applying for an account with the Alliance, and what are the eligibility requirements for a sponsor role?

The two main types of roles are 'sponsor' roles, often referred to as Primary Investigators (PIs), and 'sponsored' roles. Only faculty members from Canadian post-secondary academic institutions who are eligible for CFI funding can be sponsors. Administrators who are not faculty but lead research projects must contact accounts@tech.alliancecan.ca for appropriate accommodations.
What are the different categories of sponsored roles available when applying for an Alliance account, and who qualifies for each?

Sponsored roles fall into two groups: internal (part of the supervisor's local group) and external (a collaborator from a different institution). Available sponsored roles include: students (undergraduate, masters, doctoral); researchers affiliated with the same institution as the PI (postdoctoral fellow, or a researcher paid by the PI's institution); non-research staff (e.g., administrators, secretaries, who typically don't need compute resources); and external collaborators, who work with the PI's group but must specify an institution different from the PI's.
What is the approval process after submitting an application for an Alliance account role?

After submitting your request, you will receive an email with a link to confirm the email address you provided. If you are applying for a principal investigator (PI) role (typically a faculty member), your application will be approved by a Federation staff member. For all other sponsored roles, the application will need to be confirmed by the principal investigator you identified as your sponsor before it is approved by a Federation staff member.
What is the primary function of the CCDB portal for users within the Alliance system?
The CCDB portal serves as the main access point to your Alliance account, providing information on your project roles, allocated resources, and usage statistics.
What specific actions can a user perform on the Alliance CCDB portal?

On the Alliance CCDB portal, users can register, manage personal information and roles, apply for the Resource Allocation Competition (RAC), and manage Resource Allocation Project (RAP) details and membership.
What is a CCI within the Alliance system, and what is its typical format?
A CCI is a unique personal and national identifier created for you upon registration with the Alliance system. It typically follows a "3 letters-3 digits" format, such as abc-123.
Who is eligible to register for a CCI with the Alliance?

To be eligible for a CCI, you must be a faculty member at a Canadian institution registered with the CCDB, or be sponsored by such a faculty member. Sponsored individuals can include graduate students and research staff.
In the Alliance system, what does a 'role' represent, and why is it necessary?

A 'role' represents the combination of a person's position (e.g., faculty, graduate student), institution, and sponsor. A valid and up-to-date role is necessary to access Alliance computational resources.
What is a CCRI in the Alliance system, and how does it relate to a CCI?

A CCRI is the unique identifier for a specific role within the Alliance system, formatted as CCI-2 digits (e.g., abc-123-01). Since a person can have multiple roles, one CCI can be associated with more than one CCRI, and every job run on a national cluster is attributed to a CCRI.
What are the two main types of Resource Allocation Projects (RAPs) available through the Alliance?

The two main types of RAPs are the Default RAP, automatically created for a PI to manage default quotas and allow opportunistic compute use, and the RAC RAP, which is established when a PI receives an award through the Resource Allocation Competition.
What is the purpose of a group name for a Resource Allocation Project (RAP) in the Alliance system?

A group name serves as an alias for a Research Allocation Project Identifier (RAPI). It's often easier for users to remember and is utilized as a POSIX group name, defining a group of users authorized to submit jobs against the RAPI and share files.
How is membership handled for a PI's Default RAP compared to a RAC RAP with HPC resources in the Alliance system?

For a PI's Default RAP, all of their activated sponsored user roles are automatically members. For a RAC RAP with HPC resources, all of the PI's sponsored user roles, all associated Co-PI roles, and all sponsored user roles of those Co-PIs are automatically added.
Who initially has access to a RAC RAP that is specifically allocated with Cloud resources in the Alliance system?
When a new RAC RAP is created with Cloud resources allocated, only the Principal Investigator (PI) is initially added as a member.
What are the various permission levels for managing membership within a RAC RAP in the Alliance system?

There are three permission levels: Owner (the PI, who can add or remove managers and members), Manager (delegated by the owner or another manager, can make membership changes and use the allocation), and Member (can use the allocation but cannot make any modifications to the RAP membership).
What should a user do if they had a previous Alliance account but their position or sponsor has changed?

If a user had a previous Alliance account (CCI) and their position or sponsor has changed, they should not create a new account. Instead, they should log in with their existing account and apply for a new role, which will result in a new CCRI.
What types of roles can an applicant select when applying for an account or new role within the Alliance system?

Applicants can select sponsor roles (typically faculty members or PIs) or various sponsored roles, including students (undergraduate, masters, doctoral), researchers at the same institution, non-research staff, and external collaborators from different institutions.
How can users obtain additional assistance for questions not addressed in the Alliance's CCDB FAQ?
For any questions not covered in the FAQ, users can send an email to accounts@tech.alliancecan.ca.
What are the essential steps for generating an SSH key pair using PuTTY or MobaXTerm?

To generate an SSH key pair, first launch PuTTYGen or MobaKeyGen. Then, select "Ed25519" as the key type (or "RSA" with 2048 bits or greater) and click the "Generate" button, moving your mouse to create random data. Next, enter and remember a passphrase for your key. Finally, click "Save private key" to save it with a `.ppk` extension, and then "Save public key", conventionally with a `.pub` extension and the same name as the private key.
What are the recommended methods for installing the public part of an SSH key pair on Compute Canada HPC clusters?

There are two main methods for installing the public part of an SSH key pair. The encouraged method is to register it with the CCDB by copying the public key content into the "Public key for pasting into OpenSSH ..." box on the CCDB -> Manage SSH Keys page. Alternatively, you can install it locally on each cluster by pasting the public key content as a single line at the end of `/home/USERNAME/.ssh/authorized_keys` and ensuring the correct permissions and ownership for the `~/.ssh` directory and its files.
How do you convert a .pem key, typically generated on OpenStack, for use with PuTTY?

To convert a .pem key for use with PuTTY, open PuTTYGen and click the "Load" button. Change the file filter to "All Files (*.*)", then select the .pem file downloaded from OpenStack and click "Open". You should also add a "Key passphrase" at this point, and then click "Save private key" to save it in PuTTY's format.
What is the primary purpose of this document concerning SSH keys?
This document provides instructions on how to generate, install, and use SSH key pairs for secure access to Alliance HPC clusters and OpenStack virtual machines.
Which software applications are used to generate an SSH key pair, as described in this document?
PuTTYGen and MobaKeyGen (accessible through the MobaXTerm menu) are the applications used to generate an SSH key pair.
When generating an SSH key pair, what is the recommended type of key to select, and what is an acceptable alternative?
The recommended key type to generate is 'Ed25519'. 'RSA' is also acceptable, provided the 'Number of bits' is set to 2048 or greater.
Why is it important to remember the passphrase entered during the SSH key generation process?
It is crucial to remember the passphrase because it will be required every time the key pair is reloaded in PuTTY or MobaXTerm to use the private key.
What are the conventional file extensions for saving the private and public parts of an SSH key pair generated with PuTTYGen?
The private key is conventionally saved with a `.ppk` extension, and the public key is saved with a `.pub` extension.
What are the two main methods for installing the public part of an SSH key pair for use with Alliance clusters?
The two main methods are registering the public key with the CCDB (Compute Canada Database) or installing it locally on each individual cluster.
What is the benefit of registering an SSH public key with the CCDB?
Registering an SSH public key with the CCDB allows the user to use it to log in to any Alliance HPC cluster.
If a user opts not to use the CCDB, how can they install their SSH public key locally on an Alliance cluster?
They can copy the public key content and paste it as a single line at the end of the `/home/USERNAME/.ssh/authorized_keys` file on the cluster they wish to connect to.
What must be ensured regarding file and directory permissions after installing an SSH public key locally on an Alliance cluster?
Users must ensure that the permissions and ownership of the `~/.ssh` directory and the files within it are correct, as specified in the provided instructions.
What command-line tool can be used as an alternative for local public key installation if available on a personal computer?
The `ssh-copy-id` tool can be used for local public key installation if it is available on the user's personal computer.
How can a user verify that a newly generated SSH key pair is working correctly after installation?
Users can test the new key by attempting to connect to the server using SSH with their chosen client, such as PuTTY or MobaXTerm.
What is the procedure for converting an OpenStack key, which typically has a `.pem` extension, for use with PuTTY?
An OpenStack `.pem` key can be converted by clicking the 'Load' button in PuTTYGen, selecting 'All Files (*.*)' to find the `.pem` file, and then saving the private key in PuTTY's `.ppk` format.
What crucial step should be performed after loading an OpenStack `.pem` key into PuTTYGen during the conversion process?
Users should add a 'Key passphrase' at this point to protect their private key for future access.
What is the purpose of a private key that has been converted from an OpenStack `.pem` file to PuTTY's format?
The converted private key can be used with PuTTY to connect to a virtual machine that was created with OpenStack.
Where can users find a video demonstration related to PuTTY SSH key setup for passwordless logins?
A video titled 'Easily setup PuTTY SSH keys for passwordless logins using Pageant' is linked in the 'Connecting using a key pair' section of the document.
What steps should a new user take to obtain an account and gain access to the national systems?

New users must first apply for a CCDB account. Once an account is established, they need to request access to specific systems such as Arbutus, Fir, Narval, Nibi, Rorqual, and Trillium through the 'Access Systems' page within the CCDB.
What are the different types of computing systems available to users, and what are their primary applications?

The available systems include Arbutus, which is a cloud site allowing users to launch and customize virtual machines. Fir, Narval, Nibi, and Rorqual are general-purpose clusters (supercomputers) comprising various nodes, including large memory nodes and those with accelerators like GPUs. Trillium is a homogeneous cluster (supercomputer) specifically designed for large parallel jobs that require more than 1000 cores.
How do users determine their username and password for logging into the national systems?
The password required to log into all new national systems is the same one used for the CCDB. After logging into the CCDB, a user's specific username will be displayed at the top of the page.
What computing systems are available through the Alliance, and what are their specific purposes?

The Alliance offers several systems: Arbutus, which is a cloud site for launching and customizing virtual machines; Fir, Narval, Nibi, and Rorqual, which are general-purpose clusters (supercomputers) composed of a variety of nodes, including large memory nodes and nodes with accelerators such as GPUs; and Trillium, which is a homogeneous cluster designed for large parallel jobs exceeding 1000 cores.
How can a user obtain access to the Alliance's computing systems, such as Arbutus or Trillium?
Users must request access to one or more of the available systems through the 'Access Systems' page on the CCDB website (ccdb.alliancecan.ca/me/access_systems).
What kind of information should a user be prepared to provide to technical support to determine the most suitable computing system for their research needs?

To help identify the best resource, users may be asked about the software they want to use (e.g., commercial license, non-interactive use, Linux compatibility), the estimated resource requirements for a typical job (e.g., memory, time, computing power, accelerators, storage, network bandwidth), and how frequently they will need to run this type of job.
Which regional partners organize workshops and offer training opportunities for the Alliance?
Workshops and training are organized by the Alliance's regional partners, including WestDRI, SHARCNET, SciNet, Calcul Québec, and ACENET.
Where can users find information about upcoming training sessions and recorded webinars from WestDRI?
Users can find upcoming sessions and browse recorded webinars on WestDRI's Training Materials website, or view videos of previous UAlberta ARC Bootcamp sessions.
Is there a centralized location to view a complete list of all upcoming training events offered by the Alliance's regional partners?
Yes, a complete and merged list of upcoming training events can be found on Explora.
What is the main purpose of this document regarding Alliance computing resources?

This document serves as an introductory guide for users to navigate and utilize Alliance computing resources, covering topics from account creation and system access to data transfer and software management.
What are the initial steps for new users to gain access to Alliance computing resources?
New users must apply for a CCDB account and set up multifactor authentication. Experienced HPC users can proceed to learn about available systems, software, and job submission.
Which topics are available for experienced HPC users seeking to use Alliance clusters?
Experienced HPC users can find information about available systems, available software, how environment modules work, how to submit jobs, and how filesystems are organized.
What introductory information is provided for individuals new to high-performance computing (HPC) with Alliance systems?
New HPC users can read about connecting to systems with SSH, an introduction to Linux systems, and how to transfer files to and from Alliance systems.
Which service is recommended for transferring large volumes of data, specifically hundreds of gigabytes, across the network with Alliance systems?
The Globus file transfer service is recommended for moving hundreds of gigabytes of data across the network.
How do users log in to the new national Alliance systems, and where can they find their username?
Users log in using the same password as their CCDB account. Their username is displayed at the top of the CCDB page once they have logged in.
What are the main types of computing systems available through Alliance, and how do users gain access?

Alliance offers cloud sites (e.g., Arbutus), general-purpose clusters (e.g., Fir, Narval, Nibi, Rorqual), and homogeneous clusters for large parallel jobs (e.g., Trillium). Users must request access to these systems via the 'Access Systems' page in CCDB.
What is Arbutus, and what is its primary function within the Alliance computing ecosystem?
Arbutus is a cloud site that enables users to launch and customize virtual machines.
Which Alliance clusters are classified as general-purpose supercomputers, and what do they offer?
Fir, Narval, Nibi, and Rorqual are general-purpose clusters (supercomputers) that include a variety of nodes, such as large memory nodes and nodes with GPU accelerators.
What is the specific design purpose of the Trillium cluster?
Trillium is a homogeneous cluster designed for large parallel jobs requiring more than 1000 cores.
How can users determine which Alliance computing system is most appropriate for their specific needs?

If the system descriptions are insufficient, users should contact technical support, who will ask about software requirements, memory, time, computing power, accelerators, storage, and network bandwidth to help identify the best resource.
Are there any discipline-specific guides available for using Alliance resources?

Yes, guides are in preparation for disciplines such as AI and Machine Learning, Bioinformatics, Biomolecular simulation, Computational chemistry, Computational fluid dynamics (CFD), Geographic information systems (GIS), and Visualization.
Where can Python and R users find specialized guidance for their programming environments on Alliance systems?
Python users can learn how to install modules in a virtual environment, and R users can learn how to install packages.
When should users consider utilizing Alliance's cloud resources instead of the HPC clusters?
Users should consider cloud resources if they wish to experiment with software that does not run effectively on the HPC clusters.
Where can users find information about training and workshops for Alliance computing resources?

Training opportunities, including online and in-person workshops, are organized by Alliance's regional partners. Users can consult the training calendars and websites for WestDRI, SHARCNET, SciNet, Calcul Québec, and ACENET, or the merged list on Explora.
What is Globus, and what are its main benefits for researchers involved in file transfers?

Globus is a service designed specifically for researchers that provides fast, reliable, and secure file transfers. It offers an easy-to-use interface with background monitoring features to automate the management of file transfers between various resources, including Alliance clusters, supercomputing facilities, campus clusters, lab servers, desktops, and laptops. Globus improves transfer performance over protocols like GridFTP, rsync, scp, and sftp by automatically tuning transfer settings, restarting interrupted transfers, and checking file integrity.
How do users log in to the Digital Research Alliance of Canada Globus portal?

To log in to the Alliance Globus portal, users should go to globus.alliancecan.ca. On the initial page, ensure that 'Digital Research Alliance of Canada' is selected in the drop-down menu, then click 'Continue'. A second page will appear where users need to provide their CCDB username (not an e-mail address) and password to access the web portal.
What is the general process to initiate a file transfer between two collections using the Globus web portal?

To initiate a file transfer in the Globus web portal, first navigate to the File Manager page. Select the second 'Panels' button on the top right to view two collections simultaneously. Next, search for and select the first collection by typing its name (e.g., 'alliancecan#rorqual'), authenticating if prompted. Repeat this process to select the second collection. Once both collections are active, navigate through the directories, highlight the files or directories you wish to transfer, and then click on one of the large blue buttons with white arrowheads to start the transfer.
What information is required to access Arbutus object storage using the Globus portal after generating credentials?

To access Arbutus object storage through the Globus portal, you need to enter the AWS IAM Access Key ID and the AWS IAM Secret Key. These keys are generated using the `openstack ec2 credentials create` command.
After selecting 'Arbutus S3 buckets' in the Globus File Manager, what are the subsequent steps to provide consent and enter credentials for object storage access?

After selecting 'Arbutus S3 buckets', you must click 'Continue' to provide consent for data access, then click 'Allow', and then 'Continue' again. Following this, you will enter the generated AWS IAM Access Key ID into its respective field and the AWS IAM Secret Key into its field, then click 'Continue' to complete the setup.
How can I obtain more information or support regarding the Digital Research Alliance of Canada's Globus service?
To get more information or support for the Alliance's Globus service, you should send an email to globus@tech.alliancecan.ca.
What details should be included in an email when contacting the Digital Research Alliance of Canada for Globus support?

When contacting the Alliance for Globus support, you must provide your name, Compute Canada Role Identifier (CCRI), institution, and a clear description of your inquiry or issue, ensuring to indicate the specific sites you are transferring to and from.
What is Globus Connect Personal, and how do users install it on their personal computers?

Globus Connect Personal is a desktop client for Windows, MacOS X, or Linux, designed to make transferring files to and from a personal computer easy. To install it, users need to log into the Alliance Globus portal, navigate to the 'Collections' icon from the 'File Manager' screen, click 'Get Globus Connect Personal', download the appropriate link for their operating system, and then install the software. Once installed, the endpoint name will be '[your username]#[name you give setup]'. The program must be running for transfers to occur.
What advanced options are available when initiating a file transfer through Globus?

When initiating a file transfer, Globus provides several 'Transfer & Sync Options'. Users can direct Globus to sync only new or changed files, delete files on destinations that do not exist in the source, preserve source file modification times, verify file integrity after transfer (which is on by default), and encrypt the transfer. It's important to note that enabling encryption significantly reduces transfer performance and should only be used for sensitive data.
On Alliance general-purpose clusters, which directories are typically enabled for Globus sharing, and what is the process to enable sharing for `/project` directories?

On Alliance general-purpose clusters, Globus sharing is enabled for the `/home` directory (except on the Rorqual cluster). It is not enabled for `/scratch` (except on Narval). To enable sharing on a `/project` directory, the Principal Investigator (PI) needs to contact `globus@tech.alliancecan.ca` with confirmation, the cluster name, the specific path to enable, and whether the sharing will be read-only or read and write. We suggest using a clear path like `/project/my-project-id/Sharing`.
How do you initiate a file transfer in the Globus File Manager?

After selecting the desired collections and highlighting the files or directories you want to transfer by single-clicking or control-clicking multiple items, click on one of the large blue buttons with white arrowheads to initiate the transfer.
How can a user select multiple files or directories for a transfer in Globus?
To highlight multiple files or directories for transfer in Globus, a user should single-click on the first item and then control-click on any additional items they wish to include.
How can you monitor the status of an ongoing or completed file transfer in Globus?
You can monitor in-progress transfers and view details of completed transfers by clicking on the 'Activity' button located on the left side of the Globus portal.
What are the general guidelines for directory sharing on Alliance clusters using Globus?

Globus sharing is not enabled on the Trillium system. For general-purpose clusters, sharing is enabled for `/home` directories (with the exception of Rorqual), not enabled for `/scratch` directories (with the exception of Narval), and available on demand for `/project` directories.
On Alliance general-purpose clusters, which directories support Globus sharing by default?

On Alliance general-purpose clusters, Globus sharing is enabled by default for the `/home` directory, except on Rorqual. Globus sharing is not enabled by default for `/scratch` directories, except on Narval. Sharing on `/project` directories is available on demand.
On Alliance general-purpose clusters, which directories are typically enabled for Globus sharing, and what is the process to enable sharing for a `/project` directory?

On general-purpose clusters, Globus sharing is enabled for the `/home` directory, except on the Rorqual cluster. Sharing on `/project` directories is disabled by default. To enable it, the Project Investigator (PI) must email `globus@tech.alliancecan.ca` providing confirmation, the cluster name, the specific path to enable, and specifying whether read-only or read-and-write access is needed.
What are the initial steps to configure a new shared collection on Globus using the Alliance Globus portal?

First, log into the Alliance Globus portal. From the transfer window, enter or select the endpoint identifier of the cluster you wish to share from (e.g., `alliancecan#fir`) and activate it if prompted. Then, select the folder you want to share, click the "Share" button, click "Add a Guest Collection," and provide a name for your new share.
What crucial steps are involved in preparing data for a Globus shared collection and then managing access permissions?

For data preparation, ensure the data is moved or copied directly to the chosen sharing path, as creating a symbolic link to the data will not allow access. To manage access, once the shared collection is created, click "Add Permissions -- Share With." You can then specify a relative path within the share, and add people by email (recommended) or username, or add entire groups. Be sure to check the "write" box if write permissions are required.
How do I add users and groups to a shared Globus collection, and what options are available for managing their access permissions?

To add users or groups to a shared collection, go to the access list and click "Add Permissions -- Share With." You can add individual users by providing an email address (recommended if the Globus username is unknown or for users without an existing account) or by searching for their Globus username. To share with multiple people, select "Group" and search by group name or UUID. To enable write permissions, select the 'write' checkbox in the form before clicking "Add Permission," or toggle the checkbox next to the user's name in the access list. Read access cannot be removed. To remove users or groups from the shared collection, click the 'x' at the end of their entry in the access list.
What are the important security best practices and considerations that should be kept in mind when sharing files using Globus?

When sharing files with Globus, it's crucial to consider several security aspects. Always ensure you have explicit permission from the data's owner before sharing the files. Double-check that you are sharing with only the intended recipients; using their email address is the recommended method for verification, as Globus usernames are not linked to Alliance usernames. If sharing with a group you do not control, ensure you trust the group's owner, as they may add unauthorized members. When granting write access, always have backups of important files that are not on the shared endpoint, as users with write access can delete or overwrite files. It is also highly recommended to restrict sharing to a specific subdirectory rather than your top-level home directory to minimize risk.
How can a Globus group be created and managed to facilitate sharing with multiple users efficiently?

Globus groups provide an easy way to manage permissions for sharing with multiple users simultaneously. To create a group, click the "Groups" button on the left sidebar, then click "Create New Group." In the window that appears, enter a group name, a description, and select whether the group is visible only to its members (private) or to all Globus users, then click "Create Group." Once the group is created, you can invite users by selecting "Invite users" and entering their email address (preferred) or searching for their username. After selecting users, click "Add" to send them an email invitation. To modify a user's membership, click on their entry in the group to change their role (Admin, Manager, or Member) or status, and then click "Save Changes" to commit the modifications.
What methods are available for sharing a Globus collection with specific individuals or groups?
When configuring permissions for a Globus shared collection, you are prompted to share with people via email, username, or by adding them to a group.
Why would someone choose to share a Globus collection with a user via their email address?

Sharing by email is a good choice if you do not know a person's username on Globus. It also allows you to share with individuals who do not currently have a Globus account; however, they will need to create one to be able to access your share.
How do you specify a subdirectory to be shared within a larger Globus collection?
To share only a subdirectory, you can specify its path (e.g., `/Subdir-01/`) in the Path field, which is relative to the shared collection, or you can use the Browse button to visually select it.
How can users be invited to a Globus group?

Users can be invited to a Globus group by either entering an email address (which is preferred) or searching for their username. Once users have been selected, click the "Add" button to send them an email invitation. They will become visible in the group once they have accepted the invitation.
What are the different membership roles available in a Globus group, and how are they modified?

In a Globus group, you can assign users roles such as Admin (providing full access), Manager (who can change other user roles), or Member (who has no management functions). To modify a user's role or status, click on their name, make the necessary changes, and then click the "Save Changes" button to commit them.
How do I install the Globus Command Line Interface (CLI) on an Alliance cluster?

To install the Globus CLI on an Alliance cluster, first create a Python virtual environment using `virtualenv $HOME/.globus-cli-virtualenv`, then activate it with `source $HOME/.globus-cli-virtualenv/bin/activate`. Next, install the Globus CLI into this environment using `pip install globus-cli`, and finally, deactivate the virtual environment with `deactivate`. To use the CLI without reactivating the environment each time, you can add it to your PATH by adding `export PATH=$PATH:$HOME/.globus-cli-virtualenv/bin` to your `$HOME/.bashrc` file.
Why are there no default Globus endpoints for cloud virtual machines (VMs) like Arbutus, Fir, or Nibi, and what are the alternative solutions?

Cloud virtual machines (VMs) such as Arbutus, Fir, and Nibi do not have default Globus endpoints because they lack a singular storage system for each VM that would allow for a universal endpoint. If a Globus endpoint is required on a VM and other transfer methods are not suitable, the two available options are to install either Globus Connect Personal or Globus Connect Server.
What is the procedure for connecting to and accessing Legacy Arbutus Object Storage using Globus?

To access Legacy Arbutus Object Storage via Globus, you must have a cloud project with object storage allocated. First, generate your storage access ID and secret key using the OpenStack command line client by importing your credentials (`source <project name>-openrc.sh`) and then running `openstack ec2 credentials create`. After generating these keys, log into the Globus portal, navigate to the File Manager, and select 'Arbutus S3 buckets'. You will then be prompted to provide consent and enter your generated AWS IAM Access Key ID and Secret Key to complete the setup.
What is Globus and what is its primary purpose for researchers in Canada?

Globus is a service specifically designed for researchers to enable fast, reliable, and secure transfer of files between various computing resources, including Alliance clusters, other supercomputing facilities, and personal devices.
How does Globus improve file transfer performance compared to traditional methods like rsync or scp?

Globus improves transfer performance by automatically tuning transfer settings, restarting interrupted transfers, and checking file integrity, while shielding the end-user from complex underlying protocols like GridFTP.
How do users log into the Digital Research Alliance of Canada's Globus portal?

What is required on a personal computer to transfer files to or from an Alliance cluster using Globus?

What are some key options available to users during a Globus file transfer?

When should file encryption be considered for a Globus transfer, and what is its impact on performance?

Which directories on general-purpose Alliance clusters have Globus sharing enabled by default?

What is the process for a Project Investigator (PI) to enable Globus sharing on a `/project` directory on an Alliance cluster?

What is the primary purpose of Globus groups, and how are they created?

How can users install the Globus Command Line Interface (CLI) on an Alliance cluster?

Why don't cloud Virtual Machines (VMs) like Arbutus or Fir have default Globus endpoints provided by the Alliance?

What are the two main options for installing a Globus endpoint directly on a Virtual Machine if needed?

What information should be included when contacting the Alliance for support regarding Globus services?

What is a crucial security recommendation for users when sharing files using Globus?

It is highly recommended to restrict sharing to a subdirectory rather than a top-level home directory, verify the identity of the person you add to the access list, and ensure you have permission to share the files.

What are the primary methods for installing academic software on Alliance systems, and when might a user opt for one over the other?

Users can request Alliance support staff to install academic software by providing a URL, making it accessible to all via a `module load` command once license and technical requirements are met. Alternatively, users are permitted to install software in their own home or project space, which is often chosen if they plan to modify the code or need to evaluate it quickly.

When installing software on Alliance systems using the `configure; make; make install` pattern, what is the common solution if `make install` fails due to permissions or attempts to write to restricted system directories?

If `make install` fails because it tries to write to shared system areas like `/usr/local` or if `sudo make install` is attempted (which requires root privileges), the standard solution is to provide a `--prefix` flag during the `./configure` step. This directs the installation to a user-specified directory, such as `/my/project/directory/some-package`, instead of a restricted system location.
How does one effectively use a software library on an Alliance system, including the steps for loading it and correctly referencing its location during compilation and linking?

To effectively use a software library on an Alliance system, first load the corresponding module using `module load library_name/x.y.z`. This automatically sets environment variables like `CPATH` and `LIBRARY_PATH`, which compilers use to find header files and libraries, often eliminating the need for explicit `-I` and `-L` options. For cases requiring explicit path specification, particularly with `cmake`, it is recommended to use EasyBuild `EBROOT...` environment variables (e.g., `-DGSL_DIR=$EBROOTGSL`) for robustness. Remember to load the library module both when building and running the software.
If users install pre-compiled binaries on Alliance clusters and encounter errors related to `GLIBC` versions, what is the recommended solution?

If pre-compiled binaries fail due to `GLIBC` version errors (e.g., `/lib64/libc.so.6: version 'GLIBC_2.18' not found`), users should utilize the `setrpaths.sh` script. This script patches the binaries to ensure they use the correct interpreter and search for dynamically linked libraries in the appropriate folders, using the syntax `setrpaths.sh --path path [--add_origin]`.
How is the centralized software stack on the new Alliance clusters structured and accessed by users?

The centralized software stack on new Alliance clusters is distributed through the CVMFS file system, primarily located under `/cvmfs/soft.computecanada.ca`, ensuring it's identical across all new clusters. The core of this stack is provided by the `gentoo/2023` module, which is loaded by default, and its path is referred to by the `$EBROOTGENTOO` environment variable. Similarly, other modules for specific libraries (e.g., `hdf5`) provide `EBROOT...` environment variables (e.g., `$EBROOTHDF5`) to specify their installation locations, including header and library files.
When working with binaries from the Alliance software stack, why is it generally not recommended to set the `$LD_LIBRARY_PATH` environment variable?

It is generally not recommended to set the `$LD_LIBRARY_PATH` environment variable because binaries under `/cvmfs/soft.computecanada.ca` are designed to use a `RUNPATH`. This `RUNPATH` embeds the directories for runtime libraries directly within the binary, making `$LD_LIBRARY_PATH` unnecessary. In fact, setting `$LD_LIBRARY_PATH` overrides this `RUNPATH` and can prevent many binaries from functioning correctly, especially if set to system library locations like `/usr/lib64` or `$EBROOTGENTOO/lib64`.
On Alliance systems, what is the naming convention for environment variables used to specify library locations, particularly when working with `cmake`, and what is their purpose?

Environment variables used to specify library locations adhere to the pattern `EBROOT` followed by the capitalized name of the package, for example, `EBROOTGSL` for the GSL library or `EBROOTGCC` for GCC. Their purpose is to allow explicit specification of a library's location, such as in a `cmake` option like `-DGSL_DIR=$EBROOTGSL`, which helps reduce the risk of linking a mismatched library.
Where can users find detailed information regarding BLAS/LAPACK and MKL on Alliance systems?
Users should refer to the dedicated page on BLAS and LAPACK for comprehensive information concerning these libraries.
What is the purpose of RUNPATH for binaries located under `/cvmfs/soft.computecanada.ca` on Alliance clusters?
All binaries under `/cvmfs/soft.computecanada.ca` use what is called a RUNPATH, which means that the directories for the runtime libraries that these binaries depend on are put inside the binary.
Why is it generally recommended not to set the `$LD_LIBRARY_PATH` environment variable for binaries on Alliance clusters?

It is generally not necessary to use `$LD_LIBRARY_PATH` because the binaries' runtime library directories are already embedded via RUNPATH. In fact, `$LD_LIBRARY_PATH` overrides this runpath, and setting it, particularly to locations such as `/usr/lib64` or `$EBROOTGENTOO/lib64`, can cause many binaries to no longer work.
When might an Alliance system user need to use the `module --force purge` command?

The `module --force purge` command can be used to remove the CVMFS environment, resulting in a bare-bones AlmaLinux-9 installation without modules. This is helpful for special situations such as compiling GCC yourself or using custom toolchains like the MESA SDK. It is only necessary during compilation, as modules can be reloaded for running the software.
Under what circumstances should an Alliance system user compile software on a compute node rather than a login node?

In most situations, compilation can occur on the login nodes. However, if the code needs to be built on a node with specific hardware, such as a GPU or a Skylake CPU, then you should start an interactive job on a host with the required hardware and compile from there.
How can users request the installation of academic software that is freely available on the internet for use on Alliance clusters?
Users can email Alliance support staff, provide them with a URL, and ask them to install the package so that it can be accessed via a `module load` command.
What are two reasons why a user might choose to install software in their own home space or project space on an Alliance cluster?
A user might choose to install software themselves if they plan to make their own modifications to the code or if they wish to evaluate it quickly.
If `make install` fails because a package expects to write to a shared area like `/usr/local` on an Alliance cluster, what is the usual solution?
The usual solution is to supply a `--prefix` flag at the `configure` step to direct the installation to a directory of the user's choice.
Whom should users contact if they encounter other errors during software installation on Alliance clusters?
Users should contact Alliance support at support@computecanada.ca if other errors arise.
What is the simplest way to make use of a library on an Alliance system?
The simplest way is to first load the corresponding module using `module load library_name/x.y.z`.
Which environment variables are set when a library module is loaded on an Alliance system, and what do they point to?
Loading a library module sets `CPATH` and `LIBRARY_PATH` environment variables, pointing to the location of the library itself and its header files.
When explicitly specifying the location of a library for tools like `cmake` on an Alliance system, what is the preferred and most robust method?
The preferred method is to use an EasyBuild environment variable, such as `EBROOTGSL`, which adheres to the pattern `EBROOT` followed by the capitalized package name.
Can users install software on Alliance clusters using instructions that involve `apt-get` or `yum` commands?
It is unlikely that users will be able to install software using `apt-get` or `yum` instructions; they should look for instructions to build from source or contact support.
How can users install Python, R, or Perl packages that are not already available on Alliance systems?
Users can use the language's package manager to install the desired extension in their home directory, following the detailed guidance on each language's page.
What common error can occur when installing pre-compiled binaries in a user's home directory on Alliance clusters, and what script helps resolve it?
A common error is `/lib64/libc.so.6: version 'GLIBC_2.18' not found`, which can often be patched using the `setrpaths.sh` script.
Where is almost all software used on the new Alliance clusters centrally distributed from?
Almost all software is centrally distributed under `/cvmfs/soft.computecanada.ca` using the CVMFS file system.
What is the core module that provides the standard software stack on Alliance clusters, and which environment variable refers to its path?
The `gentoo/2023` module provides the core software stack, and its path is referred to by the `$EBROOTGENTOO` environment variable.
What is the recommendation regarding the `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` environment variable when working with the Alliance software stack?

It is generally not necessary to use `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, and users should not set it to locations like `/usr/lib64` or `$EBROOTGENTOO/lib64`, as it overrides the runpath and can cause many binaries to stop working.
In what specific situations might a user need to use the `module --force purge` command on Alliance clusters?
Users might need to use `module --force purge` for special situations like compiling GCC themselves or using custom toolchains such as the MESA SDK.
When should code be compiled on a compute node rather than a login node on Alliance clusters?
Code should be compiled on a compute node if it needs to be built on a node with a GPU or a Skylake CPU, by starting an interactive job on a host with the required hardware.
What protocol is primarily used to connect to compute servers, and what type of user interface should individuals expect to work with upon connection?
Connections to the compute servers use the SSH protocol, and users should expect to work in a text-mode console environment rather than a graphical user interface (GUI).
How can users obtain help or documentation for UNIX commands and specific executables once they are connected to the compute servers?

Users can access documentation for UNIX commands by using the `man command` in a terminal. For help specific to an executable, they can generally invoke it by using the command-line argument `-h`, `--help`, or in some cases, `-help` (e.g., `ls --help`). Users must press `q` to exit the `man` program.
What are the fundamental UNIX commands for listing directory contents, navigating the filesystem, and performing basic file and directory creation or deletion tasks?

To list directory contents, use `ls`. To navigate the filesystem, use `cd` (e.g., `cd my_directory` to enter a directory, `cd ..` to go to the parent directory, or `cd` to return to your home directory). To create a directory, use `mkdir directory_name`. To remove an empty directory, use `rmdir directory_name`. To remove files, use `rm file_name`, and to recursively remove a directory and its contents, use `rm -r directory_name`.
In a UNIX-like system, what does the 10-character string at the beginning of each line, displayed by the `ls -la` command, indicate about file permissions and file types?

The first character of the 10-character string indicates the file type: `-` for a normal file, `d` for a directory, and `l` for a symbolic link. The remaining nine characters, read from left to right, show the read (`r`), write (`w`), and execute (`x`) permissions for three classes of users: the owner, the group, and all other users, respectively.
How does one modify file and directory permissions in a UNIX-like environment using the `chmod` command, and what are some practical examples of its use?

The `chmod` command is used to change file permissions by specifying which permissions to add or remove for specific user types. You specify the user types (u for owner, g for group, o for others, a for all), followed by a `+` to add permissions or `-` to remove them, and then the permissions to modify (r for read, w for write, x for execute). For example, `chmod go-rwx secret.txt` prevents group members and all others from reading or modifying `secret.txt`, while `chmod a+x script.sh` makes `script.sh` executable for everyone.
How can the `grep` command be utilized to search for a specific text pattern within one or multiple files on a UNIX-like system?

The `grep` command allows you to search for a given expression within files. To search for 'tata' in a single file named `file1`, you would use `grep 'tata' file1`. To search for 'tata' in multiple files, for instance, all files starting with 'fil', you can use `grep 'tata' fil*`. In Linux, the `*` wildcard matches zero or more characters, allowing for searches across multiple files.
What are the three types of permissions supported by UNIX systems, and what do they allow for files and directories?

UNIX systems support three types of permissions: read (`r`), write (`w`), and execute (`x`). For files, `r` allows reading, `w` allows modification, and `x` allows running the file. For directories, `r` allows listing contents, `w` allows adding or removing files, and `x` allows changing into the directory.
To which three classes of users do file permissions apply on UNIX systems?
File permissions on UNIX systems apply to three distinct classes of users: the owner (`u`), the group (`g`), and all others or 'the world' (`o`).
What command is used to display the permissions associated with files and subdirectories in the current directory on a UNIX system?
To view the permissions associated with files and subdirectories in the current directory on a UNIX system, you can use the command `ls -la`.
What is the primary function of the `grep` command in a UNIX environment?
The `grep` command is primarily used to search for a given expression within one or multiple files. For example, to search for the string 'tata' in 'file1', you would use `grep 'tata' file1`.
How do wildcards function when using the `grep` command in Linux?

In Linux, when using `grep` or similar commands, the `*` wildcard matches zero or more characters, and the `?` wildcard matches exactly one character. This enables searching across multiple files with patterns, like `grep 'tata' fil*` to search in files starting with 'fil'.
How can one use the `grep` command to search for a variable pattern, such as 'number 10' or 'number 11', within files?

To search for a variable text pattern, such as 'number' followed by any number between 10 and 29, you can use regular expressions with `grep`. An example command for this would be `grep 'number [1-2][0-9]' file`.
How can one use the `grep` command to search for a text pattern that includes numbers within a specific range, such as 'number 10' through 'number 29', in a file?
To search for patterns like 'number 10', 'number 11', up to 'number 29' in a file, you can use the `grep` command with a regular expression like this: `grep 'number [1-2][0-9]' file`.
What type of expression is required for the search text when using the `grep` command?
A regular expression must be used for the search text when utilizing the `grep` command.
Where can users find additional resources to learn about regular expressions for use with commands like `grep`?
Users can refer to guides on regular expressions, such as the one found at http://www.cyberciti.biz/faq/grep-regular-expressions/, to learn more.
What is the primary purpose of this article for Windows and Mac users who are new to UNIX environments?
This article aims to provide the necessary basics for Windows and Mac users with little to no UNIX experience to access and quickly use compute servers.
How do users connect to the compute servers described in this guide, and what type of interface is typically used?
Connections to the servers use the SSH protocol in text mode, meaning users will utilize a console rather than a graphical interface.
Is there a recommended self-paced course available for learning about the shell environment?
Yes, SHARCNET offers a self-paced course on this topic called 'Introduction to the Shell'.
How can a user access reference manuals for UNIX commands directly from a terminal?
To access reference manuals, users can type `man command` in a terminal, and press `q` to exit the `man` program.
What common command-line arguments are used to obtain help on how to use a specific executable in UNIX?
Generally, the command-line arguments `-h`, `--help`, or in some cases `-help` are used to invoke help for an executable.
What is the initial directory a user is directed to after connecting to a Linux system, and what is the UNIX term for it?
Upon connection, a user is directed to their `$HOME` directory, which is the UNIX word for 'folder'.
What naming convention is strongly discouraged for files and directories on a Linux system?
Users are strongly discouraged from creating files or directories that contain names with spaces or special characters, including accents.
How do you list all files in a directory, including hidden files, and display detailed information such as permissions and ownership in a UNIX terminal?
To list all files, including hidden ones, with detailed information, you can use the command `ls -la`.
What command is used to navigate the filesystem in UNIX, including changing to a specific directory, moving to the parent directory, or returning to the home directory?
The `cd` command is used for navigation: `cd my_directory` to change to a directory, `cd ..` for the parent folder, and `cd` to return to the home directory.
How do you create a new directory and remove an empty directory in UNIX?
To create a directory, use `mkdir directory_name`. To remove an empty directory, use `rmdir directory_name`.
What command is used to delete files, and how can you recursively remove a non-empty directory in UNIX?
To remove files, use `rm file_name`. To recursively remove a directory, use `rm -r directory_name`.
How do you copy a file and recursively copy a directory using UNIX commands?
To copy a file, use `cp source_file destination_file`. To recursively copy a directory, use `cp -R source_directory destination_directory`.
What command is used to rename a file or a directory in UNIX?
The `mv` command (move) is used to rename a file or a directory; for example, `mv old_name new_name`.
What are the three types of permissions and the three classes of users associated with file permissions on UNIX systems?
The three types of permissions are read (`r`), write (`w`), and execute (`x`). The three classes of users are the owner (`u`), the group (`g`), and all others (`o`).
How do you use the `chmod` command to make a file named `script.sh` executable by all users in UNIX?
To make `script.sh` executable by everyone, you would use the command `chmod a+x script.sh`.
What UNIX command allows a user to view a file in read-only mode, search within it, and exit the viewer?
The `less` command views a file read-only. Users can search by typing `/what_to_search_for` and quit by pressing the `q` key.
What command is used to compare two files in UNIX, and how can they be displayed side-by-side?
The `diff` command compares two files, and the `-y` option can be used to show both files side-by-side, such as `diff -y file1 file2`.
How do you search for a given expression within one or multiple files using a wildcard with the `grep` command in UNIX?
To search for 'tata' in a single file, use `grep 'tata' file1`. To search in multiple files matching a pattern, use `grep 'tata' fil*`.
What is the recommended method for transferring a significant amount of data between different clusters?
For transferring data from one cluster to another, especially when the amount of data involved exceeds a few hundred megabytes, the use of Globus is recommended.
When moving to a new cluster, what common user-installed software and configuration files need to be re-established due to filesystem independence?

When moving to a new cluster, any Python virtual environments, R and Perl packages installed in your directories, or programs you've installed locally will need to be re-installed. Additionally, modifications made to your `$HOME/.bashrc` file on one cluster will need to be re-applied on the new cluster, as filesystems are independent between clusters.
What key differences should users consider when adapting job submission scripts for a new cluster, despite all clusters using Slurm?

Users should be aware that the number of CPU cores per node or per GPU, and the amount of memory per node or per core, can vary significantly between clusters, necessitating adaptation of job scripts. Also, special compute allocations (like RRG) or contributed allocations are tied to specific clusters and will not be available on others, although default allocations are accessible on every cluster.
How do users generally access Alliance clusters?
Users generally access Alliance clusters via SSH by changing the cluster name, using the same username and password across all clusters.
Are there any special steps required to access the Niagara cluster?
Yes, accessing Niagara does require a further specific step beyond standard SSH access.
Is data mirrored between the filesystems of different Alliance clusters?
No, there is no mirroring of data between Alliance clusters; the contents of home, scratch, and project spaces are independent on each cluster.
Can filesystem quota policies differ between Alliance clusters?
Yes, filesystem quota policies may differ between Alliance clusters, although generally not by much.
If a research group has a special storage allocation on one Alliance cluster, will it automatically be available on other clusters?

Are globally installed software modules generally the same across all general-purpose Alliance clusters?
Yes, the collection of globally installed modules is the same across all general-purpose Alliance clusters, distributed using CVMFS, assuming the same standard software environment.
What happens to user-installed Python virtual environments or R and Perl packages when moving to a new Alliance cluster?

If a user modifies their `$HOME/.bashrc` file on one Alliance cluster, will these changes automatically apply to another cluster?

What system do all Alliance clusters use for job submission?
All Alliance clusters use Slurm for job submission.
Will job submission scripts generally work across different Alliance clusters without modification?
Many parts of a job submission script will work across Alliance clusters, but users should check for differences in CPU cores, memory per node/core, and internet access.
What critical cluster-specific details should users verify regarding CPU cores and memory when submitting jobs on Alliance clusters?
Users should verify the number of CPU cores per node or per GPU and the amount of memory per node or per core, as these may vary significantly between Alliance clusters.
Do compute nodes on all Alliance clusters have direct Internet access?
No, on some Alliance clusters, compute nodes may not have direct Internet access, so users should check site-specific policies for the cluster they are using.
Are default research group compute allocations available on every Alliance cluster?

Are special compute allocations like RRG or contributed allocations universally available across all Alliance clusters?
No, special compute allocations like RRG or contributed allocations are tied to a particular Alliance cluster and will not be available on other clusters.
What is multifactor authentication (MFA) and what types of second factors can be used to access services?

Multifactor authentication (MFA) allows you to protect your account with more than a password. Once your account is configured, you will need to enter your username and password, and then perform a second action (the "second factor") to access most services. You can choose any of these factors for this second authentication step: approving a notification on a smart device through the Duo Mobile application, entering a code generated on demand, or pushing a button on a hardware key (YubiKey).
Why is it strongly recommended to configure multiple options for your second factor when enabling multifactor authentication?

When you enable multifactor authentication for your account, it is strongly recommended that you configure at least two options for your second factor. This ensures that if you lose one factor, you can still use your other one to access your account. How do you register a smartphone or tablet for multifactor authentication using the Duo Mobile application?

Under "Register a device," click "Duo Mobile," enter a name for your device, and click "Continue" to display a QR code. Finally, in the Duo Mobile application, tap "Set up account" or the "+" sign, tap "Use a QR code," and scan the QR code shown to you in CCDB, ensuring your mobile device is connected to the internet.

What are the initial steps for configuring a YubiKey for Yubico OTP if you do not already possess its Public ID, Private ID, and Secret Key?

How can Linux and macOS users configure their OpenSSH client to reduce the number of times they are prompted for their second factor during a session?

Linux and macOS users can reduce the frequency of second factor prompts by editing their `~/.ssh/config` file to include `ControlPath`, `ControlMaster auto`, and `ControlPersist 10m` for a specific host. This configuration allows a first SSH session to handle both authentication factors, while subsequent SSH connections on the same device can reuse this session for up to 10 minutes without requiring re-authentication.
How can a user configure FileZilla to minimise repeated multifactor authentication prompts during file transfers?

Afterwards, change the login method to 'Interactive' and attempt to connect again, which will then display the 2FA prompt.
How can I prevent MobaXterm from prompting for multifactor authentication twice during file transfers when connecting to a remote server?

When connecting to a remote server with MobaXterm, the file browser defaults to SFTP, which triggers a second multifactor authentication prompt. To avoid this, switch the "SSH-browser type" to "SCP (enhanced speed)" or "SCP (normal speed)" in the session's Advanced SSH settings.
How do I configure Cyberduck to avoid being prompted for multifactor authentication multiple times during file transfers?

By default, Cyberduck opens a new connection for each file transfer, leading to repeated multifactor authentication prompts. To change this, go to Cyberduck's preferences, select "Transfers," then "General." From the "Transfer Files" drop-down menu, choose "Use browser connection" and ensure the "Segmented downloads with multiple connections per file" box is unchecked.

What is Secure Shell (SSH) and what are its primary uses?

What information and preparations are necessary to successfully connect to a remote machine using an SSH client?

To successfully connect via SSH, you must know the machine name (e.g., `fir.alliancecan.ca`), your username (which is not your CCI, CCRI, or email), and your password or have an SSH key. Additionally, you need to be registered for multifactor authentication with your 2nd factor available and have requested access to the specific system you wish to connect to.
How can users enable graphical applications (X11) when connecting via SSH, and what software might be required on their computer?

To enable graphical applications via X11 when connecting with SSH, users need an X11 server installed on their computer. Linux typically has one by default. macOS users often need to install an external package like XQuartz, while Windows users can use MobaXterm (which includes an X11 server) or VcXsrv for PuTTY. On the command line, the `-Y` option is added to the SSH command, such as `ssh -Y username@machine_name`, to enable X11 communications.
What action should I take if I receive an SSH connection error message like "no matching cipher found" or "unable to negotiate a key exchange method"?

If you encounter error messages such as "no matching cipher found" or "unable to negotiate a key exchange method" when connecting via SSH, you will need to upgrade your operating system and/or SSH client. This ensures that your client supports strong ciphers, key exchange protocols, and MAC (message authentication code) algorithms.
Are there any specific older versions of SSH clients that are known to fail due to outdated security protocols?
Yes, two specific older versions of SSH clients are known to fail and require an upgrade: OpenSSH running on CentOS/RHEL 5 and PuTTY v0.64 and earlier on Windows.
Should I be concerned if my SSH client displays a warning stating "connection is not using a post-quantum key exchange algorithm"?

No, it is recommended to ignore this warning. It suggests that encrypted traffic recorded today could potentially be decoded by a hypothetical future computer, such as a quantum computer. This is considered a matter of key length rather than an urgent security issue, and no immediate system reconfiguration is planned. You can suppress this warning by configuring your SSH client with `WarnWeakCrypto no`.
What action should a user take if an SSH host key fingerprint does not match the published list when connecting to an Alliance cluster?

To simplify the login to an Alliance cluster like narval.alliancecan.ca, you can modify your local SSH configuration file, located at `~/.ssh/config`. You should add a `Host` block for 'narval', specifying your `User`, the `HostName narval.alliancecan.ca`, and the path to your `IdentityFile` (e.g., `~/.ssh/your_private_key`). Once configured, you can log in by simply typing `ssh narval`.

What are the common SSH command line forwarding options (`-X`, `-Y`, `-A`), how can they be set in the `~/.ssh/config` file, and what are the associated risks?

The common SSH command line forwarding options are `-X` for X11 forwarding, `-Y` for trusted X11 forwarding, and `-A` for agent forwarding. These can be set in your `~/.ssh/config` file by adding `ForwardX11 yes`, `ForwardX11Trusted yes`, and `ForwardAgent yes` respectively. However, enabling them by default is generally not recommended due to risks: X11 forwarding can slow down sessions, trusted X11 forwarding carries a risk of keyboard activity interception by a compromised server, and agent forwarding could allow a compromised server to use your agent to connect to other hosts. These features should only be used when necessary, and for agent forwarding, combining it with `ssh-askpass` is recommended.

What are SSH keys, and how do they utilize public-key cryptography for security?

SSH keys are based on public-key cryptography (PK), which involves a secret private key and a freely distributable public key. The public key can encrypt messages, but only the corresponding private key can decrypt them. On Alliance systems, this mechanism is used to verify the authenticity of the server, establish an encrypted session for secure traffic, and allow users to log in by verifying their identity.
What is the recommended method for installing an SSH public key on Alliance systems?

The recommended method for installing an SSH public key on Alliance systems is through the CCDB. You should navigate to https://ccdb.alliancecan.ca/ssh_authorized_keys, retrieve your SSH public key (which is a long single line of plain text), and then paste it into the CCDB form, providing a descriptive comment for the key.
Why is it important to use a strong passphrase when generating an SSH key pair?

It is crucial to provide a strong passphrase, ideally 15 characters or more, when generating an SSH key pair. This passphrase encrypts the private key, offering protection against unauthorized access if the private key file is ever stolen or compromised.
What is the typical appearance of an SSH public key?

An SSH public key usually appears as a single, very long line of text. It typically starts with 'ssh-rsa' or a similar identifier, followed by a long alphanumeric string, and often concludes with a comment such as 'user@machine'.
What is a critical warning regarding the use of example SSH public keys found in documentation?

It is essential to generate your own unique SSH public and private key pair for security purposes. You must not copy or use any example SSH public keys provided in documentation, as they are for illustrative purposes only.
What is the process for installing an SSH public key on Alliance systems using the CCDB form?

To install your SSH public key using the CCDB form, first navigate to the CCDB SSH Authorized Keys page at https://ccdb.alliancecan.ca/ssh_authorized_keys. Next, retrieve the plain text of your public key; for example, on a Unix-like system, use `cat .ssh/id_rsa.pub`, or for PuTTY/MobaXterm, use their respective key generator to obtain the 'Public key for pasting into OpenSSH authorized_keys'. Finally, paste this public key into the CCDB form, add a description, and click 'Add Key'.
What is the difference between installing an SSH public key using the CCDB method versus the `authorized_keys` file method on Alliance systems?

The CCDB method provides convenient access by making your public key available across all Alliance HPC systems, although it is not accessible by OpenStack cloud systems. In contrast, the `authorized_keys` file method allows you to install a key only on a specific target system by copying it into the `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` file in your home directory on that particular system.
How can I retrieve the plain text of my SSH public key for installation on Alliance systems?

To retrieve the plain text of your SSH public key: if you are using a Unix-like environment (such as Linux, Mac, Windows Subsystem for Linux, or Cygwin), you can use the command `cat .ssh/id_rsa.pub`. For Windows PuTTY or MobaXterm clients, open the PuTTY Key Generator or MobaXterm SSH Key Generator, load your private key via `File --> Load private key`, and then copy the content from the 'Public key for pasting into OpenSSH authorized_keys' section.
Why is it recommended to use an SSH key agent?

An SSH key agent is highly recommended because it offers both convenience and enhanced security. Instead of repeatedly entering your private key's passphrase for every connection, you only enter it once when starting the agent. The agent then supplies the private key for subsequent connections, avoiding the need to store the unencrypted private key on permanent storage, which makes it less vulnerable to theft or copying.
What are some common options for customizing the generation of an SSH key pair?

When generating an SSH key pair, you have several customization options. You can add a comment to the key for easier identification (e.g., `ssh-keygen -C 'Alliance systems'`), specify a custom file name for the key files (e.g., `ssh-keygen -f alliance-key`), choose a different key type than the default RSA (e.g., `ssh-keygen -t ed25519`), or strengthen certain key types like RSA by setting a longer key length (e.g., `ssh-keygen -t rsa-sha2-512 -b 4096`). These operations should always be performed on your own secure computer, not on a shared cluster.
How can SSH key constraints be utilized to limit a public key's capabilities or access points?

SSH key constraints offer a powerful way to limit what a public key can do, enhancing security. By default, an unconstrained public key can perform any action. However, you can add constraints to restrict it to specific commands (e.g., `restrict,command="squeue --me"` or for SFTP using `restrict,command="/usr/libexec/openssh/sftp-server"`). Additionally, you can limit the key to only be used when connecting from specific hosts (e.g., `restrict,from="d24-141-114-17.home.cgocable.net"`). These constraints minimize the risk if a key is ever compromised.
How do I install an SSH public key on a single, specific system rather than making it available on all HPC systems?

To install an SSH public key on a single, specific system, you can add your public key to the file `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` located in your home directory on that particular system. For example, to install a key only on the Fir system, you would copy your public key into the `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` file on Fir.
What command is recommended for conveniently installing an SSH public key on a specific system, such as Fir?

On systems using OpenSSH, the `ssh-copy-id` command is the most convenient way to install an SSH public key on a specific system. For instance, you could use the command `ssh-copy-id -i alliance-key username@fir.alliancecan.ca` to install a key on Fir.
What are the recommended best practices for managing SSH key pairs to ensure security and convenience?

To manage SSH key pairs effectively, it's recommended that keys be unique to each user and never shared or copied to remote systems. Private keys should always be encrypted with a strong passphrase of 15 or more characters and stored in a location accessible only to you, such as on external storage if using a shared computer. For convenience, use an `ssh-agent` to handle passphrases, and consider creating dedicated, named key pairs for different devices (e.g., `Laptop_RSA4096`). Additionally, apply constraints to public keys to limit their scope and enhance security.
What is the Key Revocation List (KRL) maintained by the Digital Research Alliance of Canada, and what steps should a user take if their SSH key is revoked?

The Key Revocation List (KRL) is a registry maintained by the Digital Research Alliance of Canada for SSH keys that are no longer trusted or are considered invalid, typically due to improper key management, theft, or a security breach. If your SSH key is revoked, it is crucial to immediately replace it with a new one to regain secure access to Alliance services and remove the compromised key from all services to prevent unauthorized access. If you believe the revocation was an error or have further questions, contact the Alliance's technical support for assistance.
What are SSH key constraints, and what are some ways they can limit a public key's scope?

SSH key constraints are provisions that limit what a public key is allowed to do. They can, for instance, restrict a key to only perform a specific command, such as `squeue --me`, or limit it to allow connections only from particular hosts, like `d24-141-114-17.home.cgocable.net`.
What is the default effect of the `restrict` keyword when used in an SSH public key constraint, and how can an interactive session be enabled with a source-constrained key?

By default, the `restrict` keyword in an SSH public key constraint turns off `pty allocation`, which can cause an interactive session to behave peculiarly. To allow pty allocation for a source-constrained interactive session, the `pty` option must be explicitly included in the constraint, for example: `restrict,from="d24-141-114-17.home.cgocable.net",pty`.

What are SSH keys and how do they function in public key cryptography?

Why does Alliance recommend using public key cryptography to connect to their systems?

What is SSH, and why are security changes being implemented for connecting to our clusters?

What specific SSH security improvements have been implemented on the clusters, and when were they applied?

What warning message might users encounter when first logging into a cluster after the SSH security changes, and how should they respond if using MobaXterm, PuTTY, or WinSCP?

Users will likely see a "WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED!" message because the cluster's host keys have been regenerated. If using MobaXterm, PuTTY, or WinSCP on Windows, this warning will appear in a pop-up window. Users should only click "Yes" to accept the new host key if its fingerprint matches one listed in the SSH host key fingerprints.
